description: Comprehensive literature review of 68 papers focusing on systematic reviews, scoping reviews, meta-analyses, and umbrella reviews.

papers.title: Work in Progress: Training STEM Graduate Students to Collaborate with Stakeholders to Address Socio- scientific Issues
papers.authors: Christina Silva, Jessica Karch
papers.abstract: Socio-scientific issues (SSIs) are complex, real -world problems that arise at the intersection of science and society . SSIs cannot be solved by one discipline alone and should engage stakeholders as part of the problem -solving process. As STEM graduate students are prepared to be scientists and address SSIs, it is imperative  that they are trained to collaborate with stakeholders. This scoping review examines how STEM graduate students are trained to collaborate with stakeholders to address SSIs.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Socio-scientific issues (SSIs) are complex, real -world problems that arise at the intersection of science and society . **Finding**: SSIs cannot be solved by one discipline alone and should engage stakeholders as part of the problem -solving process.

papers.title: Scoping Review of Knowledge-Creation Practices Supported by AI: Identification of Research Strands of Different Communities
papers.authors: Jun Oshima, Shotaro Naganuma
papers.abstract: This scoping review examines how AI supports collaborative learning as knowledge creation in varied educational contexts. Unlike previous reviews that discuss learning more broadly, this study focuses on the epistemological and methodological foundations of AI - supported collaboration. Using the PRISMA protocol, the authors analyzed 72 empirical studies published between 2020 and 2025, employing bibliographic coupling and ENA to identify research communities and their research strands. Six research communities emerged, each representing different strands —ranging from cognitive and sociocultural to design -based and systemic approaches. These communities reveal diverse perspectives on AI’s role. The findings indicate that much of the current research centers on individual learning and distal outcomes, while studies oriented toward knowledge creation, especially within CSCL and the LS, remain limited but are increasing. papers.title: Personalized Learning Analytics Dashboards in Higher Education: Fostering Self -Regulated Learning and Student Agency
papers.authors: Wei Yan, Hyejeong Lee, Donna Dancer, Wonjin Yu
papers.abstract: This rapid scoping review examines how personalized learning analytics dashboards (LADs) foster self-regulated learning (SRL) and student agency in higher education. Following the PRISMA guidelines, it synthesizes findings from twelve articles (2023-2025) grounded in SRL theory and student agency theory. Key f indings indicate: (1) personalized feedback in LADs promote metacognitive reflection  and goal setting , and (2) data visualization enhanc e metacognitive awareness . This review highlight s the benefits  while also acknowledg ing limitations in overlooking potential challenges.

papers.title: Bridging Hearts and Minds: A Scoping Review of Reciprocal Relationships Between Social -Emotional Skills and Socioscientific Issues-Based Learning
papers.authors: Yujing Chen, Shuang Li
papers.abstract: This scoping review maps the integration of Social and Emotional Learning (SEL) with Socioscientific Issues -Based Learning (SSI -L). Following a systematic search of three databases, 57 empirical studies from East Asia/Southeast Asia, Europe, and North America met inclusion criteria. All 57 studies measured SEL outcomes; 50 (88%) embedded deliberate SEL integration—26 (52%) explicit (targeting named SEL skills), 24 (48%) implicit (SEL emerged as byproduct). papers.title: Maximize Learning and Fun: How to Integrate In-game Learning Supports into Digital Learning Games
papers.authors: Seyedahmad Rahimi, Mahboobeh Mehrvarz, Samaneh Abdoli, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Bruce McLaren
papers.abstract: Digital learning games have significant potential to enhance student learning by combining engaging gameplay with academic content. While previous reviews have explored learning supports in games, none have specifically focused on in-game, content-related supports in pre -K-12 settings. This systematic review, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, addresses this gap by analyzing 58 studies to examine the design, delivery, and impact of these supports. Findings reveal diverse outcomes, ranging from cognitive to mixed cognitive and non- cognitive goals. Serious games were the most studied genre, followed by puzzle games. A strong link emerged between the integration level of supports —intrinsic inte gration—and positive learning outcomes. The delivery method (system -controlled, user-controlled, or mixed) also influenced effectiveness. Most studies (n = 30) used system-controlled delivery, followed by user-controlled (n = 21) and mixed ( n = 7). These f indings offer guidance for designing learning games that balance engagement and learning.

papers.title: Living the Impossible: Designing Life Happens, an AI-Supported Budget and Justice Simulation
papers.authors: Devan Walton, Haesol Bae, Jaesung Park, Yingru Zhao, Raymond Weiss, Susan Tashjian
papers.abstract: This paper reports on the design of Life Happens, a classroom simulation in which students manage household budgets across twelve months while encountering criminal justice– related financial obligations. Grounded in situated learning theory, the simulatio n develops quantitative reasoning and perspective -taking through authentic financial dilemmas. Initial prototypes relied on large language models, producing inconsistencies and outputs that reinforced harmful stereotypes. Informed by a trauma -aware framework, the team restructured the system into a three -layer architecture: a deterministic core, a curated event layer, and a bounded AI layer limited to brief affective text messages. This paper focuses on design principles that emerged from documented failures during deployments at a Hispanic -Serving community college and a Minority-Serving state university. Context, theoretical framing, and focus Faculty at a Hispanic -Serving community college and a Minority- Serving state university in the northeastern United States identified a need for experiential tools conveying how criminal justice involvement compounds household financial hardship (García et al., 2019). The interdisciplinary partnership brought together computer science pedagogy and criminal justice education to serve predominantly first-generation college students (Penuel et al., 2013). Institutional constraints, including limited class time,  variable devices, and diverse student demographics, shaped every design decision. We conceptualize learning through situated learning theory (Lave & Wenger, 1991), which holds that knowledge develops through participation in authentic practices. Life Happens situates students within household financial management under justice- system co nstraints, requiring arithmetic computation, budgeting, and quantitative trade-off reasoning as disciplinary competencies that emerge through meaningful decision- making (Gee, 2007). Simultaneously, students develop perspective -taking as they experience cascading consequences of systemic inequities (Belman & Flanagan, 2010). This paper focuses on the simulation’s design and AI integration, tracing how concrete prototype failures led to the principled architecture presented here. Simulation design and learning affordances Life Happens positions students as household decision- makers managing limited resources across twelve simulated months. Each cycle requires allocating funds across housing, food, transportation, healthcare, and phone services. Justice -related obligations such as probation fees, court -ordered payments, and commissary contributions impose additional mandatory costs (Harper et al., 2020). Five well -being indicators update transparently based on decisions, with visible arithmetic enabling students to anticipate  consequences (Chernikova et al., 2020). Quarterly reflection prompts emphasize metacognition and discussion (Squire, 2011). The system employs a three -layer architecture. The deterministic core maintains authored family compositions, income parameters, and cost data from regional economic sources, ensuring reproducibility and enabling instructor customization. The event layer introduces curated disruptions ranging from routine expenses to justice -related challenges, each with specified costs and well -being consequences. The affective AI layer generates brief text messages that translate numerical outcomes into personal narratives, adding emotional context while the core mechanics remain fully deterministic. AI integration: From unconstrained generation to bounded use Initial prototypes relied on large language models to generate family scenarios, event narratives, and financial parameters (Yan et al., 2024), producing three categories of documented failure. Generated family compositions contained logical inconsistencies that confused students and undermined budgeting strategies. AI- produced cost structures varied unpredictably across similar scenarios, making it difficult for students to develop reliable 2865 quantitative intuitions. Generated content also perpetuated harmful stereotypes about poverty and justice involvement, particularly affecting overrepresented communities (Lee et al., 2024). These failures demanded a framework for addressing stereotypes and trauma. Drawing on trauma - informed pedagogy (Carello & Butler, 2015), we committed to ensuring that scenarios allow full participation independent of personal history, that content represents systemic patterns while honoring individual complexity, and that instructors retain the ability to modify or disable any element they judge inappropriate. This framework guided the restructuring of AI’s role. Because educator control over sensitive elements is a pedagogical and ethical requirement, all factual elements became authored content maintained in versioned databases (Gibson, 2023). AI was retained solely for generating 280- character text messages formatted as communications from family members, employers, and service providers (see Figure 1). Prompts incorporate strict constraints on tone, relationship dynamics, and prohibited content, and each message passes validation filters before display. Pre - authored fallback messages activate when outputs fail validation or when instructors operate in non -AI mode (Aldrich, 2005). This bounded application introduces meaningful variation across simulation runs and supports empathy-building, all while the deterministic mechanics remain fully intact. Figure 1 The Phone Message Interface Displays AI-Generated Communications from Family Members and Service Providers. Design principles traced to practice The following principles emerged from the documented failures and institutional constraints above, and we trace each to its originating episode (Wang & Hannafin, 2005). Separation of deterministic and generative components arose because AI -generated cost s tructures produced inconsistencies that undermined learning objectives. Educator authorship of core mechanics resolved this while confining AI to a role where variability adds value and fairness is preserved. Trauma- aware content governance emerged from en counters with AI outputs that stereotyped justice-involved families. Instructor override, scenario review, and explicit content boundaries ensure that every version of the simulation actively interrogates these patterns. Privacy-conscious architecture responded to institutional review board concerns, and the minimal state approach transmits only current meter values and recent decisions (Pardo & Siemens, 2014). Redundancy and fallback systems became essential after pilot-session technical failures disrupted  engagement, so pre -authored alternatives for every AI feature ensure continuity. Reflection over scoring prioritizes metacognition because early testing revealed that competitive scoring distracted students from systemic insights (Li et al., 2024). Conclusion Life Happens demonstrates that AI can enhance educational simulations when carefully bounded by pedagogical goals and equity commitments. The most consequential design decisions centered on preserving educator authority over content touching systemic inequality, trauma, and identity. These transferable principles confirm that thoughtful AI integration remains accessible across diverse educational settings when guided by clear learning objectives. 2866 References Aldrich, C. papers.title: Are We There Yet? The Roles and Development of GenAI-Based Tools Supporting Collaborative Learning: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Maya Persico, Daeun Hong, Jerika Miller, Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver, Freydis Vogel
papers.abstract: Tools based on generative AI (genAI), i nteracting with learners in a human -like manner, such as conversational agents and ChatGPT, offer potential to develop adaptive support for collaborative learning. Following PRISMA guidelines, after screening results of searching three databases, our scoping review identified 239 relevant records reporting about genAI tools in CSCL including 138 empirical articles this paper focuses on. They  were analyzed in depth regarding genAI tool’s maturity level of implementation in collaborative learning, and the role genAI takes within . Results show  studies at different levels of maturity  in implementation of the genAI tool ranging from designing the tool or investigating its usability to studies focusing on human learning outcomes.  GenAI takes multiple roles  simultaneously, mostly providing epistemic and metacognitive scaffolding  to individuals or groups. Our results indicate substantial development in the growing number of empirical articles , while pointing out gaps in specific support type provision, especially for school learners.

papers.title: Encouraging Deeper Learning with GenAI: A Review of Pedagogical Constraints on GenAI and Their Impact in Higher Education
papers.authors: Shuang Geng, Di Fan, Juhong Eom, Gahyun Callie Sung
papers.abstract: This paper reviews how generative AI (GenAI) can be pedagogically constrained to promote deeper learning in higher education. A nalyzing 15 intervention studies comparing constrained GenAI use with free or no GenAI use, we found  three delivery methods (process, activity, and tool levels), operationalized through five mechanisms. Results show primarily positive impacts on performance, motivation, and higher order thinking, though nearly half rely on self-reports. The findings highlight the role of constraints in GenAI use, and invite further research explicitly linking constraints to outcomes. Setting There has been rapidly growing interest in finding ways to integrate generative AI (GenAI) into higher education classrooms. Meanwhile, there is little clarity on how  GenAI use can be moderated to better facilitate learning. Existing reviews have either explored strategies for GenAI use or evaluated the impact of having GenAI in learning as a whole, but have yet to distinguish the specific moderating or constraint mechanisms and their impact on learning (Batista et al., 2024; Almasri, 2024). To bridge this gap, our review goes beyond a binary view (use versus no use) with the following guiding questions: ● What student-facing constraint strategies for GenAI have been tested in higher education? ● What impact has been observed so far, on what types of learning outcomes? The current paper presents preliminary findings from an ongoing systematic review. We screened journal articles from 2022 (i.e., release of ChatGPT) to 2025, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) standard (Page et al., 2021). To be included, studies had to 1) investigate the impact of GenAI in higher education learning; 2) design and clearly describe a constrained or moderated GenAI use condition; 3) employ a (quasi -)experimental design, where academic or cognitive outcomes were compared between a treatment group of constrained use and a control group of free or no use of GenAI. Systematic search across Scopus, Web of Science, and ACM yielded 1,910 articles, among which 30 met the inclusion criteria. The present analysis reports findings based on half (15) of the final dataset, selected alphabetically by the first author's last name (see full list in References). All studies were collaboratively coded by the first author and at least one other author, with discrepancies resolved through discussion for this preliminary analysis. Results Context of Studies: Interventions showed a balanced representation between eight in STEM and seven in non- STEM disciplines. ChatGPT (or its API) was the primary tool in 14 of 15 cases. Constraint Delivery: Our coding process revealed three main GenAI delivery methods. First, process - level guidelines  (n=10) explicitized expectations for use, by delineating permissible forms of assistance (e.g., guiding usage with metacognitive support prompts; Xu et al., 2025). On the other hand, activity -level scaffolds (n=10) embedded constraints within the design of a learning activity, specifying the stages, timing, and conditions under which GenAI may be used (e.g., requiring independent initial attempt, followed by interaction and revision with GenAI; Jiang & Nakatani, 2025). Lastly, tool -level constraints  (n=11) configured tools for specific interaction modes, such as limiting outputs to hints (Lee et al., 2024). Constraint Mechanisms: Across interventions, five mechanisms emerged across the four stages of problem-solving: understanding, planning, execution, and revision (Polya, 1945). One mechanism constrained GenAI use to the early stage of draft or brainstorming, with the expectation that these ideas would be refined by the learner. The second and third mechanisms applied to GenAI use in the execution stage: solution first required students to create their own solution first, while no answers  primed GenAI to not give out whole answers and instead provide Socratic guidance. Lastly, in the revision stage, mechanisms included revision and verification , 734 as well as attributing and reflecting, where learners were either required to revise and verify AI output, or required to reflect on, and potentially report, how they used GenAI to perform the task. A single intervention often had multiple constraint delivery methods and/or mechanisms, reflecting layered approaches rather than reliance on a single lever. Overall, the pattern indicates a shift from merely restricting access to deliberately structuring how GenAI participates in learning, with mechanisms intuitively chosen to externalize cognition, require evidence-seeking, and align tool behavior with instructional intent. Impact on student learning Learning Outcome: On average, 4.4 outcomes were measured per study. The most common outcome category was Performance (e.g., exam grade, skill evaluation score), totaling 28 outcome measures across 13 (86.7%) studies. Other outcome categories included Motivation and Affect (e.g., intrinsic motivation and engagement), Higher Order Thinking (e.g., critical thinking), Quality of Student Artifact, and Metacognitive Skills. Direction of impact: Treatment groups showed largely positive impacts across student learning outcomes compared to control groups: 75% positive on Performance, 75% on Motivation & Affect, 80% on Higher Order Thinking, and the remaining two categories showed more mixed results.  Figure 1 shows the breakdown of directions of impact for each outcome category, combined with a second- level breakdown of measurement type. Measurement Type: Nearly half of the 66 outcomes (48.5%) relied on self-reports, which may have led to positive bias. Notably, outcomes related to Higher Order Thinking and Motivation & Affect, while showing predominantly positive results, relied exclusively on self-report (see Figure 1). Figure 1 Outcome Categories by Direction of Impact and Measurement Type Main bars: Count and percentage breakdown of direction of impact for each outcome category (X -axis). Side bars with hatching patterns: Percentage breakdown of measurement type for each main bar segment. Discussion Empirical findings point to a generally positive impact of constrained GenAI use on student performance, with more mixed results for metacognitive skills or quality of work. However, this direction may be influenced by several biases. In addition to common sources of bias such as the observer effect, limitations of self -reports, or the novelty effect, a unique issue was that in some cases, assessments were made on the GenAI-assisted task itself. Students may have shown higher performance because they had assistance, and not because they truly learned more. Another limitation was that most of these results were gained from comparing constrained GenAI use to no GenAI use. There was a surprising dearth of research (20%) that compared free versus constrained use  of GenAI (c.f. comparing no and constrained use of GenAI), which could help provide stronger evidence of pedagogical value by isolating the effects of constraint design rather than GenAI presence alone. Our ongoing analysis of the full dataset aims to delineate such emerging design insights with greater granularity. 735 References Studies included in the review are marked with an asterisk (*). papers.title: Generative AI for Creative Learning in K-12 Education: Insights from a Systematic Scoping Review
papers.authors: Seyedahmad Rahimi, Maryam Babaee, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Chris Dede
papers.abstract: The rapid rise of generative AI (GenAI) presents both opportunities and challenges for fostering creativity in K –12 education. This systematic scoping review synthesized 45 studies (2017– 2025) to examine how GenAI has been applied in creative learning. Fou r categories emerged: (1) creativity assessment, (2) human –AI co-creativity, (3) stakeholders’ perceptions, and (4) creativity enhancement. Findings show strong potential for GenAI to support idea generation, multimodal expression, and assessment of creati ve outputs, but highlight concerns about equity, authorship, and theoretical grounding. While most applications focus on text -based creativity, multimodal and culturally inclusive approaches remain underexplored. This review provides a foundation for responsible and equitable integration of GenAI into K –12 classrooms and captures a field in transition, where new forms of creative expression are emerging and educators are rethinking assessment, authorship, and pedagogy. This review provides a foundation for ethically grounded, developmentally appropriate and theory-driven GenAI designs that enhance, rather than automate, human creativity.

papers.title: Equitable Learning Analytics Dashboards: Roles and Mechanisms in Personalized Learning
papers.authors: Wei Yan, Hyejeong Lee, Donna Dancer, Wonjin Yu
papers.abstract: This poster presents a rapid scoping review of equitable learning analytics dashboards (LADs) for personalized learning. Grounded in the integration of self-regulated learning (SRL) theory and situated learning theory, the review synthesizes findings from ten  journal articles published between 2023 and 2025. The findings outline four roles and eight supporting mechanisms through which personalized LADs promote equity. This preliminary synthesis highlights inclusive design consideration to support equitable LAD development.

papers.title: Youth Climate Storytelling as Transformative Learning: A Scoping Review of Designs, Contexts, and Digital Practices
papers.authors: Asli Sezen-Barrie, Yuxi Huang
papers.abstract: This scoping review synthesizes 30 peer -reviewed studies (2014– 2024) on youth storytelling in climate change education, illuminating how storytelling  approaches foster transformative climate change learning. Findings reveal that storytelling functions as relational infrastructure while relating  climate complexity into lived experience, cultivating eco - emotional awareness and agency, and sustaining Indigenous and community knowledge. Across formal and informal settings, educators and youth partnered to co- create stories that merged data, emotion, and cultural meaning. Digital tools such as participatory video, multimedia, and augmented reality expanded access and impact but also raised questions of equity and authorship. By mapping designs, scaffolds, and digital practices, the review offers design implications for research -practice partnerships that nurture belonging, imagination, and civic participation through climate storytelling. The need and the goal As the climate crisis intensifies, educators face an urgent challenge: how to cultivate young people’s capacity to understand, feel, and act in relation to a rapidly changing world. Traditional climate change education often privileges scientific facts, da ta, and predictive models but rarely engages the emotional, cultural, and ethical dimensions necessary for sustained transformation (Walsh, 2022 ). Transformative climate change education reframes learning as an ethical, relational, and action -oriented process that centers justice, hope, and collective capacity (Leite, 2024; Sezen -Barrie et al., 2025). Within this reframing, storytelling emerges as a powerful pedagogical and epistemological approach that binds scientific sense-making with identity, emotion, culture, and community (Gottschall, 2012). Storytelling makes climate data meaningful, futures imaginable, and collective agency possible (Bentz & O’Brien, 2019; Bloomfield, 2024). It allows youth to relate abstract climate concepts into local experiences and shared narratives of resilience, repositioning them as authors of change rather than passive recipients of information. Yet, despite growing interest, the field lacks a compr ehensive synthesis of how storytelling is designed, scaffolded, and studied across learning contexts. Moreover, as digita l media and participatory technologies proliferate from personal storytelling platforms to augmented reality, the need for design frameworks that ensure equity, authenticity, and purpose becomes more pressing. This review addresses a central gap in the learning sciences: the absence of an integrated understanding of how storytelling, across diverse designs, pedagogical functions, and digital practices, shapes transformative climate learning. While storytelling is increasingly recognized as a catalyst for connection, agency, and inclusion, its implementation remains fragmented across specific areas of social science research. Drawing on 30 peer - reviewed studies (2014– 2024), this scoping review was guided by the following research questions:  (1) What research designs and learning contexts characterize studies on youth storytelling in climate change education? (2) How do storytelling function and are scaffolded to support climate change education? (3) In what ways do digital tools and frameworks support engaging in storytelling related to climate change? Conceptual framework: Storytelling in climate change education “We are the authors of our lives. We compose our self -narratives and we are composed by them” (Gottschall, 2012, p. 147). In The Storytelling Animal: How Stories Make Us Human, Gottschall (2012) argues that stories are not only how we communicate experiences but also how we construct meaning, identity, and belonging. Storytelling, the structuring and sharing of lived or imagined experiences through narrative form, is thus foundational to human cognition, culture, and communication (Gottschall, 2012). Within education, storytelling functions as both an epistemological and pedagogical approach : a way of knowing the world and of teaching it. In climate change education, it extends beyond communication to become a transformative learning practice , weaving scientific understanding with emotional relations, ethical inquiry, and socio-cultural meaning. Mainstream climate change education often privileges technocratic and positivist paradigms, emphasizing data, models, and prediction (Krasny & Schneider, 2021). While such approaches are essential for understanding biophysical mechanisms, they rarely foste r the emotional, ethical, or civic engagement necessary 1877 for meaningful transformation. Storytelling intervenes by humanizing climate knowledge  while translating complex systems into situated experiences and relationships. By embedding abstract concepts in personal or community narratives, it deepens comprehension and fosters empathy (Bloomfield , 2024). In this sense, stories “relocalize” climate learning, situating it within histories of place, culture, and justice rather than abstract global metrics. Storytelling aligns with transformative climate change education frameworks (Sezen-Barrie et al., 2025; Leite, 2024), which highlights attention to learning across epistemologies and improving emotional well -being. Climate stories , especially those from marginalized or Indigenous communities , which operates as counter- hegemonic discourses  that challenge dominant narratives of progress and environmental relationships  (Leite, 2024; Tuck, McKenzie, & McCoy, 2014). These narratives open epistemic space for lear ners to question assumptions about development, responsibility, and belonging in the Anthropocene. Through engagement with such stories, learners cultivate more pluralistic and justice -oriented understandings of socio- ecological systems. Indigenous storytelling traditions exemplify this transformative potential. In many Indigenous epistemologies, story is both method and ethic: a means of transmitting knowledge and sustaining reciprocal relationships among humans, nonhumans, and the land (Whyte, 2017). Integrating Indigenous storytelling into climate curricula enacts decolonial praxis, repositioning learners as participants in relational webs of care rather than as detached observers of climate data (Tuck et al., 2014). Empirical research reinforces the pedagogical value of storytelling. Pahl et al. (2019) found that climate messages conveyed through stories were significantly more effective at fostering emotional engagement and pro- environmental intentions than statistical presentations. Educational research further shows that storytelling supports identity work: when students create or analyze stories about climate change through oral narratives, filmmaking, or digital media, they articulate their roles, values, and hopes within broader ecological systems (Leite, 2024). In sum, storytelling is far more than a communication tool; it is a transformative framework for learning. It bridges the cognitive, affective, and ethical domains —helping learners think, feel, and act with relational awareness. By integrating storytelling into climate change education, educators can nurture imagination, agency, and care, cultivating learners who are not only informed about the planetary crisis but also empowered to participate in r eimagining its futures. Storytelling, in this sense, becomes both pedagogy and praxis —a way of composing more just and livable worlds.

papers.title: AI/ML Education in Motion: Embodied Machine Learning with Wearable Technology in Informal Contexts
papers.authors: Manav Sharma, Ji Shen
papers.abstract: Systematic reviews on the application of AI technologies in STEM Education recommend the use of age -appropriate AI/ML tools in primary and secondary school settings, in contexts that appeal to students’ interests. In this pilot we incorporate a new modality (body movement) and tool (BBC micro:bit) into an AI/ML unit for young learners to understand how they engage with machine learning concepts. Students articulated novel uses for ML tools, drew connections to other practices, demonstrated metacognitive awareness, and described their roles as designers. These findings highlight the value of scaffolded, collaborative, embodied learning designs in supporting emerging AI literacy.

papers.title: Conceptualizations and Mechanisms of Teachers’ Learning to Notice
papers.authors: Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem, Thorsten Scheiner, Heather
papers.abstract: This symposium brings  together a set of posters that focus on science and mathematics teachers’ learning to notice. Teacher noticing is a core construct of teaching, and refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making amidst the “blooming, buzzing confusion” of classr oom interactions. The goal of the session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” is conceptualized and unpack mechanisms that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Symposium overview: Goal, structure, and highlights Teacher noticing, a core construct of teaching (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023), broadly refers to teachers’ attention, interpretation, and decision-making of classroom interactions (Jacobs et al., 2010; Sherin et al., 2011). With the growing recognition of noticing as a core practice of teaching, there is an expanding line of research that seeks to understand how to support teachers’ learning to notice (Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021). Prior research shows that well -designed professional learning opportunities can foster teachers’ learning to notice students’ thinking and teaching in interaction with student learning (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa et al., 2018; Warshauer et al., 2023). As this knowledge has grown, it has prompted scholars to investigate what constitutes learning of noticing. In this symposium, we  pause and ask: How do we think about what constitutes learning to notice? While efforts to support teachers’ learning to notice is evolving, less is understood about the mechanisms of teacher learning to notice (Walkoe & Luna, 2020). Some research investigates how video tagging tools focus teachers’ attention on particular features for further analysis (e.g., Walkoe et al., 2020). Others have considered how different kinds of video clips are selected and situated in professional learning and how collaborative analysis of particular types of clips can shape teachers’ learning (e.g ., Sherin & Dyer, 2017). Recent  work has pointed to the role of discourse as a mechanism of teachers’ learning to notice (van Es et al., 2024). However, there is more to be understood about how teachers come to notice complexities of teaching and learning, and designs to better 2318 support that. Going beyond the descriptive account of noticing, in this symposium, our work collectively explores: What drives teachers’ learning to notice? All in all, the goal of our session is to examine different ways “learning to notice” has been conceptualized, and unpack the "mechanisms" that drive teachers’ learning to notice. Using multiple methods such as participatory  design research approach and typological analysis of artifacts of teaching , these studies document shifts in teachers’ learning to notice, factors that contribute to teachers’ learning of noticing, and the design choices in facilitating teachers’ learning this complex practice. T he studies identify mechanisms of teachers’ learning to notice such as coding schemes that serve as epistemic mechanisms and collective sensemaking of the complexity of teaching through analysis of classroom videos in professional learning contexts. While some papers zoom in on  noticing subprocesses that different video processes afford, others seek to understand teachers’ learning to notice when teachers worked on making links to socio-ecological issues relevant to their lives.  Together, these papers advance theory on teachers’ learning to notice, while also considering the situated and relational features of teacher learning. At the same time, they offer methodological tools and frameworks to advance research on learning to notice across math and science. This 90-minute structured poster session will consist of a brief introduction to the session by the session co-chairs (5 min), followed by the interactive discussion of 10 posters (60 min), 10-minutes of commentary from a discussant, Adam Lefstein from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, who brings expertise on teachers’ learning in professional development. We will conclude with 15-minutes of questions and discussion. The discussant will consider commonalities and differences across these studies, surfacing the considerations and tensions for supporting teachers’ learning to notice and mechanisms that drive learning of noticing among math and science teachers across the trajectory of teaching careers. Poster 1: Grounding prospective mathematics teacher noticing in socio- ecological issues: learning to notice in turbulent times Alf Coles, Sigal-Hava Rotem This study addresses the gap between current turbulent times and the seeming ‘objectivity’ of mathematics. We explore what constitutes prospective teachers (PTs) of mathematics learning to notice, during a time of war, the links they make to socio- ecological (Coles et al., 2024) issues of relevance to their lives,  and the role of the mathematics teacher educator. Following van Es and Sherin (2002), we conceptualize teacher noticing as attending to and interpreting students' mathematical thinking. Following Mason (2002), we emphasize attention to event details for in -depth interpretation. We focus on “critical events” - moments when teachers notice students' mathematical thinking has potential for deepening. We also bring a notion of “authenticity”, which relates to teachers’ task design choices, and the extent to which tasks include social or ecological issues of relevance to their lives and the extent to which the mathematics includes opportunities for generalization. The study was conducted during wartime, heightening turbulence and data significance. We employed a case study methodology, to research a year- long problem-solving course in a B.Ed. mathematics program. The course focused on a reform in mathematics educati on emphasizing "mathematics in everyday life" and incorporated two design-teach-reflect cycles where participants: 1) photographed and discussed socio- ecological concerns (photovoice method); 2) designed mathematical tasks; and 3) taught and reflected on critical events they identified. Among 23 participants, we focus on Nadin (Bedouin community member) as an illustrative case. Our analysis examines shifts in her articulation of event details, interpretations, the social- ecological issue's authenticity and the role of the teacher educator. The analysis revealed three key findings. First, Nadin was able to bring a highly relevant socio-ecological issue to her classroom, surfacing deeply held beliefs and engaging with students about their beliefs. Secondly, Nadin wrote in great detail and we observed subtle and shifting relationships between detail and interpretation in her accounts, which is of significance to how noticing might be supported. Thirdly, in examining the role of the teacher educator, we uncover the significance of the way space w as offered on the course for PTs to discuss and work on socio-ecological issues of relevance to their lives. Through examining the particulars of one case, our findings offer an example of how teacher preparation, during a time of war, can still support the noticing of prospective teachers, in connecting mathematics to relevant socio-ecological issues. We tentati vely point to a role for prospective teachers’ sharing stories from their lives, and to the power of engaging in design-teach-reflect cycles, in supporting their noticing. 2319 Poster 2: Learning to notice students’ strengths: Coding schemes as epistemic mechanisms in design-based teacher education Thorsten Scheiner This investigation addresses a critical challenge in teacher education: developing teachers’ capacity to recognize and build upon students’ strengths rather than defaulting to deficit -based orientations. While research demonstrates that strength -based noticing practices foster more equitable learning environments (Louie et al., 2021), significant gaps remain in understanding the mechanisms through which teachers develop these sophisticated ways of seeing. This study examines how structured coding schemes function as epistemic tools that bridge cognitive and socio- cultural dimensions of professional learning, offering insights into design -based approaches for transforming teacher noticing practices. The study advances an integrated framework synthesizing professional noticing theory, transformative learning mechanisms, and frame analysis. Professional noticing encompasses attending to critical aspects of student reasoning, interpreting student thinking, and deciding how to respond instructionally (Jacobs et al., 2010). Frame analysis illuminates how interpretive schemas shape what teachers notice and value in student work (Sherin & Russ, 2014). Transformative learning theory provides mechanisms for frame shifting through critical reflection and conscious reorientation of perspective (Mezirow, 2000). The framework positions coding schemes as mediating artifacts that operationalize frame orientations while scaffolding transformative professional development through the dynamic interplay of cognitive restructuring and socio-cultural meaning-making. This exploratory study used a participatory design research approach within an intensive professional learning context. Prospective teachers engaged in three iterative cycles of analysis using a structured coding scheme distinguishing deficit-based, strength-based, and uncommitted orientations across noticing practices. Each iteration incorporated fine -grained examination of transformative mechanisms through structured reflective prompts targeting frame awareness, conscious reframing, and progressive integr ation. Data collection utilized standardized noticing tasks, complemented by reflective journals documenting participants’ evolving interpretive frameworks. Analysis combined quantitative tracking of orientation patterns with qualitative mapping of transformative processes. Analysis revealed three primary mechanisms driving teachers’ learning to notice strengths. First, epistemic visibility emerged through the coding scheme’s dual function as analytical tool and pedagogical scaffold, rendering implicit interpretive frames explicit and actionable. Participants demonstrated systematic shifts from deficit- based toward strength- based noticing practices. Second, collaborative meaning -making facilitated frame shifting through structured protocols that created social spaces for negot iating alternative interpretations of student thinking. Third, reflective reframing supported progressive integration of strength-based orientations through systematic comparisons of deficit-based and asset-oriented perspectives. The iterative design revealed how these mechanisms operated synergistically, with cognitive restructuring mediated by socio-cultural practices of professional discourse and collective analysis. The findings illuminate coding schemes as powerful epistemic mechanisms that render interpretive frames both visible and actionable in teacher education. By functioning simultaneously as analytical tools and pedagogical scaffolds, structured coding schemes  support the cognitive work of frame identification while creating social spaces for collaborative meaning -making. This dual functionality bridges individual cognitive transformation and collective professional development, revealing how participatory desi gn research can systematically develop teachers’ capacity for strength- based noticing. The study contributes methodological insights for designing equity- oriented professional learning experiences that leverage the sophisticated interplay between cognitive and socio-cultural dimensions of transformative practice. Poster 3: From noticing to navigating: Pre-service teachers' expansive sensemaking in science instruction Heather Johnson, Tara Barnhart Teacher noticing—especially of student thinking—has become central in teacher education research (Weston & Amador, 2023). Noticing can be cultivated during teacher education (van Es, 2011), but connecting it to student - centered instruction requires space to reflect on the interplay between interpretations, decisions, and institutional contexts (Schwartz et al., 2021). In this study, we explore what pre -service teachers apply from their noticing of expansive sensemaking in videos of accomplished teachers to video analysis tasks in which PSTs design and enact student-centered science experiences. We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who 2320 share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We ground this study in previous work that theorizes that noticing is a learnable skill (van Es, 2011) and that learning to notice is a social activity that takes place when individuals who share a common interest collaboratively engage with tools and tasks intrinsic to their professional context (Barnhart, 2021). We conducted a typological analysis (Miles et al., 2014) of written coursework and fieldwork from PSTs enrolled in a secondary methods course prior to student teaching. Data included their planning documents, video analysis templates, and written reflections for four video tasks: one around an accomplished teacher’s classroom and three around their own teaching. Analysis of what teachers noticed in their own and others’ videos was guided by the Expansive Sensemaking framework (Bautista & Davis, 2024). By applying this framework, the study illuminates how PSTs bridge noticing of student thinking with enacting responsive science teaching. Accomplished teacher video When analyzing videos of accomplished teachers, PSTs attended to how classroom culture shaped student participation. They noticed who was given access to share ideas publicly, how ideas were taken up by the teacher and peers, and how norms and structure supported collaborative learning. PST Videos In their own lesson planning, PSTs designed inclusive tasks that positioned students as epistemic agents and included multimodal participation strategies. They also aimed to expand what "counts" as science and promote diverse ways of knowing. However, enac ting these plans surfaced asset -oriented, equity- oriented, and participation-oriented challenges. Though each PST intended to empower students, their enactments did not always lead to the anticipated engagement. These realizations revealed a gap between in tention and impact, especially in balancing student agency with institutional constraints such as pacing guides and test preparation. Equity-related challenges emerged as PSTs attempted to make lessons culturally relevant. Some PSTs reflected on how their examples did not resonate as expected. PSTs also identified challenges in fostering student-to-student interactions. They reflected on classroom dynamics, noting the need for psychological safety and clearer norms. Importantly, they attributed participation issues to instructional design, not student deficits—demonstrating asset - oriented thinking. Prior work on noticing student thinking has presumed that teachers will apply what they learn to notice in coursework to their own practice. These results support this hypothesis while also highlighting the challenges of responsive instruction and affirming the importance of reflection and collaboration in preparing teachers to sustain asset-based noticing through opportunities to analyze their own artifacts of practice and contribute to the research base for preparing teachers to teach responsively in diverse, authentic contexts. Poster 4: Noticing in college mathematics: Development of noticing discourse in a video-based professional development Patricia Fuentes Acevedo, Christina Kimmerling, Rossella Santagata, Alessandra Pantano, Roberto Pelayo College mathematics classrooms can be marginalizing spaces, particularly for women and students of color (Riegle-Crumb & King, 2010). Persistent inequalities motivate the call for more responsive and equity- oriented college teaching. Teacher noticing is at  the core of responsive teaching, with substantial research primarily conducted in K-12 settings (Santagata et al., 2021). Building on K-12 evidence, we developed and tested a video- based curriculum for instructors and graduate and undergraduate teaching a ssistants that fostered expansive noticing of students' mathematical thinking and participation (Santagata et al., 2025). Recent work has emerged suggesting that evidence of learning to notice includes uptaking a particular form of discourse (van Es et al. , 2024). We seek to unpack the relationship between participants' discourse during PD sessions and observed changes in the groups' noticing. We ask: What are the features of participants’ discourse around video- based noticing tasks? Except for a few characterizations of exemplary cases (e.g., Louie et al., 2021), little is known about how educators can learn to notice for equity. We adopt a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000) and draw on van Es et al.’s (2024) work on learning to notice by engaging in discourse-rich spaces where educators collectively make sense of instruction. Their model characterizes discourse practices that enable participants to learn how to attend to and interpret student thinking. We extend this to student participation. The authors define features of generative noticing for the different purposes that the discourse practices serve. 2321 Participants include three college instructors, five graduate and four undergraduate assistants. They engaged in whole and small group discussions around video clips during four PD sessions. For this study, we selected all segments where small groups discussed noticing prompts after watching a video clip (20 in total) and subsequent whole-group discussions. We portioned the transcribed data into conversational turns and idea units and created analytical memos. Finally, two of us deductively coded the data using van Es et al.'s (2024) features of noticing discourse (Table 1), allowing for emergent codes as well. Table 1 Features of Noticing Discourse Feature of a Noticing Discourse Definition of Feature Negotiating noteworthy phenomena A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending activity, defining what is and is not worthy of attention, and supports learning to decide what to call out and what to ignore. Problematizing and puzzling over objects of teaching and learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support interpreting and sense-making activity, which is adopting an inquiry stance toward objects of focus, such as offering conflicting viewpoints of what is observed or grappling over intent and meaning. Creating moments for further inquiry of objects of attention A collection of discursive practices that intend to support shaping interactions to gather more information for further attending and interpreting. Being accountable to evidence A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending and interpreting activity by supporting one’s claims with concrete observations, using artifacts of teaching and learning to advance an idea, and elaborating one’s ideas with more specific and precise explanations. Positioning students’ ideas and actions as resources in learning A collection of discursive practices that intend to support attending, interpreting, and shaping activity by requiring an openness to seeing what might appear as mundane, or correct/incorrect, as something important and meaningful that can be figured out and used toward understanding. Connecting to their experiences of teaching and learning (emergent A collection of discursive practices that intend to extend the discussion from what was observed in the video to their own past experiences when teaching and/or learning, or with potential future teaching scenarios. Participants discussed aspects related to student thinking and participation, primarily focusing on problematizing objects of teaching observed in the clips, and less frequently engaging in negotiation of noteworthy phenomena. An emergent and predominant feature of their noticing discourse was making connections to their own experiences, which included extending the observed episode to past or potential future teaching scenarios. Additionally, although there is little evidence of positioning students' ideas  as resources, participants maintained an asset-based perspective as required by the facilitators. The identified features in our data provide evidence that PD video prompts supported productive noticing discourse among participants and shed light on the processes through which their collective sensemaking contributed to their learning to notice. Our findings reflect the PD emphasis on noticing as multidimensional and are encouraging as they suggest tangible implications for participants' future instruction. This work contributes to the limited literature on how mechanisms for learning to notice take place at the college level. Poster 5: Attending, interpreting, and shaping: How varied ways of working with video connect with subprocesses of teacher noticing Jennifer Richards, Miriam Sherin, Sarah Larison 2322 Research has documented how video- based environments can provide rich opportunities for teachers’ learning, including learning to notice student thinking (e.g., Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; Santagata et al., 2021).  Further, advancements in video-related technology have expanded how teachers can engage with video — moving beyond watching and discussing videos to filming and editing their own clips. In this poster, we extend a prior exploration of how teachers noticed student thinking as they engaged in multiple video processes (Richards  & Sherin, 2025) by specifying ways in which these video processes map onto posited subprocesses of teacher noticing, contributing to understandings of potential drivers for noticing. The framework we animate specifies several interrelated subprocesses of teacher noticing — attending, interpreting, and shaping (van Es & Sherin, 2021). “Attending” refers to what teachers focus on in classrooms, acknowledging that humans cannot pay attention to everything. “Interpreting” refers to how teachers reason about classroom events. “Shaping” refers to what teachers do in order to support their noticing during or after instruction. While these subprocesses dynamically interact with and influence one another, we think they also reflect important opportunities for learning in their own right. Data come from three iterations of an online, video- based course for early elementary teachers in the United States on mathematical argumentation (Lomax et al., 2017). Twenty -nine in-service teachers participated in the course, in which they engaged in four sequential video processes  — recording video in their own classrooms, watching and reflecting on the video, editing clips to share in the course, and interacting with others around their clips. Data sources  included interviews and think- alouds with teachers about these video processes and video annotations on clips. Our prior analysis explored the affordances and constraints of each video process for teachers’ noticing of student thinking (Richards & Sherin, 2025). Here, we build on this prior analysis to characterize the noticing subprocesses that different video processes seemed to afford. When teachers recorded video in their classrooms, all three noticing subprocesses seemed to be in play as teachers iteratively focused on student ideas that required attention, sought to make sense of them in real time, and shaped interactions to test working interpretations and gather  more information. Watching and reflecting on the video tended to afford continued “interpreting” and “shaping,” as teachers primarily used the  video as a tool to make sense of and gain more evidence about student ideas that had intrigued them. Editing clips , in contrast, afforded “attending” with some further “interpreting” as teachers selectively identified moments of  student thinking to make visible to colleagues. Finally, when interacting with others around clips , all three subprocesses were again in play as teachers highlighted specific student ideas to consider, discussed varied interpretations, and at times reviewed the video to seek more information. These findings suggest potential implications for targeted video-based designs to facilitate specific noticing subprocesses (e.g., cultivating teachers’ attending by providing multiple opportunities to edit clips). Further research could deepen understandings of how engaging with varied sequences of video processes drives teachers’ learning to notice over time. Poster 6: Developing professional vision through negotiating understanding of videorecorded whole-class talks in mathematics Håvard Johnsrud Evang, Inga Staal Jenset Supporting teacher candidates’ development of ambitious and equitable mathematics teaching is a key challenge in teacher education (Louie, 2018) and requires that teachers adapt their instruction in response to students’ content-specific ideas and ways of participating in the talk (Jacobs & Empson, 2016). Prior research has studied this situation -specific competence through concepts such as ‘noticing of students strengths’  (Jilk, 2016) and ‘equitable noticing’ (Louie, 2018) demonstrating how video- anchored activities may support candidates developing this capacity (Jenset et al., 2024). Building on a recent socio- cultural turn in noticing research (Scheiner et al., 2026), the present study extends this work by investigating how teacher candidates’ professional vision develops as they engage in discussions of video-recorded mathematical classroom talk in Grade 8 settings. This study draws on Goodwin’s (1994) concept of professional vision, defined as the ability to construct relevant knowledge through socio-historically developed practices of highlighting and coding. This framework is used to examine how teacher candidates interpret students’ utterances and actions within recorded episodes of classroom discourse. Adopting a socio- cultural perspective, the study assumes that cultural frames —that is, culturally and historically shaped interpretive lenses regarding school mathe matics, mathematical teaching, and learning (Goffman, 1974; Scheiner, 2021) —function as mediational means that shape these practices. Consequently, the negotiation and adaptation of cultural frames to make sense of students’ mathematical contributions are understood as mechanisms that drive the development of teachers’ professional vision. The study investigates how video- anchored discussions contribute to the development of mathematics teacher candidates’ professional vision. Data consists of approximately 30 hours of video recordings from five 2323 seminars integrated into an existing mathematics-didactics course across one academic year (24 candidates). The seminars were structured to progressively broaden candidates’ highlighting and coding practices, with the goal of fostering increased attention to students’ diverse mathematical reasoning and forms of participation. Candidates’ discussions were scaffolded through an observation rubric and prompts encouraging them to focus on the qualities of students’ contributions, rather than on perceived defici encies or errors. Through reflective thematic and discourse analysis, the study examines how these practices evolved over time and how cultural frames informed candidates’ interpretations of students’ mathematical work. The study yielded three insights into candidates’ professional vision development: (i) a shift from “glossy” to complex understanding of students’ participation, (ii) an expanded understanding of students’ multiple mathematical competencies, and (iii) pers istent privileging of an authoritative view on valuable mathematical outcomes. Video-anchored discussions supported candidates develop richer framing of students as valuable resources in building mathematical knowledge. However, persistent cultural frames constrained candidates’ appreciation of student’s mathematical thinking (Louie,  2018) highlighting the need for teacher education to explicitly challenge these frames to support the development of professional vision for ambitious and equitable teaching. Poster 7: Teacher-designed cases as a tool to support pre-service teacher noticing Tracy E. Dobie, Liza Escobar Aquino, Bailey N. Ondricek, Raven Burton, Angela Warnock Extensive research illustrates the value of supporting teachers’ noticing of student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010). We respond to the call for more research that investigates learning to notice from an equity frame (van Es et al., 2017) by examining cases (Shulman, 1992) as a tool to support pre-service teachers’ noticing for equity. Teacher noticing is commonly described as having three components – attending, interpreting, and responding (Jacobs et al., 2010). Research on noticing for equity explores various facets of this construct including noticing of individual student histories, anti-deficit discourses, and status and positioning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2017). Challenges include supporting pre -service teachers (PSTs) to attend to individual students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and notice more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Cases are written narratives describing authentic and complex teaching situations (Shulman, 1992) that can be intentionally designed to investigate certain themes (Dobie et al., 2024). We use cases to help PSTs grapple with the challenges of enacting equitable mathematics and science instruction —or leveraging students’ multiple strengths, honoring students’ diverse lived experiences, dismantling classroom power and status hierarchies, and challenging dominant perspectives (e.g., Aguirre et al., 2013). We partnered with local U.S. teachers, who designed cases exploring themes such as assumptions about multilingual students, inequitable group dynamics, and school structures that disadvantage minoritized students (Dobie et al., 2024). Data include PSTs’ written responses (N=1,036; 224 PSTs) to prompts for six cases that were implemented 2 -4 times each in an elementary math or science methods course. Our team deductively and inductively developed a coding scheme (Miles et al., 2014) capturing a) case details  (what PSTs attended to), b) equity-oriented interpretations (PSTs’ reasoning), and c) solutions (ideas about how to respond). Two coders coded every response, and discrepancies were resolved. We highlight three findings: 1) Cases support PSTs to attend to details about students and their actions, 2) Cases and prompts can be designed to support PSTs to make wide-ranging equity-oriented interpretations, and 3) Case prompts elicit solutions that include in-the-moment actions, changes for future instruction, and advocacy- based actions including gathering data and research. We offer frequency counts across the dataset, PST quotes, and case comparisons. As an example, we explore how a subtle difference in prompts influenced PSTs’ breadth of interpretations in two similar cases focused on group dynamics: In one case, 83% of responses offering equity- oriented interpretations focused on a general imbalance in group dynamics; in the other, PSTs reasoned about a general imbalance in group dynamics (39%), as well as the roles of friendship (46%), language (43%), prior school experiences (24%), and gender (15%). Cases have significant potential for supporting PSTs’ noticing for equity including details of specific students’ participation (Wager, 2014) and more critical dimensions of equity (Graham & Roth McDuffie, 2023). Questions remain about trajectories of noticing over time and the impact of noticing in cases on noticing in classrooms. 2324 Poster 8: Accounting for teacher learning in a video club: Learning a noticing discourse Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Elizabeth van Es, Melissa Luna Video-based professional development has been shown to support mathematics and science teachers’ learning to notice for responsive and equitable instruction (Santagata et al., 2021). This vision of teaching calls on teachers to attend to the substantive contributions students make toward the learning goals and adopt an inquiry stance to validate and interpret student thinking to position students’ ideas as resources for their own and others’ learning. What is less understood is how and why these settings support teacher learning. Thus, we ask what might be mechanisms of teacher learning to notice in the context of video- based professional development centered on noticing student thinking? We conceptualize video-based professional development as complex activity systems in which the video clips, the norms for participation, and the cultural and historical practices of professional development all coordinate to influence teachers’ opportunities to learn in these settings (Barnhart, 2021). Our research is informed by an often overlooked feature of complex activity systems of professional development that may be supporting teachers’ learning to notice: the nature of talk that takes place in video- based professional learning contexts. Professional discourse plays a central role in teacher learning (Lefstein et al., 2020), yet less is known about the character of talk that results in teachers’ learning to notice. Data include video recordings and transcripts from two video clubs to support teachers to learn to notice the complexity of teacher -student learning interactions. Video club facilitators prompted teachers to explore the details of student thinking, potential interpretations of their ideas, in relation to teaching. One video club included nine 4th and 5th grade mathematics teachers that met ten times for about one hour over the academic year, approximately once a month. The second video club focused on supporting six middle school science teachers’ learning to notice student thinking and teaching in seven hour -long sessions throughout an academic year. We analyzed an early and late video club meeting for both groups to identify features of a noticing discourse that were present in each meeting (van Es et al., 2024; Table 1). To account for teachers’ learning a noticing discourse, we coded the video club data and wrote analytic memos for evidence and disconfirming evidence of the noticing discourse features, also noting who enacted the talk moves that represented the noticing discourse features. Findings show that both groups shifted in their enactment of a noticing discourse over time. Both groups shifting their talk to highlight more ideas represented in the clips as worthwhile for noticing (i.e., negotiating noteworthy phenomena), pursue these ideas as objects of inquiry for the group to analyze (i.e., creating moments for further inquiry), anchor their analyses of student thinking in classroom evidence (i.e., being accountable to evidence), and demonstrate an openness to explore students’ ideas as resources for learning. Moreover, teachers demonstrated an accountability to the learning community by enacting talk that balanced respecting and honoring teachers' practice represented in the video, while also pressing on what was going on to further understand student thinking and teaching. This finding offers additional insights into features of talk that are enacted to support teachers’ learning to notice, which we argue represents the importance of collective sensemaking  as a critical component of noticing discourse in professional learning. Looking across both video-clubs, this study provides evidence for a noticing discourse as key to teachers’ learning to notice, and has implications for design features, such as creating moments for further inquiry, to make video club discourse generative for teacher learning. Poster 9: Science teachers’ learning to notice expansively Miray Tekkumru-Kisa, Jennifer Richards There is growing agreement in the field that teacher noticing is critical in ambitious forms of teaching that center students (König et al., 2022; Weston & Amador, 2023). Joining other scholars in exploring the complexities of noticing (e.g., van Es et al., 2022), our ongoing work considers the multidimensionality of teachers' noticing for facilitating students’ sensemaking in science classrooms (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). However, there is much to learn about what supports teachers to develop multidimensional noticing practices. In this study, we explored whether a group of science teachers shifted their noticing through engaging in a specific video- based professional learning (PL) design. Briefly, with multidimensional noticing, we bring together key threads from prior work on noticing, such as the importance of noticing student thinking (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010) as well as pedagogy connected to student thinking (e.g., Tekkumru-Kisa & Stein, 2015), and working toward anti -deficit ways of noticing disciplines and 2325 students (e.g., Louie et al., 2021). Taking a situative perspective on teacher learning (Borko et al., 2000), which emphasizes learning through interaction in activity systems, we sought to embody these noticing practices in PL tools and routines (Greeno, 2006; Sandoval, 2014). This study was conducted within the context of an NSF -funded project, Implementing Practices of Ambitious Teaching for Complex Assessment Tasks (IMPACT). IMPACT PL is centered around the implementation of science performance assessments, providing a laboratory for teachers to work with students’ ideas. Five 8th -grade science teachers from different schools in a large urban district in the United States participated. Teachers engaged in collaborative analysis of performance assessment video clips intentional ly selected to highlight relations between student thinking and ambitious teaching principles (Windschitl et al., 2018) and were consistently asked to focus first on student thinking, then aspects of teaching that seemed to support student thinking. To explore changes in teachers’ noticing, we analyzed teachers’ baseline and exit interviews during which they were asked to share what they noticed and how they might respond to events in a ~7- minute video clip. We separated teachers’ interview transcripts into  idea units and coded each idea unit with respect to teachers’ noticing, using the multidimensional noticing framework as an analytical lens (Tekkumru- Kisa & Richards, 2025). At the end of the IMPACT PL, there was growing attention to student thinking among all five teachers. When they noticed student thinking, they began to see what students were saying or appeared to be thinking as valuable, taking an asset-based frame. Moreover, in the exit interviews, teachers focused more on ways to work with students' ideas as opposed to only correcting those ideas. In short, the video- based PL tools and routines seemed to hold promise for supporting shifts in multiple dimensions of teache rs’ noticing in concert with each other. Future research can elaborate on the dynamics of teachers’ noticing practices throughout the PL, particularly how teachers iterated among noticing student thinking and pedagogy. Poster 10: A learning to notice for equity framework Jose Mendez, Elizabeth A. van Es Descriptive accounts of teachers’ noticing for equity contribute to theorizing the complexity of teachers’ in the moment attention and sensemaking to advance responsive and equitable instruction (e.g. Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). What is less understood is how teachers learn  to notice for equity. Teacher noticing for equity is characterized by teachers ’ attention to multiple dimensions of the classroom environment including linguistic resources, power dynamics, relational interactions, social i dentities, and sociopolitical narratives (van Es et al., 2022). We theorize that learning to attend to equity involves the ability to name these classroom dynamics and see them as interconnected (e.g., Rubin & van Es, 2025). The second dimension involves the development of an interpretive practice , which entails continuously engaging with evidence to better understand and support students’ needs (Sherin & Russ, 2017). The third dimension involves embodied engagement , drawing on recent noticing-as-embodied c onceptualizations that highlight the nuanced and multi -sensory aspects of noticing (Mason, 2002; Scheiner, 2021). Embodied engagement of one’s noticing includes both actions, such as shaping, to position oneself to notice more expansively, and choosing to ignore particular aspects of classroom interactions that are less generative for student learning (Louie et al., 2021; van Es et al., 2022). Embodied engagement that disrupts inequities is a reflection of developing one’s noticing for equity (Scheiner, 2021). We qualitatively analyzed data from a research practice partnership that explored whether and how co - designing and analyzing practical measurement data could provoke a mathematics teacher’s learning to notice for equity (Mendez & van Es, 2025). We adopt sociopolitical perspectives to theorize teachers’ learning to notice as tied to their personal histories and the power -laden environments they teach in (Louie et al., 2021). We also theorize learning as a progression that can support teachers and teacher educators formatively documenting changes in teachers’ noticing over time (e.g., van Es, 2011). Data included transcripts of co- design meetings to develop a survey as a form of practical measurement data and data discussions of iterative cycles of survey implementation. This poster will present a framework for learning to notice for equity that consists of four levels. Each level is characterized by shifts in noticing along the dimensions of attending to equity, interpretive practice, and embodied engagement. As the case study teacher shifted in his noticing for equity, he came to see noticing as multidimensional and integrated, shifting frames to interpret events from an asset- and evidence-based stance. He also made connections to his practice and considered how to disrupt persistent inequities to create a responsive classroom through shaping noticing interactions focused on students’ ideas and patterns of participation. This framework moves from descriptive accounts of teacher noticing for equity to characterize the prog ression of learning to noticing from an equity lens over time. In doing so, this tool offers a framework to study teachers’ 2326 learning to notice for equity, while also providing guidance for designing experiences to support teachers’ expansive noticing. papers.title: Concepts, Approaches, and Outcomes in Computational Thinking and Mathematics Integration in K -12: An Umbrella Review
papers.authors: Lingna Xu, Chungsoo Na, Jody Clarke-Midura
papers.abstract: Despite growing interest in integrating Computational Thinking (CT) into K -12 mathematics, the research remains fragmented. To create a cohesive overview, this umbrella review synthesizes 18 literature reviews, meta- analyses, and scoping reviews published between 2006 and 2025. Our analysis focuses on the what (concepts), how (approaches), and why (outcomes) of CT-Mathematics integration. Our findings reveal a consensus on the benefits of CT -Mathematics integration but a lack of specificity. While common concepts (e.g. , abstraction, geometry) and tools (e.g., Scratch) are identified, the synergistic links between them and the pedagogical strategies for implementation are underexplored. Furthermore, learning outcomes are often studied in broader STEM contexts, obscuring the CT-Mathematics link. We conclude that future research must move beyond demonstrating if integration is effective to explaining how, when, and under what conditions CT -Mathematics integration fosters deep, synergistic learning.

papers.title: AI Tools in Arts Learning: A Scoping Review
papers.authors: Jaycee Sansom, Safinah Ali
papers.abstract: With the proliferation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in art making, AI knowledge and skills have made their way to arts learning. However, an assessment of the current state of AI tools in arts learning is lacking. This study used scoping review methodology to identify current research trends in AI applications in arts learning, and what gaps exist for future research. 58 papers were reviewed revealing four trends and five gaps and opportunities.
