papers.title: A three-prong framework for designing theory-based math games
papers.authors: Robin Sharma, Adam K. Dubé
papers.abstract: A common critique of ineffective learning games is their lack of theory-based design and integration of instructional features. While  a few  game-design frameworks have been proposed, they tend to take a limited approach. Some do not consider emotional aspects of games; others do not consider links between gameplay and learning. An approach that brings together the multiple aspects of educational game design is needed . This is important to build domain-specific thinking, build connections between gameplay and learning, and tap into the emotional and motivational aspects of games. This article describes an iterative approach to math game design by bringing  together decades of previous research. It outlines how this approach is applied to create a game for secondary mathematics, specifically geometry. Progression of puzzles based on mathematical complexity, connections between learning objectives and gameplay, and inclusion of emotional elements are described. The challenges, opportunities, and outcomes of the approach are discussed. Gaps in math game design Interactive digital experiences like games can be useful tools for mathematics education as they can transform abstract mathematical concepts into concrete experiences (Potega vel Żabik et al., 2024). For example, games can simulate the abstract nature of mathematical concepts and provide low -stake and real -time interactive environments for mathematical problem solving (Hui & Mahmud, 2023; Klopfer & Thompson, 2020; Sharma et al., 2022). However, it is difficult to design games that incorporate such elements  in a meaningful way to create an enjoyable and effective learning experience for adolescents (Vandercruysse et al., 2016). Despite their potential as engaging learning tools, research has shown that math games and interactive experiences have lacked theoretical foundations (Sharma & Dubé, 2024). More generally, researchers have regularly identified the need for theory -based development of educational games to make them more effective in achieving their intended learning goals (Dubé & Dubé, 2021; Vandercruysse et al., 2016). However, the challenge is to integrate learning into games while not taking away the “fun” (Garris et al. , 2002). From the learning perspective, ineffective educational games are criticized for lack of guiding theories and instructional features (Plass et al., 2015). From the fun perspective, ineffective games are criticized for their bad, unintuitive design,  and a mismatch between learning goals and gameplay (Plass et al., 2015). It is important to bridge these gaps by grounding the design of math games in discipline and gameplay related theoretical frameworks. In their systematic review, Ke (2016) found that game-based learning (GBL) research has predominantly focused on evaluating the effectiveness of digital games. However, researchers should also elaborate and provide descriptions of theoretical foundations, design decisions, and rationales for their choice of game -interactions (Kiili & Lainema, 2008). In this article, we describe three dimensions to educational game design based on relevant theoretical frameworks. We present a three-prong approach to math game design. It builds on previous frameworks and suggests an iterative process of math game design that considers 1) mathematics instruction and thinking, 2) gameplay interactions tied with learning, and 3) the emotional aspects of games tied with learning. We describe this approach with an illustrative example of our process of creating GeometryBOX, a geometry game for adolescents. Three aspects of educational game design Discipline-specific theory Many researchers have called for educational games to be informed by learning theories guiding their designs (Plass et al., 2020). This can refer to a discipline-agnostic theory of learning (e.g., Constructivism). While such a theory can inform the game type and mode of learning, it does not address disciplinary needs. I t does not inform how the progression and order of in -game tasks align with the development of mathematical thinking. This requires a discipline-specific theory.  A discipline -specific theory should be chosen to serve two purposes. First, it guides the in-game instruction and progression based on the requirements and the “ways of thinking” associated with the discipline (Honey & Hilton, 2011; Turkay et al., 2014). This can ensure that the game enables thinking processes in the player that are aligned with the requirements of the discipline (Mayer, 2020). Second, it informs all the subject matter -related aspects of the game, like operationalizing learning objectives for the in- game 61 problems. A discipline -specific theory informs how the in- game problems and gameplay intend to achieve the target learning outcomes (Plass et al., 2020). Gameplay-specific theory As opposed to the discipline specific theory that focusses on progression of in- game problems in line with the thinking process of the discipline, a gameplay specific theory informs the overall design of the game environment and specific player actions tied with the learning objectives. In their systematic review, Ke (2016) identified five themes and ways for integrating learning and playing in digital games. These provide a starting point for how learning goals could be mapped to the interactions offered by the game environment. The five themes are listed in Table 3 later in this article. However, it must be noted that these themes are not mutually exclusive, and one game can integrate learning opportunities in more than one way. The themes identified by Ke (2016) inform broad areas and approaches for integrating learning in games. In addition, it is also important to identify how learning content can be intrinsically embedded into the gameplay and mapped to player’s actions. This is needed to inform how all types of in-game player actions are associated with learning processes and to avoid unnecessary gameplay that can cause distractions and enhance extraneous load which can be detrimental to learning (Mayer & Moreno, 2003). Here, the Learning Mechanic – Game Mechanic (LM-GM) Framework (Arnab et al., 2015) can be a useful tool. It can be used to build a map of learning elements in a serious game with its mechanical/gameplay elements. Here, learning mechanics refers to the objectives, activities, and thinking processes focused on the context of learning. Game mechanics refers to the type of gameplay, game elements, and objects available to the player. This framework provides a starting point for designers to consider these mechanics and identify how gameplay and pedagogy are interrelated in their game. Educational game designers should carefully consider how each interaction a player makes in the game (game mechanic) is associated with the intended learning objective and processes (learning mechanic). This is useful to describe how the actions taken by the players in the games activate the thinking processes required for learning. Emotional design principles Games have the capability to induce achievement emotions that can support learning. Loderer and colleagues (2020) identified five emotional design principles to promote experiences and emotions that aid learning. Carefully considering emotional design principles to inform educational game design can help balance the “fun” and learning in games. Additionally, they can induce emotions conducive to learning like enjoyment and alleviation of boredom. Finally, emotional design principles in games can alleviate t he association of negative emotions, negative math attitudes, and math anxiety in children (Wen & Dubé, 2022; Young et al., 2012). The five principles are visual aesthetic design, musical score, game mechanics, narrative, and incentive system. Visual aesthetic design refers to the in -game visual elements that create engaging and immersive experiences. Musical scores in educational games refer to background tunes, sound effects, and audio feedback to enhance players’ experiences and learning. Game mechanics refer to the interactions and rules that drive the gameplay. Narrative refers to storylines and contextual problem solving that enhance engagement. Finally, the incentive system refers to the rewards and penalties to induce motivation during gameplay. Educational game designers should consider these five aspects at all stages of game development. When thoughtfully applied to its design, emotional design principles can make the game “fun” and “appealing” to the players while keeping intact the intended learning objectives (Mayer & Estrella, 2014). We propose an approach based on the three theoretical aspects of educational game design . Critically, all three should consistently inform design decisions across all aspects of the game (Figure 1). They are applied iteratively and inform the design process at all stages, which can include level design, characters, and in-game problems. Figure 1 Three-Prong Approach to Theory-Based Educational Game Design 62 GeometryBOX – a theory-based game for geometry “GeometryBOX” is designed for students in secondary grades, the game targets  the topic of quadrilaterals. It specifically focusses on the following general learning outcomes: (a) to understand the relationships between properties of special quadrilaterals, and (b) to classify special quadrilaterals based on their properties.  The game begins with the players assuming the role of a robot that is tasked to control a spacecraft while navigating outer space to collect as many stars as possible. The number of stars collected represents the overall game- score of the players. As they fly, they run out of resources which  takes them to the internals of the ship. Here,  they solve geometrical puzzles of increasing complexity to rebuild resources and return to the navigation gameplay. Players switch between these two primary types of gameplays as they increase their score (stars). The game finishes after they solve all geometrical puzzles. Discipline-specific theory in GeometryBOX As described previously, we aimed to identify a discipline -specific theoretical framework aligned with the intended learning objectives (geometry learning) and the target audience (adolescents). Additionally, it should inform the progression of in -game pro blems and enable the thinking processes needed to achieve learning objectives. To address these aspects, we used the Van Hiele Model (VHM) of geometric thinking (Hiele, 1999) as the guiding discipline specific theory for our game. It is a hierarchical framework establishing the existence of five different levels of geometric thinking of increasing complexity (Arnal -Bailera & Manero, 2024) . The increasing complexity of levels informed the increasing complexity of puzzles and specifically informed the “level design” of the game. Second, Hiele (1999) outlined the focus of the VHM on visual and non- verbal thinking and exploration which make it appropriate to inform the design of play- and game-based instruction. Finally, VHM is a topic-agnostic theoretical model. GeometryBOX targeted “classification of quadrilaterals”, a sub-topic in plane- geometry, generally included in middle and secondary geometry curriculum (Vízek et al., 2025) . The five levels of VHM are (a) visualization – referring to visual perception and recognition of mathematical objects; (b) analysis – referring to the ability to recognize and name properties of geometrical figures, (c) abstraction – referring to identification of properties and relationships between geometrical figures, (d) formal ded uction – referring to deduction of geometric proofs and understanding hierarchical nature of mathematical properties, and (e) rigor – referring to identification, comparison, and interrelation of different geometrical systems. VHM has previously been used to inform the design of several curricular and instructional materials for geometry (Senk et al., 2022). Table 2 shows how the definition of the VHM levels were operationalized for this topic (Crowley, 1987). Such operationalization is necessary to map how a theoretical model is applied to define the context of gameplay in association with the intended learn ing objectives. It breaks down the overarching aspects of the theoretical framework (VHM levels in this case) in relation to the target topic within the discipline. Table 2 VHM Levels Operationalized in GeometryBOX Van Hiele Level Key learning outcomes (Crowley, 1987) Learning outcomes operationalized for “classification of quadrilaterals” New game mechanics (1) Visualization Recognize and compare geometrical shapes. Compare, classify, and name geometrical shapes. Drag and drop geometrical shapes into respective bins. (20 puzzles) (2) Analysis Discern properties of geometrical figures. Progressively discover key differences between quadrilaterals of different types based on their properties. Drag and drop special quadrilaterals into respective bins. (27 puzzles) (3) Abstraction Establish interrelationship of properties between geometrical figures. Interrelate properties and relationships among different quadrilaterals. Target labels: see the label of the target bin (e.g., rectangles) to drag and drop shapes into. (20 puzzles) (4) Formal Deduction Deduce relationships and new properties based on axioms. Deduce properties of different quadrilaterals based on their diagonals. Slicing: “slice” a quadrilateral along one of its diagonals to get two triangles. (20 puzzles) 63 (5) Rigor Compare and operate within different geometrical systems. Make new shapes based on given conditions. Slicing: “slice” a quadrilateral along its altitudes to get two triangles and a rectangle; Combining shapes: certain triangles can be combined to obtain quadrilaterals. (20 puzzles) Gameplay specific theory in GeometryBOX Themes identified by Ke (2016) provide educational game designers with a tool to define how learning is integrated in the different aspects of the game. The example of GeometryBOX demonstrates integration of learning via all five themes in the context of mathematics. Table 3 describes how learning was integrated into the game based on Ke’s (2016) framework. Framing the in- game learning experiences in association with the five themes provides a clearer picture of how disciplinary learning objectives are integrated within the gameplay (See Figure 2 later in this article). Educational game designers should clearly identify how learning is integrated within their games. The themes identified here also inform the LM-GM map of the game. Table 3 Integrating Learning in GeometryBOX based on Ke (2016) Theme Description Integration in GeometryBOX game Learning as knowledge activation and acquisition Games with problem solving instances as contexts for retrieving previous knowledge and acquiring new knowledge. The game builds players’ knowledge of quadrilaterals, their properties, types, and relationship among properties through puzzles of increasing complexity. Each set of puzzles requires the players to retrieve knowledge acquired from the previous set. Learning via representation, simulation, or contextualization Game objects and rules embody the focus concepts and learning objectives. The game objects are tied to the narrative theme. The puzzles are contextualized in an overall narrative theme. The game objects (e.g., jewels) represent the mathematical objects (e.g., quadrilaterals) targeting the intended learning objectives. Learning via game mechanics and game world Game interactions and mechanics intrinsically represent the learning content. The game mechanics and interactions are centrally associated with the intended learning objectives. In- game puzzles require the players to sort and categorize geometrical shapes, this primary game mechanic mapped to the central learning objective: “classification of quadrilaterals”. Reflective and iterative learning moments in gameplay Learning happens via strategizing and reflective use of knowledge. Specific learning moments are repeated in gameplay. At least 20 puzzles are mapped to each learning outcome mapped to a Van Hiele Level (Table 2) providing iterative learning moments. Higher levels require strategizing, more complex thinking, and use of previous knowledge to solve puzzles. In-game learning supports Game provides cues, feedback, clear instructions, and in-game prompts. The game provides audio and textual feedback based on the players’ moves. It provides explicit hints and definitions associated with the learning objectives. An LM-GM map based on the framework by Arnab and colleagues (2015) is one of the most important parts of the educational game design process. It informs and presents a clear map of player interactions (game mechanics) and how they translate to learning rel ated actions (learning mechanics). All educational games should aim to create and describe the LM- GM map of their games. Table 4 shows the LM -GM map for GeometryBOX  (also see Figure 2 later in this article). An LM-GM map lists the corresponding learning and game mechanics, the ways in which they are integrated, and “how” they are integrated. This framework provides a summary to educators and administrators and helps them make decisions about the suitability of the game for their use. When building the LM-GM map of the game, implementation and usage of learning mechanics and game mechanics is described in the context of game features. The exercise of creating an LM -GM map of the game is essential to reflect how different interactions and gameplay are linked to learning. Additionally, it is important to clearly communicate to users and other researchers the reasoning for their design decisions. 64 Table 4 LM-GM Map of GeometryBOX Game mechanic Learning mechanic Implementation via Usage Cut-scenes Story Motivation Feedback Narrative Game environment Levels 1) The overall guiding context and story of the game refer to the narrative theme. 2) The game has additional, story-related gameplay levels and cut- scenes beyond the geometrical puzzles that refer to the narrative theme. 3) Game scores (stars), health bars (shield and energy), and other visual elements (backdrop of game puzzles) also refer to the narrative theme. 4) The game provides textual and audio feedback based on the player actions associated with math learning and the narrative theme. Strategy/Planning Resource management Explore Discover Identify Hypothesize Plan Feedback In-game health bars Puzzles Levels 1) Puzzle solving encourages exploration and discovery by not giving any learning-outcome related instruction. 2) Exploration and discovery are encouraged by not penalizing initial incorrect moves. 3) Players hypothesize an approach to puzzle solving and plan their next move based on game feedback. 4) Complexity of puzzles and learning outcomes follows a hierarchical system where new knowledge is built on the previous. 5) In-game health bars represent the two types of resources available to the players. 6) Players need to identify the best strategy that optimizes resource usage when solving in-game puzzles. Rewards/Penalties Game turns Incentive Repetition In-game health bars Drag and drop action 1) Game turns refer to the action of dragging and dropping geometrical shapes into correct bins and locations. 2) Gameplay provides an incentive for taking the minimum number of turns when players solve a puzzle. 3) Incorrect moves beyond a threshold are penalized, correct moves are rewarded, and successful puzzle solving is rewarded. This is reflected by changes in available resources represented as health-bars. Feedback Motivation Feedback Game task Textual and visual prompts 1) Encouraging and motivational textual feedback prompts based on players’ in-game action (e.g., after a correct/incorrect move). 2) Learning outcome related textual feedback after successful completion of the game-task, i.e. solving a puzzle. Levels Analyze Simulation Repetition Reflection Puzzles Drag and drop action 1) Puzzles with game objects that simulate properties of geometrical objects. Shapes can be dragged-and-dropped on interactive elements to simulate their geometrical properties. 2) Correctly solving a puzzle requires analysis of shapes and application of knowledge. 3) Subsequent puzzles build on learning outcomes of previous puzzles. 4) Similar types of puzzles, referring to similar learning outcomes associated with VHM levels, are repeated several times. 5) Players can retry until the correct solution is found. However, too many incorrect moves deplete health and reduce progress encouraging reflection. Emotional design principles in GeometryBOX 65 Visual aesthetic design We used bright, warm, and contrasting colors in the visual design of the game. All the geometrical figures, that were the primary objects of gameplay, were bright purple in color to create a visually appealing interface (Wen & Dubé, 2023). The overall theme of “outer space” was consistently depicted through all the game objects. For example, the cursor was styled as a “crosshair”. Players solved geometrical puzzles to fix batteries and repair their ship. On the “progress map” screen of the game, the batteries were represented as “lightbulbs” that changed color from orange to green after successful completion of a puzzle. This aimed to create a sense of curiosity and break- down the overall game into smaller goals inducing a sense of achievement  (Garg & Baroody, 2024). Musical score Audible feedback from a learning environment has the potential to enhance the perceived pleasantness of gameplay by extending the sensory experience (Nacke et al., 2010). A consistent, low, buzzing sound was used to convey the sound as their ship navigated outer space. Different types of audio feedback were used when players made correct/incorrect moves in the game, successfully completed a level, depleted their energy or shields, collected stars while navigating, an d shot enemy objects. Dynamic sounds along with encouraging phrases like “You’re good” (with a bright audio cue) after a correct move and “Try again” (with a dull audio cue) after an incorrect move were used to keep the players motivated during gameplay (Cayari, 2022). This way, the audio was also aligned with the game situation to induce immersion and emotional engagement (Andersen et al., 2021). Such acoustic characteristics were used in the game to draw attention to important content associated with learning (Collins, 2009; Plass et al., 2020). Game mechanics The central puzzle solving mechanic of the game was to “drag and drop” geometrical shapes into the correct bins to fix the batteries (Figure 2a, 2b). This built energy for the players’ ship to navigate and collect as many stars as possible. Sorting geometrical objects can engage students to build new knowledge based on their existing conceptions (Kobiela et al., 2018). It can help them identify and un derstand the properties of geometrical objects by noticing similarities and differences (Kobiela et al., 2018; Roth & Thom, 2009). Hence, sorting via “dragging and dropping” geometrical shapes into bins was built as the central game mechanic. Other game mechanics in the puzzles were primarily informed by the learning objectives at each level. New mechanics are introduced as players progress to puzzles at higher levels of the Van Hiele Model. They aim to sustain curiosity and enjoyment while preventing boredom and predictive gameplay (Loderer et al., 2020). They also create a sense of excitement as players progress in the game. For example, at puzzles from VHM level four, players are introduced to the “slicing” mechanic. They can break quadrilaterals into smaller diagonals by “slicing” them along a diagonal of their choice. Table 2 shows new mechanics introduced in puzzles at each new VHM level.  In addition to inducing positive emotions that aid learning, the game mechanics are introduced in a structured order that is informed by the discipline-specific theory, the VHM model. This avoids a mismatch between progression of gameplay and learning which can enhance self -efficacy and reduce negative emotions such as frustration (Plass et al., 2012). This is associated with the recommendations of (Masek et al., 2017) where “fun” and “excitement” in the game are fundamentally grounded in the problem solving associated with learning. Narrative Narrative in educational games can provide a framework for structural representation of problems (Dickey, 2011). There can be many ways of including narrative in learning games. This is based on the genre of game and core game-mechanics (Ke, 2016) . Our game had a focus on mathematical learning outcomes. The core mechanic involved was “logic and thought during puzzle solving”. Additionally, it was categorized as a “casual puzzle” game as players solve geometrical puzzles to progress. In GeometryBOX, narrative was embedded via environmental storytelling and backdrop missions. Elements of the game environment focused on conveying the narrative theme of the game. Nomenclature for points, rewards, and penalties referred to the narrative theme. Additional gameplay puzzles for the game incentive system were created and were also situated in the overall narrative theme of the game (Figure 2c, 2d). In our game, narrative was integrated as a broadly defined goal with a background plot and adventure missions (Jenkins, 2002). An overarching narrative can create expectations about upcoming events and build suspense that sustains attention for learning  (McNamara et al., 2010) . The narrative in GeometryBOX of “fixing batteries” to “repair the ship” and “navigate the outer space” was designed to contextualize learning and provide an overarching story connecting in- game progression, gameplay loop, rules, events, rewards, and penalties (Loderer et al., 2020) . Through all these aspects, narrative was tightly and meaningfully associated with gameplay and learning. It was not included as an afterthought where the story and narrative are only depicted through one aspect (e.g., cut scene and videos) and not tied to gameplay (Naul & Liu, 66 2020). On the contrary, the primary narrative related objective of “fixing batteries” was tied to the central learning objective of solving geometrical puzzles. Figure 2 Examples level screenshots from GeometryBOX Incentive system Rewards and penalties at the center of GBL can help keep the players motivated (Loderer et al., 2020). The incentive system in GeometryBOX is applied in three layers. First, every “game turn” of “dragging and dropping” an object costs a certain number of resources. In this way, players are nudged towards solving the puzzles in minimum possible moves to pres erve the available resources. Hence, they are incentivized for adopting mathematical strategies and discourage “trial and error” based strategy. Second, when  players deplete all their resources by making too many incorrect moves, they need to replenish it by completing another game level where they “shoot the debris to clear the boosters” (Figure 2d). This resets their available resources to 100%. This incentive system of managing resources and performance-based progress is dependent on individual learning and gameplay strategy. It aims to increase perceived autonomy and learner control and induce positive achievement emotions (McNamara et al., 2010). The third layer of incentive system is based on collecting “stars” to increase overall points. This layer in tends to enhance the value of learning through “internal compensation”, i.e. achievements in the game (Loderer et al., 2020). After players solve enough puzzles to bring their available resources above a certain threshold, new gameplay is unlocked in which the player controls their spaceship and steers it through an “asteroid field in outer space”. This three -layered, cyclic incentive system in GeometryBOX is intended to create positive achievement emotion of anticipation through feedback, novelty, and repe tition (Pekrun et al., 2014). It also aims to promote optimized gameplay linked with learning as thoughtful, strategized, and mathematical gameplay is rewarded. In sum, GeometryBOX is designed for adolescents to understand the properties and relationships between special quadrilaterals. It is tightly aligned with the learning objectives associated with this topic. This aspect was primarily informed by the VHM, the  discipline-specific theory guiding its design. The gameplay and learning were integrated based on the five themes identified by Ke (2016) and are described via its LM-GM map. Emotional design principles were applied to all five features of the game to create a positive and enjoyable learning experience for the players. Discussion This article suggests a three -prong approach to educational game design with an elaborate example of a math game. Educational game designers should follow an iterative process of applying this approach to their design. They should bring these three theoretical approaches together by going beyond previous approaches to educational 67 game design that only consider these aspects independently. In their review of existing educational game design frameworks, Sasupilli and colleagues (2019) identified six prevalent game design models. However, none of them focused on domain specific, play specific, and emotion specific theoretical foundations simultaneously. They were limited to either one or only two of these aspects. For example, the experiential gaming model (Kiili, 2005) does not consider blending learning through game mechanics. In the context of mathematics education, the application of a theoretical framework of math instruction is critical to promote students’ domain -specific mental models for learning (Pirnay -Dummer et al., 2012). This factor becomes much more critical in the context of math as it relies on students’ development of mental models of mathematical objects, their properties, and their relationships (G arg et al., 2025 ; Prayekti et al., 2020). Additionally, the use of Ke’s (2016) framework is needed to address the “what, how, where, and when learning is embedded” in games. This framework helps game designers answer broader questions about leaning in games. It informs design decisions like choice of game genre (simulation versus puzzle), absence or presence of narrative, narrative design (environmental backdrop versus roleplay), representation of learning content (content as game objects versus simulation of concepts), frequency of learning moments in games (exploration and discovery versus immediate feedback), and presence or absence of in-game learning supports. Further, at a finer level, the LM-GM framework (Arnab et al., 2015) helps designers address how all game features (game mechanics) are linked to learning mechanics. Creating an LM-GM map of the game during its design process is crucial to establish granular relationships between pedagogy and gameplay. Finally, to leverage the potential of games to induce emotional experiences for learning, the application of emotional design principles is essential. This can ensure a balance between fun and learning by fostering positive emotions (Byun & Joung, 2018). Specifically for mathematics, enhancing the overall learning experience can be transformative to address concerns with the negative perception of math as being too challenging and uninspiring (Wen & Dubé, 2023). Careful integration of emotional design principles that meaningfully and systematically induce enjoyment, anticipation, and excitement (Putwain et al., 2018) can counter negative impressions of math like fear and anxiety (Budhathoki et al., 2022). Navigating challenges While there are theoretical benefits of applying the three- prong framework to educational games, it also comes with its own challenges and opportunities. It is possible that there is overlap, friction, and conflict when certain game elements are informed by two approaches. The design process for GeometryBOX serves as an example to illustrate how such challenges can be overcome. This is mainly exhibited by two elements: game mechanics and narrative. We describe how all game mechanics were linked to learning via the LM-GM map of the game. The LM-GM map describes the way in which mechanics were implemented and their link with learning processes. In addition, a range of game mechanics were built to create anticipation and excitement as an outcome of the emotional design principles. Further, the addition of new mechanics to create anticipation and excitement was based on the increasing complexity of the discipline -specific VHM model. This way, the design of game mechanics was grounded in all three frameworks that each supported learning through different dimensions. Similarly, learning was integrated through an implicit narrative in the game via environmental storytelling, backdrop, textual and visual references to narrative theme. This was based on Ke’s (2016) framework. Narrative can be beneficial for math learning by providing learners with a framework for representation of problems (Irmayanti et al., 2024; Junkin, 2019). Here, narrative was not included as explicit framing but, rather, the action of solving geometry puzzles to achieve learning outcomes was implicitly linked to the game narrative (solving puzzles = fixing “batteries” = repairing “ship”). Moreover, narrative served as a tool to create an immersive and enjoyable learning experience based on the emotional design principles. This demonstrates how the inclusion of narrative was also informed by two distinct frameworks. Yet, it aimed to avoid contradictory and conflicting experiences. In this case, grounding the narrative in multiple theoretical argument s is likely to strengthen its effects on learning rather than weakening it. Conclusion The GeometryBOX game described in this article is an example of applying distinct but relevant theoretical frameworks of educational game design to create a geometry game. It bridges the gaps between cognitive and domain-specific, gameplay-specific, and emotional foundations of game-based learning. Thoughtful and implicit design of game features tightly tied to learning objectives have the potential to result in positive learning outcomes and make learning an enjoyable experience. We aim to  conduct evidence -based, experimental  studies on the effectiveness of GeometryBOX on geometrical understanding of adolescents . Game designers should consider this approach to create educational games that are not only grounded in theories of learning and instruction but also harness the power of play in a holistic way. 68 References Andersen, F., Danny, King, C. papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: A common critique of ineffective learning games is their lack of theory-based design and integration of instructional features. **Finding**: Despite their potential as engaging learning tools, research has shown that math games and interactive experiences have lacked theoretical foundations (Sharma & Dubé, 2024). **Relevance**: While  a few  game-design frameworks have been proposed, they tend to take a limited approach.

papers.title: A Scoping Review of Interdisciplinary Learning Research in Higher Education Contexts
papers.authors: Shotaro Naganuma, Go Shoji, Jun Oshima
papers.abstract: This study conducted a scoping review on 19 interdisciplinary education/learning research articles in higher education contexts. Citation network analysis and qualitative analysis revealed that 1) the articles were categorized into three clusters, 2) only 14 articles were cited more than t wice, and 3) each cluster cited different articles with different focus es. These findings suggest that interdisciplinary education/learning research is in the phase of establishing shared vocabularies and engaging with conceptual tools.

papers.title: Thematic Issues: Three Design Models to Address The Challenge of
papers.authors: Selma Hamdani, Elizabeth S. Charles, Annie-Helene Samson
papers.abstract: The increasing complexity of societal challenges requires interdisciplinary approaches in education to cultivate critical thinking, adaptability, and a holistic understanding of global issues. In response, the  Quebec college system’s Social Science program introduced the Thematic Issues course (TI), a single -instructor course designed to engage students in interdisciplinary inquiry through instructor- selected themes and three prescribed social science disciplines. To navigate the challenges of teaching across disciplines in an unstructured framework, instructors formed a Faculty Learning Community (FLC) to collaboratively refine course design and instructional strategies. This paper e xamines three TI course models: the serial model, offering compartmentalized insights; the spiral model, promoting cumulative, integrated learning; and the jigsaw model emphasizes collaborative synthesis by combining specialized disciplinary perspectives into a cohesive understanding. By analyzing these models, this practice-centered study highlights the pedagogical affordances and constraints of single-teacher interdisciplinary instruction. Context As societal issues grow more complex, interdisciplinary education is increasingly recognized as a way to help learners make sense of them. Curricula must prepare students for real -world challenges by fostering critical thinking, adaptability, and transferable skills (Peiqi & Xionghu, 2003). This paper presents a practitioner-centered perspective on the development of a multidiscipline course aimed at fostering interdisciplinary thinking. The course was collaboratively designed through the efforts of nine instructors (practitioners) at a large urban college in Quebec, part of the province’s unique 2-year post-secondary CEPEP system (1). These individuals were tasked with developing and teaching the first cohort of a 45-hour, third semester Social Science course called Thematic Issues (TI), which prepares students for a self- directed interdisciplinary project in their final ( fourth) semester. As a core course within the program, the TI is offered in 20 sections annually, serving approximately 500 students. Operating as a Faculty Learning Community ( FLC; to be defined shortly), the nine instructors brought expertise from six disciplines: psychology, anthropology, philosophy, religious studies, sociology, and business administration. These instructors had no experience working within an explicit theoretical framework to prepare for the design of the interdisciplinary course. Beginning in late May 2024, the instructors held initial meetings of the FLC before pausing for the summer, during which independent course planning took place. Bi-weekly meetings resumed in Fall 2024, leading to the course's first large scale offering that semester. This piloting phase is currently ongoing (Winter 2025) and will extend into Fall 2025. Early design decisions were driven by pragmatic reasoning and practitioner insights. However, one FLC member––the first author —was simultaneously involved in a research-practice partnership focused on interdisciplinary instruction, allowing for the integration of research-informed insights of this process. Inasmuch, her role is characterized as that of boundary spanner (Akkerman & Bakker, 2011), bridging theory to practice and enriching the FLC’s pedagogical approach to interdisciplinary course design. The faculty learning community Drawing on the Cox model of Faculty Learning Community (Cox, 2004), an FLC is a structured, collaborative group of educators who engage in an ongoing, scholarly, and collegial process to enhance teaching, learning and professional development (Richlin & Essington, 2004). This participatory approach offers several advantages including fostering interdisciplinary collaboration, enhancing teaching practices and building a supportive 2223 professional network that drives innovation in pedagogy. Participating in an FLC not only enhances individual teaching practices but also fosters a sense of community and professional growth among instructors (Cox, 2004). The FLC participants consisted of instructors who were either assigned to teach the TI course or who were involved in its initial design. Course development began with a shared understanding of the course competencies. Over the summer, each instructor independently designed their course based on their interpretation of the  course competency and learning o utcomes. In Fall 2024, during biweekly FLC meetings, instructors collaboratively refined their course designs, addressing challenges and aligning their approaches before implementing them in their classrooms. As noted earlier, the central challenge faced by this FLC stemmed from the nature of the TI course itself. With its open framework and minimal prescriptive guidance, the course placed the responsibility on individual instructors to independently design innovative pedagogical approaches that integrate diverse disciplinary perspectives. This task w as further complicated by the fact that, like many post -secondary educators, the instructors lacked formal training in teaching and learning (Ramolula, & Nkoane, 2024) —what is often referred to as the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL). Moreover, the course required them to engage with content and perspectives beyond their own disciplinary expertise. These were just some of the issues the nine FLC members grappled with during their many meetings, which ultimately shaped the course design described in the next section. Course design The initial results of the FLC were five proposals for the TI course design, these were subsequently refined to three models—Serial (Figure 1), Spiral (Figure 1), and Jigsaw (Figure 2)—each representing one of possible ways of addressing the interdisciplinary teaching challenge . These models were developed through instructors' experiential insights and collaborative brainstorming sessions . In large part, the FLC  instructors’ pragmatic practices and considerations of feasibility were the driving decision makers to settle on choosing these three designs as the models to be piloted . Once decided by the FLC, the first author brought them to the research - practice group for deeper study, leading to the identification of feature s that suggest alignment with known learning sciences theories and instructional strategies. Case 1: Serial model The serial model (Figure 1) follows a low-integration multidisciplinary structure, where students explore themes sequentially, with instructors acting as content experts (Jacobs, 1989).  In this model, each discipline is presented independently, allowing students to engage with multiple perspectives before drawing comparisons. This compartmentalized approach provides clarity but limits synthesis, positioning students as passive observers . While some instructors viewed this structure as a barrier to interdisc iplinary learning, others found it beneficial for students unfamiliar with interdisciplinary work, as it offers a structured introduction before deeper integration. Case 2: Spiral model The spiral model (Figure 1)  adopts a high- integration interdisciplinary approach, reinforcing cumulative understanding through iterative learning cycles, reminiscent  of Bruner’s (1960) spiral curriculum  approach. It engages students in recursive knowledge  construction, aligning with authentic complexity of real -world issues (e.g. mental health and wellbeing, climate change). This course design begins by establishing foundational knowledge of a central theme. It then progressively incorporates additional layers, examining how various factors —such as cultural contexts, developmental stages, and systemic influences —shape and inte ract with the core concept. These elements are explored as interconnected components that contribute to a broader understanding. Each stage builds upon the previous one, creating a cohesive framework that enables students to apply their earlier learning to increasingly complex ideas. 2224 Figure 1 The Serial and Spiral Models The serial model (left) presents disciplines sequentially, examining themes in isolation before drawing connections, while the spiral model (right) interweaves disciplines, revisiting core themes at increasing depths for a cumulative and integrated understanding. Case 3: Jigsaw model The jigsaw model (Figure 2), rooted in the cooperative learning framework (Aronson, et. al 1978; Johnson, et al., 2000), structures the TI course into two distinct phases. In the first phase, spanning the first 10 weeks of the semester, students are introduced to disciplinary concepts sequentially , much like in the serial mode. This phase establishes the foundational understanding of the course material. The final five weeks , the second phase, adopts a Jigsaw approach, where students are divided into groups  to explore a specific social science discipline’s perspective. This model engages students in collaborative synthesis, requiring them to actively contribute while instructors balance facilitation with content e xpertise. The Jigsaw model fosters student agency and interdependence, deepening critical thinking through peer teaching (Aronson et al., 1978). Figure 2 The Jigsaw Model This figure begins with a serial presentation of religion, introducing foundational concepts through three distinct components of the scientific study of religion. This is followed by an example showcasing the anthropology team's focused analysis, demonstrating their exploration of religious practices. The exemplar represents the discipline- specific deep dive, a critical step in the collaborative integration process that defines the jigsaw model. Conclusion 2225 Designed as a foundation for interdisciplinary learning, the TI course guides students in examining contemporary issues from multiple disciplinary perspectives, helping them develop the analytical skills needed for integrative thinking. The development of the TI course models emerged from ongoing collaboration between a practitioner FLC and a research-practice team, mediated by a facilitator who acted as a boundary spanner . Using an FLC approach, nine instructors collaborated to identify key challenges in interdisciplinary instruction and develop practical solutions for the TI course design. These discussions, informed by insights from the facilitator––working with the research team ––led to the identification of three pedagogical models —serial, spiral, and jigsaw —each offering a distinct approach to the challenge of interdisciplinary learning. Importantly, they demonstrate that the grounded and pragmatic solutions generated by practitioners can also be  justified by the learning sciences research. In doing so,  these models could act as boundary objects that allow both the FLC and the research - practice groups to examine the implications of the course designs on interdisciplinary learning. Results from the initial pilot of the TI course revealed that most instructors adhered to the serial model, likely due to its simple structure. However, two instructors from the FLC took the opportunity to experiment with the more interdisciplinary approaches – one implementing the spiral model and the other the jigsaw model. The instructor who opted for the spiral model highlighted its effectiveness in fostering knowledge integration . In reflecting on the experience of working within this model the instructor stated that it allowed her to reflect more "authentic real -world situations" into her class activities (Participant 2, personal communication, [2025]) . By examining core themes from different disciplinary perspectives, it helps students integrate the knowledge in meaningful ways that resemble solving authentic problems. The Spiral model was praised for its effectiveness in fostering deep understanding and sustained engagement. The instructor also noted that it required significant time to plan the curricular activities . The other instructor, who adopted the jigsaw model, reported high student engagement. However, during an FLC discussion, concerns were raised about the challenge of managing the integration of the six disciplines within the exercise (recall Fig 2) disciplines within this model. Despite the challenges, he was encouraged by the results of the jigsaw model and proposed exploring modifications to improve its feasibility, including a more purposeful selection of disciplines to enhance the coherence of the activity. From the perspective of the practitioner, these three TI course models offer flexible feasible frameworks that can be adapted to various institutional and disciplinary contexts and offer valuable insights for educators seeking to foster integrative learning across disciplines. The Serial Model, with its discipline-specific sequencing, may be most suitable for institutions where interdisciplinary coordination is limited but can serve as a first step toward integration. The Spiral Model, which builds on iterative engagement with interdisciplinary themes, requires sustained collaboration but offers a scalable approach for programs aiming to deepen integration over time. The Jigsaw Model, emphasizing cooperative learning, is highly adaptable to settings that prioritize student- centered learning and active engagement. From the perspective of learning sciences, these models are opportunities for research to examine how they function across different educational contexts and their impact on student learning outcomes, allowing us  to better understand their effectiveness in fostering interdisciplinary thinking. Additionally, further investigation could explore the extent to which the models align with constructivist and social constructivist principles, identifying potential affordances within their designs that may enhance interdisciplinary learning. From a facilitation perspective, the FLC approach proved to be a valuable mechanism for supporting interdisciplinary course design. It enabled the development, refinement, and implementation of the three course design models while fostering a collaborative space for pedagogical innovation. The role of the facilitator was particularly crucial in maintaining a focus on interdisciplinary learning objectives. A key challenge involved balancing instructional design priorities with the traditionally content- driven orientation of higher education instructors. As this project continues, ongoing analysis in collaboration with the research- practice group will further examine the effectiveness of these models and refine their implementation, particularly within the context of an FLC. It offers two- year pre-university programs or three-year technical programs. CEGEPs emphasize accessibility and affordability. They offer ablend of specialized as well as general education. papers.title: The Effects of Digital Games on Pre-K-12 Students’ Growth Mindset: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Seyedahmad Rahimi, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Ran Gao, Deniz Ercan, Supharoek Keawphonkrang
papers.abstract: The concept of a “growth mindset” refers to the belief that one’s abilities and intelligence can be developed through effort, learning, and persistence. This systematic review examines the impact of digital games on fostering a growth mindset in pre-K- 12 educational settings. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, we analyzed 13 studies focused on digital games designed to enhance a growth mindset. Findings indicate that most games positively influence growth mindset along with other competencies (e.g., creativity and persistence), while a minority show mixed or negligible effects, often linked to the game design or context. The review identifies trends across various game genres, targeted skill s, and geographical regions, reflecting a growing interest in growth mindset research. It suggests that digital games represent a valuable avenue for educational interventions which emphasize the need for thoughtful design informed by evidence on effective game features.

papers.title: Design and Play in Real Time: A Participatory Design Approach for Autistic Children to Design Online Play with Peers
papers.authors: Yiqi Xiao, Jiabei Xu
papers.abstract: This paper presents a participatory design approach for children, designers, and educators to collaboratively create inclusive digital play environments that foster interactions between neurodiverse and neurotypical children. Integrating generative AI (GenAI) empowers children to actively contribute to game design while engaging in the play with their peers without adult mediation, highlighting the potential of such methods to foster inclusive collaboration among children, between children and adults, and between children and technology. A Call for creating inclusive social opportunities online Like other children, autistic children often desire peer friendships (Rodda & Estes, 2018) yet frequently face social challenges (Lord & Magill-Evans, 1995). These include difficulties with language, sensory processing, and interpreting social cues—such as jokes, eye contact, or facial expressions (Ghanouni et al., 2019; Aherne, 2023)— which can lead to reduced or atypical peer interactions. Given these challenges in face-to-face communication, online spaces offer alternative avenues for social expression. Research shows a strong preference among autistic children for screen-based media, especially video games (Mazurek & Engelhardt, 2013). As Barrington Campbell, an autistic adult, shared: “If you are autistic, this can feel more than stressful... Online gaming means autistic people can play in an environment we feel comfortable in and can control” (National Autistic Society, 2024). However, autistic children also face heightened online safety risks compared to peers (Macmillan et al., 2020). Mainstream digital spaces rarely support neurodiverse communication and often neglect their well-being in interactions with non-autistic users. Few games, whether commercial or academic, are designed to connect autistic and neurotypical children through shared interests in gameplay (Spiel & Gerling, 2021; Xiao, 2024). The research team that designed Zopy, a collaborative iPad game that successfully fostered friendship among autistic students without adult mediation, encouraged designers to create more games that reflect the diverse spectrum of social behaviors in peer collaboration (Boyd et al., 2015). Building on this, more design approaches are needed to guide the development of such inclusive applications. This paper proposes a participatory approach to digital play, involving collaboration among children, educators, designers, and GenAI. The rationale and methods for each type of collaboration are illustrated through the design case Together Tales, a collaborative storybook making game (Xiao, 2024). Collaboration among children, educators, and designers Why involve children? Traditionally, adults have controlled all aspects of the design process, even when the intended users are children. As Druin (2002) noted, children have distinct preferences, curiosities, and needs that differ from those of adults. Their input is therefore essential for designing effective products. Involving children not only improves outcomes but also ensures they feel valued and heard. Despite growing recognition of children as design partners, research involving autistic children remains limited. Most games for this group adopt top-down approaches with educational or medical goals, often overlooking their interests (Spiel & Gerling, 2021). Given the social challenges autistic children face, it is vital to include them in designing social games tailored to their needs. It is also worth noting that autistic children, like other neurodiverse groups, may be natural design partners. They often exhibit traits commonly labeled as “gifted,” such as excelling in creativity, visual-spatial skills, and attention to detail (Armstrong, 2010), making them highly capable contributors to design processes. How to involve children? In many participatory design (PD) practices, researchers acknowledge that children often struggle with verbal communication, particularly when dealing with abstract concepts (Druin, 2002). This issue is likely to be even more pronounced in collaborations between autistic children and adults. As a result, drawing is frequently used as an alternative form of contribution to the design process (Hunt et al., 2023). In the approach proposed here, children express ideas through drawings and then select AI-generated elements that match their vision. These are directly incorporated into the final design. The technical implementation of this GenAI collaboration is discussed in later sections. In Together Tales, children are prompted by animations within the game to draw characters they imagine appearing in specific story scenarios. They then select the generated images that best match their vision. The selected images retain certain features and are integrated into the subsequent storylines, influencing the progression of the narrative. Why involve educators? It is a common practice to involve educators in the participatory design process involving children (Piedade et al., 2024; Ey & Spears, 2020), to leverage their expertise and insights, which help ensure pedagogical guidance. In the context of this paper, educators primarily function as stakeholders, providing critical insights that bridge pedagogical goals with the needs and interests of the children. How to involve educators? While understanding why educators should be involved is relatively straightforward, addressing how to involve them effectively requires deeper consideration. Excessive involvement by educators may reduce the freedom and space for children to contribute, while insufficient involvement risks a lack of critical information in the design. How can we achieve an appropriate level of participation? The participatory design process proposed in this paper borrows from the concept of guided play (Weisberg et al., 2016). It highlights the strategy that adults create a setting that emphasizes a specific learning goal while still allowing children the freedom to explore and interact within the environment independently. Research shows that compared to a free setting and a highly structured setting, children’s active participation in discovery, combined with appropriate scaffolding from a knowledgeable adult, a higher level of engagement and better learning result (Sim & Xu, 2015). In Together Tales (Fig. 1), educators define the overarching storyline—the goal of the journey for two players, structure of activities in which children engage during digital play. These activities may include collaborative drawing, assembling puzzle pieces, organizing photos to reconstruct a story, or other creative tasks. While the framework provides guidance, the specifics—such as what to draw, the themes of the photos, or the approach to completing the activity—are shaped by the children’s prior choices and left open for their exploration. This balance between structure and freedom ensures meaningful engagement and allows children to take ownership of their creative process. Figure 1 A Demonstration of The Mechanism of Together Tales. The role of designers/researchers Rather than focusing solely on the final product, designers and researchers should prioritize creating innovative processes and frameworks that position users and stakeholders as active, independent contributors. They are also responsible for assessing the technical feasibility of stakeholders’ ideas to ensure the process runs smoothly. Collaboration between autistic and neurotypical children Why involve both groups? Peers support autistic children’s play in ways adults cannot (Jones, 1991), yet few digital play environments reflect neurodiverse interests. Many games focus narrowly on autistic children’s social challenges rather than fostering inclusive or neurodivergent-centered experiences (Spiel & Gerling, 2021; Xiao, 2024). Two major misconceptions contribute to this gap. The first is that only autistic children benefit from peer interaction. Jones (1991) identified self-disclosure, trust, and companionship as key to friendship satisfaction. A global study of 2,555 autism experts emphasized traits like morality, trustworthiness, and kindness in autistic individuals (de Schipper et al., 2016)—qualities that make them valuable friends. Without opportunities to engage, neurotypical children may miss out on meaningful relationships, thus they too need to learn how to interact and collaborate with autistic peers. The second misconception is that autistic children are not capable of forming strong friendships. Though their styles may differ, research increasingly shows that autistic children build meaningful relationships with both neurotypical and autistic peers (Rodda & Estes, 2018). Therefore, creating more opportunities for positive interaction is essential to support relationship-building between neurodiverse children. How to involve both groups? Collaborative play—where players coordinate actions toward a shared goal—effectively fosters social interaction between autistic and neurotypical children (Reuter et al., 2014; Khatab et al., 2024). Moreover, Piedade et al. (2024) found that creating such artifacts enhances self-determination in autistic children. While few studies compare artifact co-design to digital collaboration within the screen in terms of social outcomes, the approach of “collaborative making through game” shows strong potential and merits further exploration. In Together Tales, children collaborate on playful design decisions, such as choosing what kind of backpack to include, determining the type of animal characters they encounter, and deciding the sequence of photos displayed on a wall. These decisions collectively weave a unique narrative. At the end of the game, children receive a co-authored, printable digital storybook as a tangible artifact of their collaboration. Collaboration between children and GenAI Why involve GenAI? The development of AI technology has significantly transformed and advanced educational practices. For example, AI can assist teachers in designing and delivering personalized, timely, iterative, and enriching learning experiences (Nguyen, 2023). However, a significant portion of current methodologies view AI as an extension of roles traditionally held by educators, behavior analysts, or other adult experts, aiming to achieve previously unattainable efficiencies (Amiri et al., 2017; Shahamiri & Thabtah, 2020). Few approaches aim to help children enhance their own abilities, limiting their opportunities to participate meaningfully in the design process and reducing their agency within support systems. Moreover, while discussions have highlighted the potential of AI as a creative assistant in participatory design (Zhao, 2024), research focusing on its application for children— especially autistic children—is scarce. Despite this, AI has been used in various contexts to support youth in creating original work outside the PD framework. Ali et al. (2021) demonstrated how GenAI supported K-12 students and educators in co-designing learning materials, boosting teacher confidence. Such cases underscore AI’s potential to enhance children’s creativity and support its further exploration in participatory design with autistic children. Figure 2 Character Creation to Collaborative Storytelling in Together Tales. How to involve GenAI? Through the versatile application of GenAI, generative image model (GIM) empowers children to transform their sketches into content-consistent images. Vision-language model (VLM) further enhances this process by converting visual outputs into descriptive text, integrating these capabilities with large language model (LLM) and carefully crafted prompts, AI can generate adaptive visual content tailored to children’s preferences, all while maintaining alignment with educator-defined scaffolds to ensure meaningful engagement. In Together Tales, generative AI is implemented using ComfyUI combined with Stable Diffusion and ChatGPT APIs (Fig. 2). Summary This paper presents an innovative design process through Together Tales—a storybook game designed to foster collaboration between autistic and non-autistic children. The process unfolds across three levels of collaboration. First, among children, collaborative making fosters neurodiverse peer-to-peer interactions, cultivating authentic and inclusive social connections. Second, between children and educators, the approach ensures that pedagogical goals are met while providing children with the freedom to create and collaborate independently, striking a thoughtful balance between guidance and autonomy. Third, between children and generative AI technologies, the integration of GenAI showcases AI’s potential to enhance their creative agency and further enables them to co- create unique experiences and products for themselves with adults and their peers. Discussion This participatory design model holds great potential for broader application—not only for autistic children but also for those with ADHD, dyslexia, and other neurodiverse profiles, in collaboration with neurotypical peers. The educational principles underpinning this design, such as collaborative play and scaffolding, are rooted in general education practices, suggesting their adaptability across various neurotypes and learning contexts. While this approach emphasizes children’s contributions to one aspect of game design, future work will explore AI integration across the full design process, building toward a more comprehensive child-centered framework. Upcoming iterations will also include structured observations and post-play interviews to assess its effectiveness. References Aherne, D. (2023). The pocket guide to neurodiversity. Frontiers in Communication, 9. https://doi.org/10.3389/fcomm.2024.1440384 Using Markov Chain Analysis to Study the Relations Between Emotions, Cognitive Actions, and Performance in Collaborative Learning Ashwin T S, Vanderbilt University, ashwindixit9@gmail.com Caitlin Snyder, University of Detroit Mercy, snydercr@udmercy.edu Srigowri Mayasandra Prasanna, Vanderbilt University, srigowri.mayasandra.prasanna@vanderbilt.edu Naveeduddin Mohammed, Vanderbilt University, naveeduddin.mohammed@vanderbilt.edu Gautam Biswas, Vanderbilt University, gautam.biswas@vanderbilt.edu Abstract: Collaborative problem-solving (CPS) in STEM+C education involves cognitive coordination and emotional regulation during joint tasks. Prior research has examined discrete affective states in learning environments but less is known about how these emotions evolve over time and affect CPS behavior. This study investigates the temporal dynamics of five emotions—engagement, confusion, boredom, delight, and frustration—using Markov Chain analysis of data from high school pairs building computational models in the C2STEM environment. Emotional transitions aligned with cognitive processes, seen in interaction patterns like PLAY, ADJUST, and BUILD, to analyze affect during modeling. Results show that emotional trajectories closely relate to cognitive actions, including construction, simulation testing, and debugging. Transitions that maintained engagement linked to productive collaboration and stronger performance, while ongoing frustration and boredom indicated disengagement progress.

papers.authors: Université de Lille, to foster Group flow.
papers.abstract: This research project aims to refine the understanding of Group flow within the context of collaborative problem solving (CPS). One systematic review and four experimental studies were carried out. Video, audio, physiological and subjective data were collected from 55 participants during CPS simulation. Data triangulation has shown its added value in corroborating the subjective perception of Group flow using multimodal data that capture collaborative dynamics. The results could serve data-driven co-design strategies, to foster Group flow.
