papers.title: A Socio-Cultural Approach to Personalization in Education: Case Studies in Empowering Learners as Knowers with AI
papers.authors: Fanjie Li, Hannah Ziegler, Abbey Gonzales, Emily Phillips Galloway, Alyssa Friend Wise
papers.abstract: In this conceptual design paper, we outline a novel socio -cultural approach to personalization that values diverse ways of knowing, learner agency, and co- construction of learning outcomes as an alternative to system -driven adaptation. We present two illustrative cases of AI agents developed to probe the viability of this approach. The TRANSLATE Buddy facilitates collaborative translation activities in multilingual classrooms aimed at empowering students as linguistic knowers and fostering metalinguistic engagement. The Scholar’s Table fosters a dialogue between post -secondary students and academic voices to promote active meaning-making of disciplinary texts. Both agents showed notable strength in supporting emergent learning directions, but variability in honoring multiplicity / relationality of meaning and positioning student-as-knower. Implications and future work are discussed. (Re)Positioning personalization in education Efforts to personalize learning for individual students have a long history of development in education, with evidence of improvements in students’ learning outcomes over a one-size-fits-all model dating back over a century (Thorndike, 1911). Earlier approaches focused on teachers’ tailoring of content, pace, and feedback for learners , while recent work has focused on technology -driven approaches for personalizing learning at scale (Walkington & Bernacki, 2020). Technology-driven personalization is either taken to subsume adaptivity (adjusting instruction to changes in students’ knowledge over time) or complement it through responsiveness to each student’s interests, affect, motivation, needs and goals (Shemshack & Spector, 2020). Rega rdless, such conceptualizations center both knowledge about the student and decision-making as to how learning should proceed in the technology. Thus, while traditional personalization  approaches embody some aspects of learner- centered pedagogy, such as responsiveness to students’ “knowledge, skills, attitudes, and beliefs ” (Bransford et al., 2000, p 133), adaptation schemes based on a uniform conceptualization of mastery can limit learner agency (McCombs & Whisler, 1997), overlook the fluid ways students think and engage the world (Li & Wise, 2025) and limit opportunities for critical, self-directed learning which help diverse students thrive (Watters, 2021). In this conceptual design paper, we address these shortcomings by proposing a socio- cultural approach to personalization that aims to embrace learners’ diverse ways of knowing and empower their agentic meaning- making. We present two case studies to probe the approach’s viability, while also introducing an alternative epistemological framework for learner-AI interaction that moves beyond the AI-as-expert paradigm. A socio-cultural approach to personalization and epistemological shifts From a socio-cultural perspective, knowledge is considered not to be fixed or universal, but co -constructed and context-dependent (Vygotsky, 1978; Rogoff, 2003) . This view casts the learner not as a passive recipient but as an active knower, engaged in self-directed, culturally mediated meaning-making that is deeply informed by their unique experiences and identity, and rich with emergent and multiple meanings (Cole, 1996; Nasir & Hand, 2006). Traditionally, personalization has been linked to an individualistic orientation (Watters, 2021), which may appear misaligned with this culturally embedded, sociohistorical stance on learning and knowing. However, recent advances in generative AI, when mobilized carefully, offer promising opportunities to bridge this divide.  AI- driven conversational agents powered by large language models have the potential to engage learners in dialogic sensemaking that surfaces student interpretations based on their existing knowledge, actively responds to student reasoning, and bring s varied perspectives to the conversation (Mollick & Mollick, 2023) . While traditional personalization supported these activities to some extent,  recognizing and building on the multiple, relational ways that students engage in meaning making is difficult within a scripted, system-driven paradigm. Generative AI dramatically lowers the barriers to engag ing with the varied and potentially unexpected, pathways of  learner sensemaking, thus enabling both emergent directions of learning process and co-construction of outcomes. Such use of Generative AI is distinct from the common AI-as-expert paradigm on multiple epistemological dimensions. Multiplicity of Meaning: Rec ognizing that knowledge is not singular or static (Greeno, Collins & Resnick, 1996), a socio- cultural approach to personalization values the diverse interpretations and understandings of 1704 phenomena that can exist. Thus, rather than helping a learner to arrive at a single, predefined understanding, this stance emphasizes navigating and embracing multiple, often culturally grounded, meanings (Warren et al., 2020). Relationality of Meaning:  From a socio -cultural perspective, knowledge is inherently relational, with meaning influenced by a learner's identity, history, and context (Gutiérrez & Rogoff, 2003). Personalization thus aims to support learners in constructing knowledge in ways that are deeply connected to their own experiences and cultural background, recognizing the importance of learners' relationship to what is learned as a core source of meaning (González et al., 2005). Student as Knower: Following from the points above, learners are seen as active agents in the construction of knowledge whose perspectives are integral to the learning process (Wetsch et al., 2009). Personalization is thus not something done for or to them, but a process that recognizes their authority and expertise within their learning journey (Miller et al., 2018). Emergent Destination of Learning:  A socio-cultural approach to personalization intentionally allows the goals and direction of learning to evolve based on the learner's engagement and discoveries (Nasir & Hand, 2006). This aligns with the core of culturally sustaining pedagogy, which emphasizes honoring students' unique cultural resources and insights, viewing their evolving contributions as essential to shaping a responsive and meaningful learning journey (Paris & Alim, 2014). In the remainder of this paper, we present two design cases of AI agents developed using this framing in order to probe the viability of the approach. The first addresses the learning of English by emergent bilingual middle schoolers while the second focuses on supporting post -secondary students in engaging with disciplinary texts. Each offers a compelling alternative to relevant AI -as-expert tools in the domain: for case 1, language learning AI-tutors such as found in Duolingo, and for case 2, paper summarization tools such as NotebookLM. Case 1: The TRANSLATE Buddy TRANSLATE is a curriculum designed for teaching middle-grade English reading comprehension in multilingual classrooms, using translingual pedagogies that strategically use multilingual students’ full linguistic repertoire — including knowledge of languages other than English—and metalinguistic knowledge (García & Wei, 2014) as resources for text understanding (Jiménez et al. 2015). Grounded in socio- cultural and dynamic bilingual lenses (García & Wei , 2014) , the TRANSLATE curriculum empowers educators to tap into students’ diverse linguistic resources, even when they do not share all their students' languages. One key activity in the curriculum is collaborative translation. In this activity, students work in pairs or groups to translate parts of culturally relevant English texts (e.g., young adult novels featuring immigrant stories) into their shared home language. Teachers scaffold students' metalinguistic noticing and thinking about language features as tools for constructing meaning, by asking language -general inquir y questions. Collaborative translation activities in TRANSLATE classrooms position students as experts in their own languages and cultures as well as provide structured opportunities to build shared understanding of text using their home language (White et al., 2024). These valuable learning experiences are unavailable to students who are the sole speakers of their home language, a common reality in today’s diverse classrooms, motivating the development of TRANSLATE  Buddy. Table 1 Excerpt from System Instruction Prompts for Each Design Case Quality   TRANSLATE Buddy   The Scholar’s Table Multiplicity of Meaning Remain uninterested in whether a translation is "correct" or "better"... Treat your views on the text as one of many viewpoints rather than a definitive source of truth... Relationality of Meaning Focus on cultural context relevant to the translation. Invite students to connect... Show that texts have socio -historical context, and people can establish their unique take on them... Student as Knower Inquire: "What do you notice as similar and different about our translations?" Recognize students as competent contributors to the discourse who bring their own valued perspectives... Emergent Destination Build on student's ideas, ask questions, follow their intellectual curiosity... Encourage students to establish their take on the paper and relate it to their own pursuits... We built the Buddy AI agent by providing ChatGPT 4o with custom system instructions and a curated knowledge base of translingual  theory texts . Applying persona prompting techniques (White et al., 2023), Buddy was instructed to act as an inquisitive and supportive peer translation partner, following a key set of conversation moves. These moves target the previously discussed pedagogical goals of collaborative translation a nd enact the four epistemological stances described above as follows: Engaging with the  multiplicity of meaning possible in language use, Buddy is told to prioritize  collaborative exploration of  the spirit of the focal text over word- for- word translation. As such, Buddy is explicitly instructed to produce multiple translations and to refrain from seeking a single “best” translation (see Table 1). Instead, it is prompted to focus on how and why translations may differ and use this as a gateway for exploring the multiple ways that language conveys meaning. The relationality of meaning underlying text comprehension approaches rejects the claim that the textual meaning depends  solely 1705 on its lexical elements (Kintsch, 1988). Rather, Buddy was prompted to pose probing questions that  invite students to draw on their lived experiences and culturally-rooted knowledge to make local meaning of the anchor texts selected for translation. Importantly, as students collaborate with Buddy to co-construct possible translations, a key interaction goal of Buddy is to constantly position students as knowers , uplifting students’ cross-linguistic noticing, linguistic expertise, and intellectual curiosity  as the primary factors that drive the emergent destination of the collaborative translation. To achieve this goal, Buddy was instructed to (i) always ask  students to share their translation before offering its own; (ii) use open-ended questions to invite students’ metalinguistic noticing; (iii) actively build on students’ noticing of word choice, syntactic construction, and discursive meaning when they compare and negotiate possible translations; and  (iv) employ inquisitive clarification prompts as invitations for students to articulate their linguistic understanding and reasons for their translation decisions. Internal testing of Buddy by multiple members of the research team, using diverse anchor texts and home languages including Spanish, Mandarin, Korean, and Turkish, reveal ed strengths and limitations of the current prototype across the four epistemological dimensions. Overall, Buddy appeared to honor multiplicity by framing its own translation as an  “alternative version for comparison”  and encouraging students to consider “ the nuance/feeling you want to convey ” (Figure 1a). This afforded emergent meaning-making opportunities during which the student and Buddy negotiated and built on each other’s ideas. For example, we regularly observed Buddy inquiring about users’ noticings or opinions in the translation process (Figure 1a ) as well as instances of co-construction where Buddy actively engaged with and expanded on users’  perspectives: “Your choice  of 没有机会 really emphasizes that external factor—how others didn’t give her the opportunity to explain.” However, the challenge of moving beyond an entrenched notion of a single “best” answer remains: Buddy often used absolute language to affirm users’  choices (e.g., “ That makes 学过 the perfect choice!” ) implying a translation hierarchy antithetical to TRANSLATE  curriculum's core values. In addition, we saw  room for improvement in positioning students as knowers as Buddy sometimes preemptively highlighted differences  in tran slations, limiting opportunities for students to make and share their own observations , a key aspect of TRANSLATE curriculum’s aim to foster their ownership and engagement in metalinguistic meaning- making. Moreover, users asking for the meaning of English words to aid translation tended to shift  Buddy into more of a tutoring role, overshadowing their home language expertise and their opportunities to engage in language construction. Finally, although Buddy responded usefully to cultural elements that highly engaged users brought to the conversation, it did not provide many invitations to make such relational text-to-self connections. Figure 1 Excerpts from (a) TRANSLATE Buddy and (b) The Scholar’s Table Chats (a) (b) Case 2: The Scholar’s Table (TST) While students often engage with academic texts as decontextualized from history and meaning (Lillis  et al., 2016), a  sociocultural perspective establishes academic reading and writing as an inherently social practice situated in sociopolitical contexts (Afdal et al., 2022 ). For instance, Lillis et al.  (2016) contend that disciplinary discourses are historically saturated and contested. The recent development of  AI-assisted writing has presented new inquiries and implications regarding students’ academic literacy and compositional skills (Nguyen et al., 2024). In the context of academic reading, students seldom utilize AI beyond summarizing papers (Liu et al., 2024), but a socio-cultural approach necessitates a fuller engagement with literature that includes active meaning- making (Gavelek & Bresnahan, 2014). In fact, college faculty often expect students to grasp complex texts, relate prior knowledge, and make connections across topics (Clark et al. , 2002). The critical need for reading support for such meaning-making at the postsecondary level motivates our development of The Scholar’s Table (TST). We built the TST AI agent by providing ChatGPT 4o with custom system instructions to facilitate a “dinner party” between a learner and two simulated scholars (designated as such, see Figure 1b) who discuss the reading in light of their own research and perspectives. TS T’s design  reflects a socio -cultural approach to engagement with disciplinary texts and the four epistemological stances in multiple ways. First, we designed TST to reflect multiplicity of meaning by providing instructions to select scholars who can offer different ways to position the text within broader cultural and academic contexts (particularly considering perspectives underrepresented in fields the paper originates from / has had impact on), making visible the heteroglossic nature 1706 of texts (Table 1). Additionally, engaging with relationality of meaning , TST was instructed to support learners in crafting their own take to engage with the paper in relation to their personal or  academic pursuits. Positioning students as knowers (and the scholars as powerful allies / resources for the students’ meaningful engagement with the text), TST was prompted to strategically end turns of talk with invitations for learners to elaborate, expand or contest the ideas shared. Lastly, instead of adhering to a set of predefined learning goals for a paper, TST wa s prompted to invite students to drive their learning trajectory through dynamic co-construction and direction of the conversation ( emergent destinations of learning). For instance, interaction is scripted to begin with scholars’ inquiries about how the ideas presented in the paper might connect to the student’s own interests and background. Internal testing of TST by multiple members of the research team to engage in article -based dialogue produced mixed success with respect to multiplicity  of meaning. Although the tool was designed to present two different scholarly views, the agent  brought in quite similar perspectives on most occasions. At times it also engaged in evaluative language such as “You’re getting to the heart of it!” implying a universal and single correct answer that the user was striving to discover. A key concern in creating simulated scholars was the possibility that TST might over -essentialize, stereotype, or misrepresent scholars' perspectives; while this requires careful ongoing evaluation, our team’s initial uses did not find any notable examples of this nor that of AI hallucinations. One concern noted however was that conversations often drifted away from specific engagement with the academic text at hand into more general discussion of the ideas within it. TST’s behavior with respect to relationality of meaning were more promising: TST consistently asked students about the application of the content to their own scholarship (e.g., “what might that look like in your field? ”) and presented each scholar’s views as a way rather than the way to look at a text. In early stages of TST development, we found a tendency of the scholars to pontificate and dominate conversations . With our goal to foster a dialogic experience, we refined the prompt to create more space for the student  through balanced turn- taking and succinct responses. The final agent did better both  in making space for student talk and positioning the student as knower but also guided the conversation strongly, inviting this knowledge in quite specific directions: “I’d love to hear more about how you think assessment systems could truly support diverse learning identities. What would a system that respects these identities look like to you?”  Still, some emergent destinations of learning were supported by the use of open- ended questions such as: “What’s your take?” While such questions by scholars were not intended to be coercive, we recognize that a learner’s identity (particularly pertaining to experience and  expertise) might shape how they either comply with or challenge TST’s probing, warranting further testing and design iterations. Overall discussion and conclusions The primary aim of this conceptual design paper was to outline a novel socio-cultural approach to personalization, offering an alternative to system -driven adaptation and the AI-as-expert paradigm. We sought to create two AI agents that would honor diverse, relational ways of knowing, recognize students as knowers and co-construct the direction of learning with students. Our development and initial use of the TRANSLATE Buddy and The Scholar’s Table reveal both the challenges of the non-deterministic nature of system prompting  and the “jagged frontier” of generative AI capabilities  (Dell'Acqua et al., 2023) where certain goals are simple to achieve while others much more challenging. Both agents showed notable strengths in supporting emergent learning directions, something that has traditionally been quite  difficult for learning technologies (Watters, 2021 ). However , they differed in the extent to which they supported multiplicity and relationality of meaning: Buddy excelled at holding multiple translations in play but rarely invited students to make text-to-self connections; TST consistently asked students how textual ideas connected to their interests but often introduced simulated scholars with very similar views. Both agents demonstrated elements of valuing students’ knowledge but also a tendency to act as  an authoritative knowledge provider . Some aspects of these limitations  can be addressed through additional prompting in the next design iteration, but others may be tied to the specific pedagogical framing of each case. In addition, it will be important to examine how the ways users engage with the agents affect conversation trajectories. Informally, we noticed users  who positioned themselves as knowledge holders and the AI a gent as a tool were more apt to receive responses recognizing them as an agentic knower, while when users engaged less confidently, the agents reverted to an AI-as-expert telling mode. This raises important concerns from an equity perspective as those who most need support to see themselves as knowers are least likely to receive it. We will explore this and other agent interaction dynamics in our next phase of work running  user studies that look  at patterns of use by students with varying profiles and backgrounds . In conclusion, this conceptual design paper presents a n initial framing of the design space for  a socio-cultural approach  to personalization  and demonstrat ion of  its viability. This approach offers an alternative to the educational paradigm of AI -as-expert and offers a broader framing of personalization than traditional approaches—not simply as an adjustment of pace or content but as a transformative practice that honors learners’ cultural context, agency, and evolving understanding. 1707 References Afdal, H. papers.title: Human-Centered Perspectives on Computational Thinking and Problem Solving in the Age of AI: How to Investigate the Changing Educational Landscapes?
papers.authors: Kateryna Zabolotna, Megumi Iwata (Co-chair, Presenter 3), Cristiana Mergianian (Co-chair, Surya Pasupuleti, Burcu Şener, Thomas B. Frøsig, Université Côte d’Azur, Margarida Romero
papers.abstract: As emerging digital technologies and AI reshape education, Computational Thinking (CT) skills such as abstraction, problem decomposition, and algorithm design are crucial for learners to navigate this landscape. This symposium brings together a set of diverse studies that highlight the relevance of CT  and problem -solving skills in the age of AI. The studies demonstrate how CT can be comprehensively addressed in learning sciences research at different educational levels from primary school to teacher education, in different learning designs spanning from individual programming tasks to collaborative activities, and through multimodal multichannel data. The discussion will focus on the relevance of CT as a core concept supporting learning with and about AI while preserving critical pedagogical values such as agency, creativity, and critical thinking with human-centered approaches. Overview of the symposium In today’s  educational landscapes driven by artificial intelligence (AI), our theoretical and empirical understanding of such transversal skills and competences as computational thinking (CT) and problem solving that are foundational for learners undergo significant transformation. CT is increasingly recognized as a specific form of problem solving that involves processes such as abstraction, decomposition, and algorithmic thinking. As digital technologies and AI tools reshape how we learn, teach, and design learning environments, there is a growing need to explore how these skills evolve in these contexts. Our symposium offers a timely and comprehensive exploration of CT and problem-solving skills in the age of AI, with a dual focus: (1) showcasing diverse theoretical and methodological approaches to investigating these skills in various educational settings, and (2) interrogating the role of these skills in AI -supported learning and teaching across different educational levels. CT refers to a competence that allows us  to solve complex problems  with a creative problem -solving approach relying on computational concepts and cognitive processes such as abstraction, problem decomposition, algorithm design, and debugging (Romero et al., 2017) . Rather than simply coding line by line , i t involves developing an approach to solve complex problems  by engaging in a reflective and creative analysis of the situation, its representation at the abstract and concrete levels, and the operationalization of a solution  that is produced with the help of metacognitive strategies  associated with CT , which can be applicable to different contexts and situations, not only in computer programming (Romero et al., 2024). While early research on CT predominantly emphasized individual learning outcomes —such as individual task behavior in programming environments (Guenaga et al., 2021) —and was often grounded in cognitivist perspectives (Agbo et al., 2021), recent studies have expanded this scope. Emerging work increasingly explores CT as a socially situated and collaborative process (e.g., Lai & Wong, 2022; Lee et al., 2019) , drawing on constructivist and/or experiential learning theories (Agbo et al., 2021). Consequently, there is an increasing interest in studying various aspects of human behavior involved in learning CT, such as participation, social interaction, and interest (Kafai et al., 2020)  as well as collaboration and regulation of learning processes (Emara et al., 2021). Despite this shift, there remains a need for more integrative studies that examine CT development in situ, capturing the interplay of individual, social, and technological dimensions. Addressing this, our symposium brings together studies that investigate CT across a range of educational contexts —from elementary classrooms to teacher education—and at different levels of analysis, i.e., from individual performance to group collaboration. By employing diverse methods, including multimodal multichannel data (e.g., log files, video, screen and audio recording), these studies contribute novel insights into the dynamic, contextual nature of CT. Collectively, they 2469 advance a more holistic understanding of CT as it unfolds in authentic, technology-rich learning environments— an essential step toward theorizing CT in the age of AI. Building on this broader view of CT as a dynamic, socially embedded, and context-sensitive competence, recent research has increasingly examined the evolving relationship between CT and AI. Studies have  not only suggested that CT and problem -solving skills positively impact AI literacy (Celik, 2023) , but also that the relationship is reciprocal—AI can in turn support the development and application of CT skills (Guggemos, 2024). However, as AI technologies become more deeply embedded in educational practices, they are reshaping core problem-solving CT processes such as  debugging (Sun et al., 2024a ). This transformation calls for deeper theoretical and empirical inquiry into how AI-driven learning environments differ from traditional approaches to CT instruction—not merely as tools but rather as co- agents in learning. Against this backdrop, our symposium’s second aim is to explore this evolving theme and its pedagogical implications. In particular, we emphasize the central role of teachers not only in integrating AI meaningfully into their classrooms (Celik, 2023; Luckin et al., 2016), but also in fostering learners’ critical engagement with computational systems. The presented studies shed light on how educators can leverage CT as a framework to both teach about AI  and teach with AI— highlighting human-centered pedagogical approaches that empower learners to navigate, critique, and co -create within increasingly algorithmic educational landscapes (Romero et al., 2024). To operationalize our two central aims , (1) understanding CT development across contexts  and (2) exploring its evolving conceptualization in AI-supported environments, we present five diverse yet conceptually connected studies. Together, they offer a rich set of methodological approaches and theoretical insights. The symposium opens with a scoping review (Poster 1; Mergianian et al., 2025) that synthesized how log data can be utilized to assess CT skills at the individual level. This work not only identifie s trends and gaps in existing research, but also builds the foundation for understanding process-based assessments of CT. From there, we shift toward collaborative learning contexts that utilize multimodal data. Poster 2 (Pasupuleti et al., 2025) explores how CT concepts can be introduced through embodied play in primary education, drawing on theories of enactive cognition to show how physical interaction and co- creation support the emergence of computational understanding in young learners. T he study compa res pre - and post -test for concept retention and epistemic emotions in two conditions, utilizing generative AI to support data collection with young learners. Poster 3 (Iwata et al., 2025)  brings together log and video data to examine how CT skills emerge within problem-solving interaction in an AI-powered robotics task in secondary education. This is done by applying a CT problem-solving model (Barendsen & Bruggink, 2019) to robotics and analyzing the interaction through a hybrid framework that integrates creative computational problem solving (Chevalier et al., 2020) with established CT dimensions (Selby & Woollard, 2013) . papers.title: Instructional Principles for Inclusive AI in K-12 Education
papers.authors: Hyojung Kim, Wei Yan
papers.abstract: As AI becomes prevalent in education, it offers transformative opportunities but also risks widening inequalities, particularly for underserved students. This study explores instructional strategies and design considerations for fostering inclusive participation in AI and technology through a scoping review. After applying screening criteria, 17 articles were analyzed, revealing five main themes and 14 pedagogical principles. These findings provide valuable insights for educators and researchers i n developing inclusive and equitable AI curricula.

papers.title: Improving Pre-K–12 Students’ Executive Functions Using Digital Games: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Deniz Ercan, Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Seyedahmad Rahimi
papers.abstract: Executive functions (EFs) are critical cognitive skills that influence learning, decision-making, and problem-solving. This systematic review examines the impact of digital games on improving EF skills in Pre-K–12 settings by following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Contributions from diverse fields, including psychology, education, and technology, reflect the interdisciplinary interest in this area. Based on the analysis of game design integrations, this systematic review organizes game design elements into two categories: high-impact, where games are purposefully designed to improve EF skills, and low-impact, where games are not intentionally designed to target EFs. The findings reveal trends in game design elements, such as adaptive challenges and feedback systems, that contribute to EFs improvements. This study highlights digital games as promising tools for enhancing EFs. Findings underscore the need for more rigorous designs and future research on higher-order EFs.

papers.title: The Future Landscape of Education: Constructing an Analytical and Application Framework for Generative Artificial Intelligence in Higher
papers.authors: Zihan Xiao, Chengliang Wang, Yutong Lai, Haoming Wang, Xiaoqing Gu
papers.abstract: The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has infused new vitality into education, making the regulation of its application in higher education a current research focus. This study conducts a systematic literature review to comprehensively assess the application landscape and challenges of GenAI in higher education, constructing an action framework encompassing four key elements: Formulate policy and regulation, Enhance  academic integrity and assessment, Advance preparation and t raining, and Develop teaching and learning strategies. The framework aims to provide structured pathways for universities to ensure the ethical and compliant application of GenAI, uphold academic standards, foster skill development, and promote instructional innovation. Specifically, by delineating action pathways according to educational entities (governmental bodies, educational institutions, educators and students), this study provides clear execution directions for each role, facilitating collaborative efforts. The framework serves as a bridge between policy and practice, offering guidance for integrating GenAI into higher education systems effectively.

papers.title: From Questions to Impact: Unveiling Teachers' Power to Support Actionable Learning Analytics Design
papers.authors: Nan Wang, Nancy Law
papers.abstract: With the widespread adoption of e-learning and advances in educational data mining and AI, research publications in learning analytics (LA) have surged in recent years. However, LA has not significantly impacted learning and teaching in authentic educational contexts. As teachers’ uptake of LA depends on whether their pedagogical concerns are addressed, it is important to understand teachers’ LA needs in relation to their learning design contexts. We report on an investigation of the nature of teachers’ LA questions at different levels of design granularity—a learning task, a task sequence, or a course —identified through a systematic review of published empirical LA studies that engage teachers at some stage of the LA research process. The findings show that  teachers seek actionable feedback on learning processes and progress. However, available LA often focus on course -level performance or task -level engagement, yet actionable insights need to consider relationships among a sequence of tasks .

papers.abstract: Electrodermal activity (EDA) is a widely used psychophysiological measure given its sensitivity to cognitive and affective processes via sympathetic arousal. Although interest in this data modality for study ing learning processes has been boosted by the advances in biosensors, its research tradition spans over a centur y. In this work, we systematically review the empirical literature using EDA in the learning sciences from both theoretical (e.g., frameworks and constructs) and methodological (e.g., collection and analysis) perspectives.

papers.title: Digital Literacy in Physical Education: A Systematic Review of Frameworks and Development Areas
papers.authors: Sua Im, Min Kyu Kim, Jinmoo Heo
papers.abstract: This review examines digital literacy in physical education (PE), an underexplored area despite increasing technological integration. We address three key questions: (1) What theoretical frameworks are used? (2) How is digital literacy reported in PE? (3) What areas need further development? A systematic review of 12 studies shows digital literacy in PE is mainly framed through digital literacy and digital competence model s. While overall levels were moderate to high, disparities emerged by gender, grade level, and experience. Key barriers include inadequate professional development and a lack of standardized assessment tools. This review highlights the need for targeted training and objective evaluation methods to better capture digital literacy in PE.

papers.title: Cultural Context and Participation in Online Learning Communities
papers.authors: in Post-Secondary Environments
papers.abstract: Critical to success in online education is the ability for students to navigate online spaces and to participate in learning communities.  If pedagogical characteristics of online learning environments emphasize, and rely upon, interaction and collaboration (Garrison et al., 2000), it is critical to examine digital spaces and resulting online learning communities for cultural inclusivity. This systematic literature review outlines some of the arguments for using critical pedagogy to design online learning communities that are inclusive of diverse learners , creating space for mu ltiple epistemologies and cultural contexts. It will begin with a brief outline of the search strategy used to source fifteen peer-reviewed journal articles, followed by benefits and challenges for students from non-dominant cultural contexts. Context A scan of relevant literature indicates that digital technology has the potential to provide access and opportunity for learners across educational systems (Eady & Woodcock, 2010; Kral, 2010; Simon et al., 2014; Phirangee, 2016; Sisco, 2010). Yet, a gap exists between the completion rates of Indigenous and non- Indigenous learners in online environments (Sisco, 2010; TRC, 2015b). Combined with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) mandates to decrease the documented disparity in educational outcomes for Indigenous peoples in Canada (2015a, 2015b), this potential has influenced educators to transform digital spaces to meet educational goals (Kral, 2010). Despite this view of online education as democratic , digital spaces are not neutral, value free or culture free (Gunawardena, 2020) and the same tendency of users and designers to include dominant paradigms can be incongruent for learners from non-dominant cultures (Caruthers & Friend, 2014). Search criteria, inclusion and exclusion process Fifteen articles were included that contained an overlap of Indigenous or critical pedagogy with  an inquiry into how diversity can be  cultivated. The following keyword combination was used: “online learning communities.” Using “ Indigenous” “critical” “cultural ” reduced  the volume of literature . Using keywords  “ online learning communities” “inclusive” and “Indigenous” resulted in 273 articles. A search of two research databases resulted in five articles through ERIC and 76 through LearnTechLib using the search string: online learning community (indigenous OR aboriginal OR "indians of north america") "first nations" from:2000 to:2020. Removing duplicates, irrelevant articles, and including only peer -reviewed studies in journal articles resulted  in the final articles chosen because they dealt with non-dominant cultures and online learning communities. Findings Expansive growth in online enrollment and low retention rates deem it important to examine the spaces in which student interaction occurs, as one aspect integral to learning (Anderson, 2017; Garrison et al., 2000) . Across disciplines, scholars explored models of participation in online discourse and how these improve learning (Jaggars, 2014; Phillip et al., 2018). Participation in online discourse may be culturally mediated, and potentially, exclusionary to those from non- dominant cultures (Caruthers & Frie nd, 2014). For example, research indicates that Indigenous education must be culturally coherent (Sanguins, 2015; Pigeon, 2018). Phirangee (2016) states that online facilitation requires a different skill set, one that requires training and professional development, and without, instructors struggle to understand which strategies and interactions are effective for online environments. Learning spaces are virtual location s in which people enter to engage in knowledge acquisition as a central activity (Oblinger, 2006). The LMS can provide an  opportunity to develop learning communit ies using technological tools that afford communication and collaboration (Castañeda & Selwyn, 2018).  Typically, the discussion space allows for multiple threads, topics, or conversations to be created by any participant.  However, responsibility rests with those that design digital educational spaces to engage in critical and progressive design, using technology to drive critical engagement. To do this, they must be aware of their own worldviews and how those impact their design choices and commitment to instructional design paradigm s (Dreamson et al., 2017) . An assimilationist approach to teaching replicates social inequities because it does not account for ways in which students create or acquire knowledge differently based on cultural background (Gutiérrez & Rogoff, 2003). Indigenous knowledge and relational ways of learning do not align with the policies and practices encoded 2825 by our institutions (Battiste, 2000; Dreamson et al., 2017; Pidgeon et al., 2014).  The LMS, where most online learning takes place, reduces collective culture to individual differences, restricting interculturality with policies that do not respect cultural diversity (Dreamson et al., 2017). Critical approaches to online discourse (Carut hers & Friend, 2014) align with Indigenous education goals, especially if they transform spaces into equitable places of discourse. Inclusive learning environments foster a sense of belonging to and participation in a learning community (Gunawardena, 2020; Morris & Stommel, 2018; Phillip et al., 2018 Benefits Multiple benefits exist of online communication and “unprecedented possibilities and combinations for learning spaces and pedagogies” (Al-Mahmood, 2006, p. 43). Flexibility, convenience, and accessibility (Bolliger & Inan, 2012; Phirangee, 2016; Sanguins, 2015) are lauded as major benefits of online education allowing students to plan around their unique circumstances (Bolliger & Inan, 2012; Hara & Kling, 2001) with the option of asynchronous, synchronous, or a combination of both modalities. For example, it affords students in remote locations the opportunity to enroll in post -secondary without relocating , reducing financial barriers ( Simon et al., 2014). Technology can improve access to online instructors (Bali et al., 2020), to other students (Hilton, 2013) and virtual communication can provide opportunities students who require/prefer to reflect and compose text communication (Phirangee & Malec, 2017 ; Bali et al., 2020) . The ability to create a social presence and space for affective expression was shown to impact persistence and potentially lead to an improved sense of belongin g (Hannon & D’Netto, 2007). The temporal aspect of the digital space offers time to engage in reflective practice and begin to foster critical consciousness. A course that is des igned to facilitate opportunities for effective critical dialogue also provide opportunities for identity formation (Phirangee & Malec, 2017).  An unlimited number of student-driven online spaces can be created for learners to study collaboratively, problem solve, critically analyze (Eliyahu-Levi, 2020; Hilton, 2013) or simply discuss assignment guidelines (Bali et al., 2020). Online spaces can be used to share resources and engage in several online discussions simultaneously without F2F “turn-taking” (Phirangee, 2016). Challenges Despite above benefits, online learners experience physical isolation, reduced sense of community, lack of interaction between and among their classmates which can foster feelings of alienation, isolation, disconnection, and distraction (Phirangee, 2016) and that this is the main cause of attrition rates in online education (Angelino et al., 2007; Kanuka & Jugdev, 2006). Gunawardena (2020) posited that online education amplified inequities, rather than creating equitable spaces. Certain interactions can weaken the sense of community (Phirangee, 2016). Low levels or a lack of interaction , minimal support (Carr, 2000) , and reduced social cues (Gunawardena, 2014; Hughes, 2015) contribute to dissatisfaction ( Hannon & D’Netto, 2007). Dominant students have the potential to crowd out alternative voices. With efforts to engage in active forms of teaching for inclusion and critical pedagogy, diversity can be improved (Phirangee, 2016) but remains  dependent upon the instructor, their worldviews and concept of their role as an instructor. Historically, barriers and even systemic violence has been experienced by those students from non- dominant groups ( Phillip et al., 2018). Redesigning online spaces to include authentic and active learning is recommended by several  scholars (Caruthers & Friend, 2014; Gunawardena, 2020) rather than  using the LMS simply as a resource repository. A transformational pedagogical (Caruthers & Friend, 2014) approach aligns with Freire’s (1972) philosophy on critical pedagogy. Conclusion Technology mediates all experiences in online communities and cultural biases shape digital tool and environment design (McLoughlin & Oliver, 2000) . With attention, these same tools can be used to create inclusive learning experiences (Gunawardena, 2020; Rice et al., 2020). Digital environments can constrain or afford opportunities for critical interaction and collaboration between participants (Caru thers & Friend, 2014; Eliyahu- Levi, 2020), leading to a rich learning community inclusive of all cultures (Al -Mahmood, 2006; Caruthers & Friend, 2014; Gunawardena, 2020; Rice et al., 2020).  The pedagogical characteristics of online learning environments emphasize, and rely upon, interaction and collaboration (Anderson & Garrison, 1998). I nstructors and skilled students can foster  environments that normalize diverse perspectives by engaging in critical discourse, making this a pedagogical priority. 2826 References Battiste, M. A. papers.title: Cultivating Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Computer Science Education: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Azibun Nuder, Chih-Pu Dai
papers.abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) into daily life underscores the need for comprehensive AI literacy education within computer science  (CS curricula. In this systematic review , we revealed  insights into educational strategies, tools, and evaluation procedures. Our findings highlight ed the necessity for a holistic  framework that incorporates ethical issues and age- appropriate tools. This study provide d recommendations for cultivating AI literacy into CS education and emphasized the necessity for additional research.

papers.title: Critical Algorithmic Literacy for LLM-assisted Decision-making
papers.authors: Ge Wang, Roy Pea
papers.abstract: In today’s information landscape, algorithm- driven technologies mediate nearly all aspects of information and communication, profoundly shaping our decisions and societal participation. This paper explores a rapidly evolving example of algorithmic influence: the role of LLMs in human decision-making. As LLMs become increasingly central to these processes, their influence extends beyond simple assistance, potentially transforming how individuals evaluate options and act on recommendations. We examine this through the lens of critical algorithmic literacy, which encompasses the ability to interpret and critically assess algorithmic systems that influence access to information and decision -making. Based on a scoping review of 45 papers, we highlight the need for autonomy- supportive LLM-assisted decision-making approaches that empower learners to critically engage with the entire process and confidently take control of their choices as transformative agents.

papers.title: ChatGPT as a Feedback Provider in Digital Learning Games: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.authors: Mahboobeh Mehrvarz, Bruce M. McLaren, Autumn Qiu
papers.abstract: This systematic review explores how ChatGPT has been integrated into digital learning games, focusing on its role as a feedback provider. Analyzing 17 empirical studies, the review found that ChatGPT is mainly used to deliver cognitive and motivational feedback, often leading to improved engagement and learning. While students generally appreciate the immediate support, concerns remain about the accuracy and depth of its responses.

papers.title: A Systematic Literature Review of Large Language Model Applications in the
papers.authors: Yajie Song, Yimei Zhang, Doina Precup, Reihaneh Rabbany, Maria Cutumisu
papers.abstract: Algebra is often challenging to teach and learn. While large language models (LLMs) are gaining attention in education, their role in algebra remains unclear. This systematic review, guided by the PRISMA framework, analyzed 21 studies from 532 records. Findings revealed that LLMs were mostly used on secondary data, for assessment, with ChatGPT, using zero-shot prompts but struggled with complex reasoning. This review offers theoretical insights and practical guidance for effectively applying LLMs in algebra education.

papers.title: Healing Metabolic Rifts Through Bridges of Conviviality: An Exploration of Urban Gardening Practices in Indian Cities
papers.authors: Deborah Dutta
papers.abstract: Diverse, interconnected socio -ecological issues beset societies with an increasing urgency to respond in meaningful, substantive ways. However, the abstract, temporally stretched, and geographically diffused and distributed nature of the issues presents a significant cognitive challenge, thereby diluting the moral imagination necessary to nurture transformative changes directed at collective wellbeing. Using the context of urban spaces in Indian cities, this study describes the ‘metabolic rift’ created in f ood systems through opaque, efficiency -driven systems of industrial agriculture and modern supply chains while exploring alternate practices that lay the ground for civic participation. Drawing on Illich’s idea of ‘tools for conviviality’, the paper descri bes a qualitative study with urban farming practitioners to argue that food gardens can scaffold affect-based, collaborative spaces based on social, emotional, and physical feedback offered through plant-care practices. Such initiatives can provide crucial grounding to challenge dominant narratives and build a praxis of relational wellbeing based on pluralistic epistemologies. Urban food systems: Broken and unsustainable By 2050, more than 70% of the global population is expected to live in cities, with the fastest expansion and growth of metropolises projected in the Global South (UNDESA, 2018). The unprecedented rate of urbanization in the past century has significantly reoriented land use patterns, employment opportunities, supply chains and energy demands. Following the conventional linear model of resource extraction and use, most cities are seen as ‘one-way resource sinks’ wherein natural resources and energy mined from far-off areas are used to sustain urban areas (Yang & Yang, 2022). Moreover, cities continue to generate massive amounts of waste, and degraded materials, thereby causing a ‘metabolic rift’ due to the imbalance between input and output of resources (McClintock, 2010). The concentration of resources and people, also make cities particularly vulnerable to increasingly common climate risks and associated socio-ecological issues of pollution, water and food insecurity, distress-induced urban migration and so on. Food systems offer a tangible manifestation of the imbalance created due to the industrial crop production techniques and supply chains that have made possible storage, transport and consumption of food over thousands of miles. However, engaging with ecological issues requires an ‘unsettling’ of the dominant, oppressive ways of being and knowing (Bang, 2020). The ontological shift demands an urgent need to pay attention to the particular histories, contexts, and perspectives underrepresented in the education discourse to create alternate imaginaries that are not dominated by superficial technocratic visions of “fixing” a problem. This study focusses on urban food systems as a context to illustrate the ways in which the conventional arrangements create an estranged and exploitative relationship with land and labour, and draws on experiences that can help reimagine one’s relationshi p with food. More broadly, the paper explores processes that can shape agency and enable actions to broaden moral horizons of collective wellbeing. Linking the act of consuming food to the conditions under which food is grown and brought to our plates requires a systemic way of thinking about the human– nature relationship.  Recognizing, and nurturing, rich urban ecosystems amidst cities presents numerous challenges, as well as opportunities. Studies on urban food systems, however, have a regional bias of countries from the Global North, with relatively less research focused  on cities of the Global South, despite their rapid expansion (Rao et al., 2022). ‘Conviviality’ as a framework to explore urban garden interactions The philosophical use of ‘conviviality’ as a term was most famously employed by Ivan Illich (1973, p.24) to refer to ‘autonomous and creative intercourse among persons, and the intercourse of persons with their environment’, with ‘intercourse’ referring to diverse interactions and engagements. Deeply critical of the industrial technology and underlying value processes of alienation it entails, Illich described convivial tools as ideas and actions that allow “each person who uses them the greatest opportunity to enrich the environment with the fruits of his or her vision” (p.25). Given that much of modern civilization  is a product of tool -making and associated technological processes that are co -shaped by socio -economic models and cultural practices (for instance, agroecology vs industrial farming, or, small-scale renewable energy vs fossil fuels), convivial processes require a critical analysis of the technology in question. Vetter  (2018) for example, suggest a criteria for a democratically controlled convivial technique. These are five levels: a) relationship quality: What kind of interactions does the technology 1175 promot e? Does it encourage or discourage knowledge/ resource sharing? b) accessibility: Is the technology accessible to everyone? Is the knowledge used to create the technology open- access? c) Adaptability: Can the technology be adapted to local contexts or can only be used at a large, uniform scale? d) Bio -interaction: What are the potential risks of the technology, and does it promote ecosystem flourishing (or atleast not harm it). e) resource intensity: What resources are consumed by the technology, and how sustainable is the use?  Adhering to convivial principles emphasizes the connections and interdependencies sustaining life, and includes non- human agency and wellbeing as an integral part of human flourishing. As a physical practice, it refers to a deep and sensory engagement with the surrounding landscape (Hamilakis, 2017). Such interactions don’t ignore the inevitable tensions, conflicts and trade -offs involved in relational sustenance; instead, recognizing the interdependencies allow for a fuller unde rstanding of relational wellbeing. Kavedžija  (2021) argues that while traditional psychological studies of wellbeing analyze factors and outcomes from individual to community level in a series of cascading impacts, social and relational wellbeing could be better understood by moving away from the individual as a focal point. The process and presence of convivial structures might help in gaining newer insights. While many studies have studied urban gardens as ways to engage with questions of food access, security and sustainability, understanding the potential of such spaces to nurture socio- political perspectives of shared wellbeing merits further research. The participatory culture in these initiatives, especially from the view of expanding notions of sustainability, is a less understood phenomenon. Grassroots community initiatives such as farming can play a role in subverting common notions of cities as being ecologically barren, and far removed from 'Nature' (which is thought as only existing in pristine places). These initiatives help reaffirm var ious kinds of ecological relationships, which are otherwise opaque, made invisible by industrial modes of production and consumption. These are projects that can grow into larger ideas and practices, which were not originally envisaged. Such a gradual expansion creates further avenues for participation by a wider group of people (rather than a small, invested group). Understanding the 'how' and 'what' of such hands -on engagement  in and through community practices can help urban environmental educators design better collaborative learning and action initiatives. This project thus sought to explore the following lines of inquiry: 1) What forms of interactions incorporate aspects of interdependence in urban gardening practices? 2) How do such practices engender perspectives on conviviality amongst the practitioners? Research context and approach The study was motivated by the need to contribute to ongoing dialogues and policy discussions on transformative educational experiences beyond the silos of classrooms and strait -jacketed syllabus. Based on her previous experiences of volunteering at community farms and facilitating school gardens  (Dutta & Chandrasekharan, 2018), the author sought to explore urban gardening practices as sites of recreation, livelihood, well -being, pedagogy and even resistance. Thus, using the opportunity of a grant 1, the study aimed to foreground the voices of practitioners and understand the scope, motivations and challenges  in sustaining food gardens across a few Indian cities. In the spirit of co -creating knowledge through the active  participation of the people interviewed, emphasis was given to particular histories, plurality of voices and geographical contexts. The approach involved interviewing diverse practitioners 2. Dimensions such as the potential interviewees’  background, experience in growing food, positionality and geographical context  were considered . Based on mutual availability, we interviewed 15 people from seven cities through reaching out via various public WhatsApp groups consisting of farming enthusiasts. Ethical protocols of seeking consent and voluntary participation were followed as approved by the Institutional  Ethics Committe e. The transcribed interview data was thematically analysed to identify patterns, structures, and relations in the data  (Boyatzis, 1998). Rich descriptions of data were connected back to the research questions, to provide an interpretation of specific points of interest such as motivation and expanding sphere of actions. Since many themes were closely associated to certain artifacts/ practices, interpretation involved going beyond the description of an occurrence, and relating it to underlying events (Ospina & Dodge, 2005). Findings The interviews provided insights into ways in which participants  began seeing their agency in farming -related activities. A ‘personal transformation’ was generated by the perspectives embedded in the practice, and these views were affirmed through peer feedback (Hards, 2011). This led to the farming practice being understood in relation to wider environmental issues, such as food miles, seed sovereignty, water usage and increasing local biodiversity. These observations are supported by recent views of sense -making, as inherently relational, and as a core component of social cognition (Jaegher, Paolo & Gallagher, 2010). These views propose social interactions as enablers of the sense- making process, which simultaneously shape normative ideas regarding the world. In a similar vein, Ramstead, Veissière, and Kirmayer (2016) argue that social learning constitutes immersion in local 1176 conte xts through what they describe as 'regimes of attention' that direct humans to engage with the environment in specific ways. Specific themes illustrating these aspects are discussed as follows: Material scaffolding through emerging affordances Respondents described how their interactions with different materials to make compost, collect biomass, grow seasonal edible plants or engage in plant care helped them expand their notions of sustainability, labour, care and community engagement. As one participant remarked, “I use whatever waste is generated in the house and sometimes make liquid ferments to use as a spray or add to the compost. I think whatever we are regularly using should be easily and locally available. I haven’t found good quality cow dung, so I have dev eloped my own recipes for nutrient mixes. Each plant responds differently, and I am always learning that way.”(VN) Visceral experiences of activities in the garden seem to engage a wider spectrum of senses and their combinations, which allows one to attend to previously ignored features of the environment. Respondents commented on how they had begun paying more attention to the weather, even as artificially controlled environments have become the norm, as they could see it impacting plant growth and health. Such diverse and consequential acts of noticing were mediated through their connection with the plants and the immediate surroundings. Broader engagement with resources Many respondents described related practices that could be understood as a broadening of sustainability perspective owing to recognising the interrelated connections constituting ecosystem wellbeing. For instance, recycling grey water for gardening purposes, and replenishing soil fertility through various methods of composting and mulching were often mentioned. Through these actions, connections between various environmental phenomena gained significance for the practitioners. Physical, social and cultural feedback – Convivial relations Most participants described feeling motivated through tangible positive feedback, in terms of harvest or encouragement from peers. The idea of being able to grow food in limited spaces, even in small quantities, seems to have helped participants actively seek groups and practices to help them sustain the effort. Further, the possibility of forming and strengthening social bonds through shared actions acted as a motivation to participate in similar activities. For instance, a participant described how people organised themselves to collect dry biomass from various localities and kickstarted a civic movement to prevent dried leaves from going to the landfill. Another connected her food growing experiments extending into her profession as a chef, wherein she had taken to introduce people to fermented food as part of her menu, as a way to reduce wastage and incorporate microbial connections into the customers’ pa late. As evident in the narratives, the experience of togetherness attached to social interaction and affiliation not only motivates individuals to seek pleasure in social interactions, but also works to strengthen social bonds. These actions are mediated through the artefacts of practice, which act as tangible media for shared interactions. Discussion Participating in practices of growing edible plants provides volunteers with a visceral sense of ecological relationships manifested in the form of plant care, pest -predator interactions, seed saving, composting, mulching and so on. These actions create a ‘coagulative’ practice ( Dutta & Chandrasekharan, 2018) – a set of actions that generate an understanding of the interdependence of elements in the environment, such as the symbiotic relationship of microbial systems and a garden, and the need for biodivers ity for a healthy ecosystem. The term ‘coagulative’ captures the quality of the practice wherein seemingly different actions are integrated. This coagulation gradually leads to amorphous ideas becoming more substantive and actionable. For instance, the need for nutrients led to the realization of nurturing healthy soils and reimagining their connection with organic waste. Such close interactions led practitioners to deeply reflect on the methods of garbage disposal in their communities. Growing food thus cr eates various associations between elements that are systematically compartmentalized in an urban set-up, in terms of production, consumption and waste disposal. By paying close attention and unearthing such interdependencies, individuals began to participate in acts of care and are motivated to deepen their relationship with the “cared-for” environment based on the response. Building a meaningful relationship with the environment requires immersive, sensorium -based experiences, which generate the rich, mor al imagination necessary to think and act in ecologically responsible ways. Given the atrophied and opaque nature of socio- 1177 ecolo gical relationships in cities, facilitating such rich experiences and understanding the challenges in acting upon them is a promising and urgent area of research.  In this project, we explored growing edible plants as a practice that allows one to embody the reciprocal relationships embedded in the health of the land, soil and living beings dependent on it. Based on our findings we argue that urban gardening can be an important way to motivate people to re-establish connections with the ecosystem. As a tool for conviviality, urban farming at personal and community level allow for social bonding, free sharing of knowledge and resources, is less resource- intensive owing to local scales of practice, and provides a lens to develop a critical perspective towards food technologies that operate in ignorance of, or against communal wellbeing. The barriers experienced only underscore the need of such initiatives to find infrastructural and policy support. Within the larger narrative of transitioning to sustainable food systems, such grassroots practices constitute significant nudge points to alter behavior and actions at a community level. The socio -political emphasis on care and reciprocal relationships manifested in convivial practices form a generative platform of transformative change. As conventional educational pedagogies based on linear, arbitrary and reductionist models of the world fail to nurture the perspectives, skills and values required to engage with an uncertain future, the need to draw on local wisdom and imagination rooted in meaningful encounters is a vital task for educators. Instead of drawing boundaries around formal educational spaces, active efforts to include diverse learning environments, and practitioners as sources of grassroots knowledge must be undertaken. This study offers an arc of such practice networks that could in turn support educational initiatives directed towards embodied forms of collective wellbeing. papers.title: Maximizing the ISLS
papers.authors: Sarah Bichler, Katharina M. Bach
papers.abstract: This interactive and practical community -based workshop intentionally spans the before, during, and after the conference. Over multiple sessions: Kick-off & Presentation Skills, Practice & Conferencing Skills, and Reflections & Pursuing Opportunities we have three goals. 1) foster exchange between (new) members while they prepare for the annual meeting and create a network to fall back on during and following the annual meeting, 2) guidance for designing research talks and working out strategies to experience the annual meeting such that it meets personal expectations, and 3) joint reflection on the annual meeting experience and implementation intentions for pursuing opportunities. The workshop works towards making interactions around the presented research highly valuable for all ISLS attendees, offers professional development opportunities for all members and especially those who do not routinely get such support in their local contexts, and sustains the Learning Sciences society through building community and motivating continued engagement. Description of the event Aligning with the 2024 annual meeting theme of learning as a cornerstone of healing, resilience, and community, we want to support community building and productive exchange. Our goals are to 1) foster exchange between (new) members while they prepare for the annual meeting and create a network to fall back on during and following the annual meeting, 2) support members preparing their conference participation, including a) guidance for designing research posters/presentations, and b) working out strategies for members to experience the annual meeting such that it meets their expectations, and 3) joint reflection on the annual meeting experience and implementation intentions for pursuing opportunities.  To achieve these goals, this is a long -tail workshop spanning the before, during and after the 2024 annual meeting. Session 1: Kick-off & Presentation Skills: beginning of / mid-May 2024, 120 min, online Session 2: Practice & Conferencing Skills: half-day 6 h June 8th or 9th, in person (hybrid/online optional) Session 3: Reflections & Pursuing Opportunities: first week of July 2024, 60 min, online Participation Anyone who thinks this workshop benefits their ISLS 2024 annual meeting experience. However, our workshops might be most beneficial for first- time attendees, such as undergraduate and graduate students and participants new to conferencing or the ISLS. The workshop will be offered for a minimum of 6 and up to 20 participants. Requirements for participation are: applied before the deadline, commitment to iterate on presentation/poster design and talk, and active participation (sharing and giving feedback). Pa rticipants must attend ISLS 2024 (in person or remotely) and ideally have an accepted paper/poster. Theoretical background, relevance and expected outcomes A conference such as the ISLS annual meeting represents an opportunity to get to know other researchers in the field and learn about their research during presentations and informal exchanges. By sharing with others and listening, a conference can provide important new insights, skills, and inspiration essential to one’s own work (Becerra et al., 2020). At the same time, conference attendance allows one to present one’s own research and receive valuable feedback from others (McCarthy et al., 2004). To have such an enriching experience and not be overwhelmed, a certain understanding of how to navigate or participate in a conference effectively would be beneficial. This is, however, not always given, especially for early career researchers (Becerra et al., 2020). Newcomer researchers benefit more from a conference when they get guidance and strategies for navigating it. Additionally, they have an advantage if arriving well- prepared for their paper or poster presentation to communicate their work understandably and convincingly (Sousa & Clark, 2017). Even though academic presentation and communication skills are fundamental for a successful academic career (Ohnishi & Ford, 2015), researchers may have little opportunity to prepare and practice for conferen ce presentations in the everyday university setting. While research papers and 84 arti cles are available that give tips on how to work towards an academic career or navigate conferences (e.g., Chatzea et al., 2022), it is not routine practice to consult these resources before attending a conference. Therefore, we propose a community approach to preparing the ISLS annual meeting, providing collaborative activities, hands-on work on participants’ own contributions, and practice with peer and facilitator feedback and guidance. The proposed interactive and practical community -based workshop is relevant to the field and annual meeting on several dimensions: First, it supports participants in delivering high -quality presentations, talks, and focused conversations around their resea rch, ultimately making interactions around the presented research more valuable for all ISLS attendees. Second, it is a resource and offers a toolbox, especially for those researchers who do get little or no guidance in their local contexts. Third, it sustains the Learning Sciences community through onboarding members, preparing them for a meaningful experience, inviting participation and motivating continued engagement with the community. Our workshop design intentionally spans the before, during, and after the conference to build community beyond supporting presentation and conferencing skills. In this workshop, we learn together how we most effectively engage in the scientific discourse, but we also bring people together to sustain the environment in which this discourse happens. Further, this workshop elicits the various expectations and goals different people have for the conference experience, fostering respect, uptake, and integration of various ways of scientificness within the community. Outline of workshop activities Session 1: Kick-off and presentation skills • Aim: Laying the groundwork for trustful interactions during the conference & presentation skills intro • Activity 1: Icebreaker and getting to know each other (20 min) Name, pronouns, conference experience, research topic (whole group or breakout rooms, depending on N); Ice-Breaker game (e.g., find similarities with your group in break-out rooms) • Resources: Presentation skills & rhetoric (60 min) Share knowledge, tips, and practical advice on “preparing meaningful conversations about your research”. How do we “make it stick”? Strategies for ensuring the audience hears and remembers the gist of your story • Activity 2: Your research story (30 min) Participants apply strategies to their own research talks at the conference (brainstorm, formulate, reflect: your research story communicated effectively in 10 or 3 minutes) • Summary and goodbye (10 min) Takeaways + preview half-day session. Optional: individual coaching sessions before session 2. Session 2: Conferencing skills & research talk simulation • Aim: Professionalizing research talks & preparing conference interactions Participants bring their (final) posters, slides, and revised drafts of talks to the 6 h in -person session. • Activity 1: Icebreaker and getting to know each other in person (25 min) Ice-breaker game (e.g., Bingo) to create a comfortable atmosphere and community among the participants, setting individual and community goals for the workshop • Activity 2: Expectations for the annual meeting (25 min) Individual work + whole group sharing: what do you want to accomplish during the annual meeting? • Activity 3 & Resources 1: How to get the most out of the annual meeting (40 min) Using digital facilitation tools, we work out plans for achieving the goals participants have set for the annual meeting. We address challenges and fears and propose strategies. Participants make implementation intentions by listing three goals they want to achieve and how/when. Collaborative viewing of the conference program and creating personal schedules. • Q & A (10 min) Room for questions and sharing. • Break (15 min) • Activity 4 & Resources 2: Body language and rhetoric (75 min) Participants give their talk in a small group. We observe and give feedback. We learn about gestures, facial expressions, posture, and linguistic aspects (e.g., choice of words, stylistic devices) that we use unintentionally and can use intentionally to ma ke our research talks more precise and enjoyable. Lead 85 by pee rs and facilitators. Individuals set goals for improving their research talks. Second round of practice talks with feedback on the specific aspects each person focused on. • Break (30 min) • Activity 5: Simulation (120 min) We simulate the presentation at the conference. Each participant gives a full presentation for the whole group. Participants and facilitators give feedback for final improvements. Optional: record the presentation (using participants’ own phones) for their  own use or short coaching with facilitators. We might split into two larger groups, depending on the number of participants. • Summary and goodbye (20 min) • Feedback from participants, questions. Session 3: Reflections and pursuing opportunities • Aim: Reflect on the annual meeting experience and takeaways + implementation intentions for follow - ups. • Activity 1: Presentation and conferencing skill reflections (30 min) Using guiding questions, we reflect on the annual meeting (Padlet or else for anonymous sharing). This reflection will be on two levels: conference experience and participants’ presentation/poster talk. Highlight accomplishments, identify the “room to grow” • Activity 2: Pursuing opportunities (20 min) Individually, participants reflect on their personal experiences and opportunities that came up during the conference (e.g., a conversation with a fellow researcher, a presentation that sparked interest, etc.). They share with the group. Participants discuss what follow -up action they can take to pursue these opportunities. Participants make implementation intentions to pursue 1-3 opportunities (what, when, and how). • Summary and goodbye (10 min) • Feedback regarding workshop format and the content. Goodbye. Call for participation We will solicit participation via the ISLS 2024 annual meeting webpage, on the ISLS homepage, through ISLS mailing lists, the Education Committee, on social media (X, Facebook, etc.), and through mailing lists at local institutions accessible to the facilitators and their personal networks. We will use our personal and professional networks, for example, of the Munich Center of the Learning Sciences, to inform potentially interested people about the opportunity to participate in the workshop. While there are definite benefits for undergraduate or graduate students, first-time conference attendees, or new ISLS members, we invite all members who want to professionalize their presentation and conferencing skills and to build community within the ISLS to participate in this workshop. We aim for all workshop members to deliver high -quality presentations of ISLS research, design personally meaningful and rewarding conference experiences, and connect with the ISLS community. For these goals to be achie ved, participants should commit to active contributions, respectful and kind feedback practices, and openness to iteratively refine their work. Workshop facilitators Sarah Bichler received her PhD in Psychology and Learning Sciences from the LMU Munich in 2019, worked as a postdoctoral scholar at the University of California, Berkeley, and is continuing her postdoctoral research at LMU München. As a member of ISLS for more than fiv e years, she actively contributes to the Education Committee and NAPLeS. Sarah has taught academic skills courses and workshops for undergrad and graduate students, organized peer feedback and collaborative conference preparation, a student conference at t he Munich Center of the Learning Sciences, and has extensive experience in teaching, advising, and mentoring. Katharina Bach started her doctoral research on learning and instruction at the LMU Munich in 2022. Prior, she graduated from the Master’s program in Psychology and Learning Sciences at the LMU and conducted research at several universities (e.g., University of Californ ia, Berkeley, and UCLA) and institutes (e.g., German Youth Institute). Katharina teaches several classes on academic skills and educational content. Moreover, she is a trainer for effective communication and rhetoric and is mentoring several students in he r free time.
