papers.title: Visualizing Learning in a Social Data Science Educational Game World
papers.authors: Jennifer Kahn, Sarah Radke, Lisa Hardy
papers.abstract: Our poster explores visualization methods for participation in an identity- aligned, multiplayer video game world for learning data science through relationship and community building. We extend methods of representing engagement and learning in both educa tional games and in data science education contexts. Using simulated game play data and screen capture records of interviews with middle school girls playing an early version of the game, we explore representations for individual and multiplayer learning. Representing learning and engagement in a virtual game world Understanding how students learn and engage in educational virtual worlds is complex (Dawley & Dede, 2014). In this poster, we explore methods for visualizing player engagement and interactions in a virtual, social game for learning data science. Our game in development, “Isles of Ilkmaar,” (Figure 1a) is a multiplayer data -rich world designed to support inclusive, identity- aligned data science learning experiences for middle school learners. Players work to rebuild community by befriending creatures and restoring the world’s ecosystem balance. Players can generate, visualize, and explore game data (through a personal data log and at specific locations) to inform game activities, such as gathering resources, investigating mysteries, and crafting and giving potions, foods, and gifts to heal or befriend creatures. Here we consider ways to represent learning data science as participation in a community of social, distributed data practices (Rothschild et al., 2022, Wise, 2019). In our game, these practices involve data moves (Erickson et al., 2019) for exploring datasets generated through gameplay, such as merging, filtering, or making selections in table and visualization forms. We consider methods for understanding individual and multiplayer, community-driven data science learning in our game Our study contributes to methods of analyzing player learning in educational games and data science learning environments. Game learning analytics typically focus on out -of-game student performance (pre -post assessments; Pellas & Mystakidis, 2020) and meas uring successful in- game task completion (e.g., time to complete a puzzle correctly in Martínez et al., 2020). Virtual worlds like ours necessitate alternative analysis and assessment methods (Dawley & Dede, 2014). We seek to build on approaches like evide nce-centered design that systematically gather and organize data to support claims about student capabilities, particularly in game - and simulation-based evaluations (Riconscente et al. 2016). Our approach to learning through participation calls for innovative methods for representing players’ social engagement with the game world, data, and each other that move beyond pre -post assessments, self -reports, and descriptions typically used to evaluate learning in  data science education environments (e.g., Lee et al., 2021). Drawing also from studies that have creatively visualized engagement with physical learning environments (e.g., Shapiro et al., 2017), we seek to develop methods for visualizing and analyzing complex, social, and distributed data science learning in a virtual world. In exploring new ways to represent learning, we also seek to develop our own engagement framework that promotes iterative design processes and qualitative development of engagement patterns, which can be assessed using learning analytics to gauge their impact on student outcomes (Mora et al., 2017). New methods and a framework will allow us to understand participation trajectories in a data community situated in the game world and hold promise for improving learning analytics and outcomes in diverse gaming and educational contexts. Figure 1b provides an example visualization of gameplay data, showing the effects (y- axis) of giving different gift items to creatures of four different factions (x -axis). We would expect that as a player uses data to become better at gifting items to creatures, they would create and gift more items with higher item effects (like a creature’s happiness or health), which would produce more items (orange dots as cases) higher on the y-axis. Such data visualizations could also reveal player preferences in gameplay, such as preferences for certain creatures (e.g., Growth tree-like creatures) or for certain item types (e.g., a player may prefer to craft and give healthy foods or treats, which have a stronger effect on mood). We are currently exploring (a) how suc h gameplay data, if aggregated across players, might reveal trends from a community of players collaboratively learning and participating, and (b) how showing these visualizations to players (playing in after- school groups) could support their learning by prompting their reflection on gameplay strategies or participation in and contributions to a community of players. 2229 Fig ure 1 (a) “Blinded” Game World; (b) Data that Players can Generate through Play; (c) Eva’s Mapped Game Activities Using screen-capture videos of gameplay, we mapped players' transitions between activities in part of the game in which players treated sick creatures in a clinic (Figure 1c). The nodes represent key activities (scanning and sending creatures for treatment; depositing ingredients; mixing potions; treating creatures) and the arrows indicate the activity sequence (1 -17). The network map, made from 15 minutes of Eva’s play, highlights her gameplay strategy: while other players crafted many potions before using them to treat creatures, Eva alternated between making a potion and treating creatures before scanning new creatures to send for treatment. Distinct modes of engagement may support different ways of engaging with game data. Subsequent visualizations will include players’ engagement with game data, such as when players access or explore in-game data tables or visualizations. Examining individual maps over time may indicate learning through changes in data use, while maps aggregated across players may reveal coordinated approaches to gameplay between players. Our poster presents methods for visualizing learning in distributed, social, multiplayer game worlds. As we recruit cis-gender girls and gender expansive youth in playing the next game version in after-school groups in coming months, we are developing representations of not only individual learning but also multiplayer collaboration. Such methods can help us understand how youth’s participation in our virtual world game community can motivate their pursuit of equitable, identity-aligned futures in STEM and data science. papers.title: Supporting Collaborative Learning and/or Knowledge Building in Initial Teacher Education Using Video: A Systematic Review with PRISMA
papers.authors: Ricardo R. Monginho, Frank De Jong, Aeres Hogeschool Wageningen, Erick Velazquez-Godinez, Computer Research Institute of Montréal, Paulo Costa
papers.abstract: This paper reviews the use of video technologies in teacher education, focusing on how they enhance collaborative learning and knowledge building. The review follows the PRISMA methodology and analyzes 35 peer -reviewed papers published in English between 2000 and 2023. Three main video modalities of use were identified: "Video Recording," "Video-Based Content," and "Live Video Conferencing." The findings show that video technologies play a crucial role in collaborative learning and knowledge building in teacher education. This review highlights the growing importance of video technologies in shaping teacher education and emphasizes the need for further research to fully unleash their potential .

papers.title: Teacher Candidates Leveraging Children’s Picture Books to Plan Equity-Oriented Instruction
papers.authors: Julia D. Plummer, Carmen Vanderhoof
papers.abstract: This study investigates how  teacher candidates  utilize children’s science picture books to design equity and social justice -oriented lessons. Teachers drew on references to diversity, equity, and social justice represented in the books, indicating the importance of high- quality resources for beginning teachers and demonstrating the teachers’ potential for criticality. Our objective in this study was to investigate how teacher candidates  (TCs) can become critical consumers of children’s science picture books and leverage these texts to develop an equity-orientation in their lesson planning. Focusing on how TCs enact anti-deficit practices will help us trace their trajectory towards enacting social justice in the classroom. Participants critiqued children’s picture books then wrote a lesson plan that built on one of the books they critiqued . We focused this work on picture books because  of the key role they  play in elementary science instruction  (e.g., Pringle & Lamme, 2005) . Picture books have the potential to facilitate teacher s in addressing issues of race and racial justice in their classrooms (Husband, 2018).  Yet, little is known about how early career teachers begin this work. Thus, we asked, in what ways do TCs recognize equity-oriented themes in children’s picture books and highlight those themes in elementary science lesson plans? Framework for equity and social justice in science education Our work takes an anti -deficit perspective by switching the focus from what learners are missing to identifying what they bring with them. In doing so, we support new teachers in broadening their understanding of what it means to “do science” and “be a science person” (Carlone, 2004). Stereotypes concerning who can do science and what counts as science persist in K-12 education, influencing what science taught and how it is taught in schools. Thus, we frame our work with TC s to engage their thinking about e quity and social justice (E&SJ). All students have the right to access to high quality science learning opportunities , thus we work with TCs to examine equity from the perspective of meeting students’ needs and avoiding deficit perspectives through culturally sustaining pedagogies, such as funds of knowledge (NRC, 2012). We apply a social justice perspective with TCs as we take a critical lens to  the societal structures in place that control the distribution of resources and actions towards students manifesting in equitable or inequitable opportunities for science education. Thus,  we collaborate with TC to explore how achieving equity in science education will occur through transformative changes within unjust contexts and not through isolated or technical means (Morales -Doyle, 2017).  Mills & Ballantyne ’s ( 2016) systematic literature review found that teacher education programs, especially those that focus on E&SJ, can change TCs’ equity and social justice perspectives.  However, barriers to change exist , such as  when TCs understandings of social justice may conflict with teaching practices or when these E&SJ perspectives were not supported in their field placements. Our study explores these issues by considering the ways an E&SJ oriented tool could facilitate TCs’ integration of E&SJ into their pedagogy through lesson plan writing.

papers.title: Scaffolding the Peer-Feedback Process: A Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Julia Hornstein, Melanie V. Keller, Martin Greisel, Markus Dresel, Ingo Kollar
papers.abstract: Peer-feedback can be supported by formal or subject -matter-related scaffolds. However, it is unclear whether these scaffolds differ in their effects on process -related and outcome-related variables. In our meta-analysis including N=22 studies with N=2.473 learners, results show a statistically significant effect only for subject- matter-related scaffolds on process-related variables. The lack of further effects might represent a power problem, i.e., more research is necessary to judge the effectiveness of the different scaffolds on process and outcome-related variables. Aims and theoretical background Peer-feedback has been shown to be an effective approach to support student learning. Through peer -feedback, students actively participate in the learning process and thus can increase their own knowledge and skill acquisition (e.g., Double et al., 2020). Typically, peer-feedback involves four sequential processes (Kollar & Fischer, 2010): Task performance, feedback provision, feedback reception, and revision. In this paper, we focus on the phases of feedback provision and feedback reception. The current st ate of research shows that peer - feedback requires instructional support (e.g., Lui & Andrade, 2022). Based on prior research (e.g., Vogel et al., 2017), at least two types of scaffolds can be differentiated: formal scaffolds (e.g., prompts how to structure feedback provision or feedback reception) and subject -matter-related scaffolds (e.g., questions related to the specific content that is being learnt). These scaffolds come in different forms, such as preparatory activities (e.g., training prior to the actual peer-feedback exercise), rubrics (e.g., in the form of a rating scheme), sentence starters, questions, or as integrated scaffolds (as a combination of different scaffolds). Single studies show that all these scaffolds can have positive effects on different process-related (e.g., feedback quality) and outcome-related (e.g., performance) variables (Zheng et al., 2020). Yet, what is missing is a systematic comparison of the effectiveness of the different scaffolds on these different process and outcome variables. Such a comparison would hold a strong potential to inform practitioners on how to optimally support their students in the peer -feedback process. Research questions Against this background, we ask: What are the effects of (1) formal scaffolds and (2) subject -matter-related scaffolds during peer-feedback on (a) process-related variables and on (b) outcome-related variables?
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: Peer-feedback can be supported by formal or subject -matter-related scaffolds. **Finding**: In our meta-analysis including N=22 studies with N=2.473 learners, results show a statistically significant effect only for subject- matter-related scaffolds on process-related variables.

papers.title: Using Digital Games to Enhance 21st-Century Skills Development in K-12 Education: A Systematic Review
papers.authors: Salah Esmaeiligoujar, Seyedahmad Rahimi, Maryam Babaee
papers.abstract: In today’s rapidly evolving landscape, 21st -century skills such as creativity and problem-solving are indispensable. Digital games present a promising medium to cultivate these essential competencies. In this systematic review, we examine the impact of dig ital games on nurturing K -12 students’ 21st -century skills, drawing on a rigorous analysis of 81 selected studies. This paper offers a synthesis of our initial findings.

papers.title: One-on-One Coaching to Support Connection Making: Moving Professional Learning to Practice
papers.authors: Chandra Hawley Orrill, Zarina Gearty, Email 2, Rachael Eriksen Brown, Penn State Abington, Shakhnoza Kayumova, UMass Dartmouth, Ramprasad Balasubramanian
papers.abstract: In this paper, we explore how one -on-one coaching supported one teacher in implementing ideas about computational thinking in her classroom. We draw from existing literature on coaching strategies but recognize those tend to have been developed in large-group or small-group settings rather than one -on-one. Our findings consider two kinds of questions that seemed to support the teacher in engaging with discourse practices that have been shown effective for coaching (Lefstein et al, 2020). Our findings suggest that coaching made the instruction and activity from PL workshops more relevant and tangible for the teacher. Purpose While researchers have done considerable work determining the characteristics of high- quality professional learning (PL; e.g., Desimone, 2009; Loucks -Horsley et al., 2010; Penuel et al., 2007), supporting teachers in translating ideas from PL into practice often remains elusive. Thus, we have been working on the development of a Model of Coherent Learning for Teaching (Orrill & Brown, 2023) that explicitly considers how to move high quality PL into practice. In the present project, we have developed an ongoing PL program, designed with the high-quality PL characteristics in mind. A group of elementary teachers met monthly, typically face-to-face, with a goal of integrating computational thinking (CT; e.g., Wing, 2006) into their regular math and science classrooms. To help support the teachers move the instruction from the workshop to implementation in the classroom, the professional developer engaged teachers in one-on-one coaching each month. In this paper, we consider coaching as a Connecting experience that supported teachers to move from their work as learners in the PL to teachers in their classrooms. Further, this study addresses the need for more evidence about the potential elements of effective coaching models (e.g., Desimone & Pak, 2017) for shaping practice. To this end, we present the case of one participant (Lisa) and considered: How might one -on-one coaching support a teacher to  Connect her learning of computational thinking to her application of it in the classroom? What strategies are used in the one -on-one coaching seemed effective for the teacher to  Connect the PL to her classroom practice? How do these strategies help a teacher move from learning about CT to teaching CT in her classroom? Perspective and background We situate this work in the Model of Coherent Learning for Teaching (MCLT; Orrill & Brown, 2023) which organizes PL in three phases: Exploring, Connecting, and Applying. MCLT asserts the need for a stage between Exploring the content (in this case, computational thinking) and Applying it in the classroom. We have found in MCLT mathematics work that teachers struggle to integrate new-to-them ideas into their teaching. Thus, the need for Connecting activities. We see one- on-one coaching as one possible approach for supporting the work of translating the experience as a learner into the experience as a teacher. To understand the coaching moves that seemed important  for connection -making, we used the lens developed by Lefstein et al (2020). In their systematic review , they considered 64 articles researching  teacher team discourse and interactions. Their goal was  to identify norms and structures of collaborative discourse in coaching that can generate teacher learning. The authors  identified five discourse practices that had potential to generate teacher learning. These were a) revealing and probing problems of practice, b) providing evidence or reasoning, c) making connections to general principles, d) building on others’ ideas, and e) offering different perspectives. This lens allowed us insight into how one -on-one coaching might be fostering the Connections we assert to be valuable for supporting teachers.

papers.title: Mapping Interventions of Teacher Reflective Dialogue Sara van der Linden (chair and co-organizer)
papers.authors: Marta Kobiela, Edel Connolly, Adia Wallace, Renato Carvalho, James D. Slotta, Marguerite Walsh, stian D. Schunn
papers.abstract: This structured poster session brings together a community of scholars who conduct research on support for teachers' reflective dialogue and its outcomes in diverse contexts. Conjecture mapping is positioned as an approach to develop a shared language around research where teachers' reflective dialogue plays a central role with the aim to advance this diverse field. Symposium introduction Teacher reflection has been recognized as a crucial (Darling -Hammond et al., 2017) and frequent practice of expert teachers (Anderson & Taner, 2022). Research indicates that reflective dialogue with colleagues or coaches and based on representations of teachers’ own practice, such as video, holds potential for improving practice (van der Linden et al., 2022; Lefstein et al., 2020). Both practitioners and researchers understand what reflection is and how it is performed in multiple ways. While there appears to be little debate about its value, questions remain how to facilitate it and what specific outcomes can realistically be expected. For example, the role of the facilitator to support reflection is of key importance, but also challenging (Gelfuso & Dennis, 2014). Within the learning sciences, scholarly discussions about teacher reflection have often taken place in different communities, each foregrounding different aspects of the design arrangements, like collaborative discourse (Lefstein et al., 2020), video clubs (van Es & Sherin, 2010), visualization tools for video- based PD (Chen et al., 2020), video coaching (van der Linden et al., 2022).  Bringing together different approaches from diverse contexts can enrich understanding of teachers' reflective dialogue, in particular because the design of learning arrangements is shaped by the theoretical background, as well as the contextual conditions (McKenney & Reeves, 2019). Building on the work from the ISLS 2023 pre-conference workshop on this theme (van der Linden et al., 2023), this structured poster session aims to strengthen scholarly dialogue by exploring synergies and differences in related, but distinct lines of resea rch. We think this is timely and important, not only to exchange ideas, but also because it can contribute to a shared language that supports the creation of argumentative grammars for how learning ensues through teachers' reflective dialogue across the varied arrangements and contexts. This is not to say that approaches and underlying theories must be assimilated, but rather that the articulation of differences and similarities, can reveal new insights, as well as important next steps for future research. This symposium positions conjecture mapping as an approach to structure systematic inquiry and to begin to develop a shared language around research where teachers' reflective dialogue plays a central role. Conjecture mapping is the work of "specifying theoretically salient features of a learning environment design and mapping out how they are predicted to work together to produce desired outcomes" (Sandoval, 2014, p.19). Conjecture maps can be seen as logic models, illustrating how design embodiments yield enactment processes, and how these result in specific outcomes. Two kinds of conjectures are distinguished: design conjectures explain why inputs influence enactment processes, while theoretical conjectures explain why enactment processes (will) lead to the targeted outcomes. This session features four individual poster contributions which together build an initial conjecture map for teacher reflective dialogue as shown in Figure 1. The first two posters focus on articulating design conjectures between design and enactment. Kobiela, Connolly, and Wallace discuss four design principles for reflective practice, namely practice being adaptive to local contexts, attention to forms of seeing, teachers as active collaborators, and the consideration of tools and norms. Van der Linden, Chen, and McKenney show how design of technology can be leveraged in video-based reflection interventions to attend to aspects of scale (depth, spread, sustainability, and shift), as well as how these scale aspects could be captured during enactment. Two other posters focus on articulating theoretical conjectures between enactment and outcomes. Carvalho and Slotta show how reflective dialogue around the design of critical action pedagogy has been of great importance to the solidification 1934 of the PLC. Finally, Walsh and Schunn show how expansive and strategic framing during teachers' reflective dialogue supports the development of adaptive expertise. During the 60-minute structured poster session, authors will first provide a short pitch to introduce their posters, followed by a breakout session where authors will discuss their poster contributions with the audience, and the session will be concluded with a panel discussion. Figure 1 Symposium Overview (individual posters in triangles) Poster 1: Conceptualizing teacher reflection as a professional practice Marta Kobiela, Edel Connolly and Adia Wallace Building upon the work of Schön (1983), teacher reflective practice is often described as an active and intentional process that enhances professional practice and identity (e.g., Farrell, 2016; Rossi & Thorsen, 2019). This conceptual poster aims to interrogate this description by drawing upon theories from the learning sciences an d scholarship about professional practice. By bringing together our varied positionalities as researchers, teacher educators, and teachers across three different countries, we hope to offer new insights that other, more siloed perspectives fail to address.  We ask: (1) What does it mean to conceptualize teacher reflection and reflective dialogue as a professional practice? (2) What are design implications for supporting and studying teacher learning of reflection as a professional practice? Drawing upon theoretical perspectives such as the situative perspective, distributed cognition, and mediational means, we conceptualize professional practice  as situated within social, historical, and cultural contexts and guided by the interactions and norms within those contexts (Greeno, 2006; Werstch, 1998). From this perspective, reflection as a professional practice is more than just a set of processes: It entails forms of activity that are shaped by one’s social, historical, and cultural context (e.g. , standards, institutional pressures). How teachers learn to engage in reflective practice is shaped by the communities of practice that constitute their profession (Lave & Wenger, 1991). We consider reflective dialogue then to capture the interactions that teachers have as they engage in reflection. Reflective dialogue occurs not only amongst individuals, but also as individuals interact with artifacts that embody socially and culturally constructed norms and perspectives. Building from these theoretical perspectives, we propose a preliminary framework of four theoretically- grounded design principles for supporting teachers in learning to engage in reflection as a professional practice (Table 1).  First, because professional practice is socially, historically, and culturally situated, educators may consider how to adapt what counts as reflective practice and how teachers learn reflective practice to local contexts (Lefstein et al., 2020). This includes attention to the disciplinary contexts and communities within which teachers are situated. Secondly, because professional practice involves developing a professional vision (Goodwin, 1994), when supporting teachers to learn reflective practice, it may be helpful to consider  the forms of “seeing” that are part of reflecting and the socially-constructed norms that shape those forms of “seeing.” Thirdly, because learning professional practice involves apprenticeship, teachers may be empowered as active and engaged collaborators in their learning  of reflective pract ice. Finally, because interactions with tools are critical to the learning  of and engaging in professional practice, reflective practice may involve flexible consideration  of norms of interacting with tools. Table 1 Preliminary Design Principles for Supporting Teacher Learning of Reflection as Professional Practice Design Principles Design Embodiment Enactment Processes Principle 1: Adaptive to local contexts Epistemic and social norms and discourses that are inclusive. Teachers position themselves as part of the professional and disciplinary community and 1935 Consultation and focus groups with teachers & other key stakeholders. are invited to engage in reflective dialogue as part of the community. Principle 2: Explicit attention to the forms and norms of “seeing” Dynamic frameworks that allow for adaptive decompositions of reflective practice (Goodwin, 1994). Frameworks for coaches that incorporate theories of teacher learning (e.g., conceptual change work, Philip, 2011). Teachers adapt frameworks to reflective particulars of discipline and local context. Coaches attend to specific ways that teachers learn reflective practice. Principle 3: Positioning teachers as active collaborators in their learning Involving teachers as co-researchers (e.g., through Design-Based Research (Hall, 2020; McKenney & Reeves, 2013). Teachers take initiative and leadership in researching their learning of reflective practice. Teachers examine their own positionalities as a practitioner, researcher, and learner of reflective practice. Principle 4: Flexible norms of interacting with tools Norms for interacting with reflective practice tools allow flexibility to adapt to local and disciplinary contexts. Teachers question and adapt norms for tool use (e.g., journaling, using frameworks). In reflecting on the nature of reflective practice, we have come to see the above design principles as one step towards imagining reflective practice in a dynamic way, i.e. as a multi -dimensional spectrum. In this poster we will address our struggles in balancing generic design conjectures and context-specific demands. For example, common issues that manifest in different ways include: time constraints and pressures, a lack of professional support to empower teachers to develop this practice, and a lack of a commitment from policy makers to include teachers in shaping future policies. We developed this initial framework by gathering literature within the learning sciences and about professional practices and discussing key tenants from these readings and our own experiences as teachers, teacher educators, and researchers. For the ISLS p oster, we will continue to develop the framework through a more systematic review of the literature following these steps: (1) keyword search of Google Scholar for articles using terms such as “reflective practice”/  “reflection”/ “reflective dialogue” AND “teachers”/ “workplace learning”/  “teacher learning” and “professional practice” AND “learning;” (2) hand search of key journals in the learning sciences (e.g., Journal of the Learning Sciences ); (3) review of abstracts to select articles that relate to the learning of professional practice and/or reflective practice; and (4) drawing upon our theoretical perspectives, analysis of articles to identify themes related to supports for professional and reflective practice and dialogue. Poster 2: Scaling technology-rich support for teacher reflective dialogue Sara van der Linden, Gaowei Chen  and Susan McKenney Video-based interventions with a focus on teacher reflection through coaching have much potential to support teacher learning and development (Gaudin & Chaliès, 2015; van der Linden et al., 2022). While these types of interventions can be effective, they are often challenging to sustain at scale, for several reasons. First, coaching interventions are costly due to the personalized nature of the  support provided (Kraft & Blazar, 2018). Second, while researchers often act as coaches in coaching studies, the availability of high -quality coaches who can provide prolonged support based on effective programs is limited (Kraft & Blazar, 2018). Third, video data can illustrate complex classroom situations and serve as input for learning, but the analysis of videos is highly labor- intensive, which can pose challenges for coaches who are already pressed for time. This poster explores how technology can help address the aforementioned challenges at scale while also providing rich, sustained learning opportunities that are tailored to local needs (Kraft & Blazar, 2018). Scale can be conceptualized according to the depth, spread, sustainability, and shift in ownership (Coburn, 2003). Depth concerns a deep change in human activity. Sustainability concerns the extent to which participants in the project have (the intention) to use project materials or pedagogical ideas after a project ends. Spread concerns the extent to which others, outside the project context, are using project materials and pedagogical ideas. Finally, a shift in ownership can be observed from external to i nternal when local systems come into place that support the adoption of materials, adaptation of materials to local needs, as well as maintenance and dissemination. Technology has the potential to support (coaching of) video-rich reflective dialogue at scale. Technology can support the analysis of discourse and text, and natural language processing (NLP) can be used to automate discourse analysis and is often used in combination with learning analytics (McNamara et al., 2017). Dashboards display this visual information on key processes and illustrate patterns, often visualized in one screen to help users achieve their goals (Teasley, 2017), and can be focused on the learner or instructor/ coach. Visual learning 1936 analy tics (VLA) combines visual and automated analysis to provide interactive, process -oriented visualizations for coaches, tutors, and instructors, facilitating them to locate and (re)examine the relevant portions of video data and enhancing their focus and efficacy of reflective dialogue (Chen, 2020). Conversational pedagogical agents are intelligent systems that can engage in a dialogue with learners in real -time, and fulfill the roles of coaches, tutors, or instructors (Gulz et al., 2011), and support student learning through the provision of metacognitive suggestions (e.g. Hayashi, 2020) or discussion prompts (e.g. de Araujo et al., 2023). Hereafter, the possible roles of the technology in relation to scale have been conceptualized (Table 2). Table 2 Possible Roles of Technology in Relation to Scale Depth Sustainability Spread Shift NLP Automate discourse analysis and support identification of patterns Provide continued automated analysis of discourse by existing users after project end Provide automated analysis of discourse to new users Process discourse data to identify development goals Dash- boards Provide compact visual overview of patterns in line with goals to support reflection/ monitoring Provide visual overviews on important processes to help existing users to sustain new practices when needed Provide visual overviews to help new users focus on important processes Signal new learning needs to guide problematization/ provide visual information to support maintenance VLA Interactive, process- oriented visualizations and analytics for supporting human reasoning and judgment Enable existing users to track changes of their teaching and make continuous data-informed decisions Transform video data into meaningful visualizations and analytics that are readily accessible to new users Visualize the similarities and differences in one another’s teaching to support teachers’ collaborative reflection and plans for teaching improvement Conver- sational agents Provide metacognitive and discussion prompts to guide learning Provide metacognitive and discussion prompts to existing users Provide metacognitive and discussion prompts to new users Provide support for high-quality discourse to new and existing users The aim of this poster is to articulate how existing tools to support video-rich  reflection (could) attend to scale, leading to the following research questions: How could technology support (1) depth, (2) spread, (3) shift, and (4) sustainability of (vide o-based) teacher reflection? Table 2 is used as an analytical lens for retrospective analysis of existing projects and prospective analysis of related literature. The retrospective analysis leads to data- based hypotheses on how technology could support the scaling of video-based teacher reflection, based on existing tools, namely: Classroom Discourse Analyzer (Chen et al., 2020; Chen & Chan, 2022), ReflAct (van der Linden et al., 2023), and TalkMoves (Jacobs et al., 2022; Jacobs et al., 2024). These projects are first analyzed deductively, meaning that the results sections of the above -mentioned articles were  coded on the four scale aspects, and then inductively,  meaning that within these sections aspects of scale are unpacked to derive design considerations in light of these projects . The prospective analysis leads to literature -based hypotheses for how technology can support scale, where data is currently lacking.  The analysis results in a revised table focusing on scaling video- based teacher reflection supports, and articulating how scale aspects could be captured during enactment. Analyses are currently underway, and the poster will articulate affordances and limitations that were observed in our cases (e.g. design principles/ decisions for scale), which are informative for design or observations that foster reflective dialogue in relation to scale. Based on the analysis, a research agenda will be provided, which defines what each facet looks like in terms of technology for teacher reflective dialogue, and points to important aspects that are currently lacking in the literature. Poster 3: Facilitating pedagogical transformation: Teachers' reflective dialogue on adopting critical action education in the classroom Renato Carvalho and Jim Slotta This study was conducted during an international professional development (PD) workshop for teachers in the Summer of 2023 in the context of a project called the Critical Action Learning Exchange (CALE; Carvalho et al., 2022, 2023). CALE has grown as a professional learning community (PLC) that connects educators from around the world engaged in designing, enacting and sharing critical action curricula. CALE curriculum aims to empower students in response to complex socio- environmental issues, such as climate change, social justice, and pandemics, that affect themselves and their communities. CALE is grounded in the theoretical framework of Critical Pedagogy, a philosophy of praxis that underscores the importance of the educational process to intertwine 1937 theo ry, action, and reflection as a means to enable societal advancement toward social change and justice (Freire, 1970; Kincheloe, 2004). One central practice of Critical Pedagogy is the negotiation of a meaningful curriculum with students. This requires a fundamental change in the social relations of discourse in the classroom: the unidirectional relationship between the teacher who detains and imparts the knowledge and the students who receive it has to give way to a dialogical method of teaching and learning that engages both student and teacher in the production of knowledge (Shor et al., 2017). Within CALE, educators take part in professional development activities, including the collaborative design of new critical action lessons as well as reflective  dialogue about their problems of practice. Since 2020, researchers have designed activities, resources, and technology environments to support the CALE PLC, testing and improving designs through iterative cycles of implementation and redesign (Carvalho et al., 2021). This poster reports on the most recent implementation of the CALE professional development model, which occurred in the Summer of 2023. Our research objective was to understand how reflective dialogue within a PLC can facilitate the epistemic shift that Cr itical Pedagogy requires. Participants ( n=34) from 15 countries were K-12 teachers from upper elementary through university level. Workshop sessions were held on Zoom for two consecutive weeks in four three-hour sessions (12 hours in total). Each session was designed to facilitate the community's advancement in three mutually reinforcing aspects: 1) the theoretical understanding of Critical Action Learning, 2) the collective design work of Critical Action curricula, and 3) engagement in reflective dialogue and development of shared identity as a professional learning community. In each session, participants watched presentations from more experienced members of the community who reported on their successful designs and implementations of critical action lessons. They then participated in reflective dialogue on problems of practice and worked in small teams to design new lessons (n =30 lessons in total) that would engage their students in critical action on topics related to climate change, diversity and inclusion, environment, health, media and technology, economy, mental health, and the future of work. We collected data from pre- and post-surveys, video recordings of the PD sessions (including Zoom breakout rooms), discussions on the CALE online platform, and the participants' design documents. We utilized a framework for assessing teachers' readiness fo r pedagogical transformation (Jones and Swanson, 2022) to analyze the data. Participants confronted the challenges entailed by change of practice to focus on critical action education. They report a low level of support and encouragement for such a change from their educational systems (ministries, boards, etc.) Nevertheless, they report that being a member of a community of practice and participating in structured PD opportunities can effectively facilitate this paradigmatic shift. In particular, the role of reflective dialogue has been of great importance to the solidification of the PLC, and often takes form in communications between teachers and peer mentors. Our presentation will focus on this aspect of the CALE professional development model. Poster 4: Reconceptualizing framing theory and research for coach-guided teacher reflection: The role of expansive and strategic framing for developing adaptive teaching expertise Marguerite E. Walsh and Christian D. Schunn Education researchers widely agree that adaptive expertise is central to facilitating student -centered instructional reforms (Munson et al, 2021). Expert-guided reflection on teaching artifacts is often cited as critical for supporting teachers to transform entrenched practices and skillfully enact new kinds of instruction (Darling-Hammond et al., 2017). However, our understanding of the specific mechanisms that facilitate teachers to develop adaptive teaching expertise in these contexts is still underdeveloped (Carbonell et al., 2014). In this conceptual poster, we describe a novel framework that draws from existing research as well as our own empirical work to study and develop coaching routines that support robust teacher learning and change outcomes. We specifically drew from prior analyses of hundreds of pages of coach- teacher reflective dialogues across disciplines (math and literacy) , conducted as a part of larger project , to identify interactional patterns that consistently characterize the work of highly effective coaches (i.e., coaches whose teacher partners showed the highest growth in instructional quality). Together with in-depth analysis of adaptive expertise theory and research, our framework specifically proposes a revised theory of frames and framing as a central mechanism for supporting teachers’ adaptive reasoning, problem-solving, and knowledge transfer in reflection-based coaching. Rooted in socio- linguistic research, frames are interpretive schemata individuals use to represent and make sense of a situation (Goffman, 1974). In our framework, we define a teaching frame as a kind of interpretive schemata comprised of 2 elements —teaching schema  and teaching principle —that jointly activate to define a particular classroom situation or problem in situ . The teaching schema refers to a basic categorical distinction 1938 involvi ng one or more components of the “instructional triangle” (i.e., interactions among students, teacher, and task) that are emphasized (or not) within a particular instructional episode (e.g., ‘students completing work’ or ‘teacher eliciting student ideas’). The teaching principle shapes the significance of these details in relationship to an envisioned goal state, particularly with respect to epistemology (what knowledges are relevant and valued) and social positioning (how participants’ expected roles in these processes;  Greeno, 2009). Because a key goal for education reform is to promote students’ active learning (Engle & Conant, 2002), teachers will likely need help to shift towards less traditional, more student-centered ways of framing their teaching interactions. As is detailed below, we propose two dimensions of frames and framing—expansive and strategic—that we argue are especially needed to support this kind of shift. Building on prior research (Engle et al., 2012), we define expansive framing in a teacher learning context as the scope of applications enabled by the teaching frame across time and settings. More specifically, we posit that enable broader knowledge retrieval and transfer across classroom situations can be enabled by connecting to common elements and alternative representations within and across teaching frames (see Table 3) Table 3 Expansive Framing Components and Examples Component Involves emphasizing… Common elements within and across teaching frames Shared teaching schema: Ex 1. common strategies for eliciting student thinking across math and literacy Co-occurring teaching principles:  Ex 2. ‘supporting students to construct their own understandings’ as an underlying principle across lesson phases Teacher’s central role in instructional triangle Ex 3. how a teacher’s choice of phrasing was consequential for students’ subsequent thinking opportunities Alternative representations within and across teaching frames A variety of teaching schema: Ex 1. past successes using open questions to ‘build student trust’ in the context of reasoning about ways to ‘elicit student ideas’ A variety of teaching principles: Ex 2. how ‘supporting students to construct their own understandings’ could vary in the context of ‘eliciting student thinking’ vs. ‘addressing student misconceptions’ Teacher’s central role in adapting: Ex 3. a variety of potential alternative strategies for addressing a student misconception in case one doesn’t work Strategic framing refers to the ‘fitness’ of a teaching frame given a teachers’ current problem -solving situation and learning trajectory. Adaptive experts deliberate and select among a variety of frames those which best meet the demands of current situation or problem scenario given emergent, shifting, and possibly ambiguous details (Bransford et al., 2005). Applied to teacher learning, we define this aspect of adaptive expertise in terms of selecting teaching frames that enable effective noticing, reasoning, and action given: 1) the current state of instructional triangle; the targeted instructional model; and the teachers’ learning trajectory (see Table 4 ). Table 4 Strategic Framing Components and Eexamples Component Involves selecting: Current teaching situation Teaching schema needed to resolve the main underlying problem:  Ex 1. focusing on task selection when current task only supports low-level student engagement Teaching principles needed to resolve the main underlying problem: Ex 2. invoking equity-related principles when the primary issue is that students are being afforded uneven learning opportunities Current teacher learning trajectory Teaching schema needed to advance teachers’ current learning trajectory: Ex 1.focusing on assessing questions if a teacher is not yet ready for advancing questions Teaching principles needed to advance teachers’ current learning trajectory: Ex 2. invoking principles for identifying student thinking if a teacher is struggling to distinguish different kinds of learning evidence This poster contributes to theory on mechanisms of teacher learning and transfer, articulating two key framing dimensions aligned with developing adaptive expertise. Specifically, we theorize that connecting to common elements and alternative representatio ns within and across in teaching frames (expansive framing) can create the expectation that: 1) teachers’ thinking and action in any one learning situation has broader relevance and applicability; and 2) there is more than one way to represent, interpret, and act with respect to any particular problem. Moreover, by increasing alignment between selected teaching frames and a teacher’s current problem - 1939 solvi ng needs and learning trajectory (strategic framing), teachers can be supported to engage in more adaptive reasoning and problem solving in response to emergent situational details, issues, and dilemmas. Concluding, this symposium brings together emerging research on teachers’ reflective dialogue from  a variety of settings to exchange perspectives on this versatile topic, to strengthen scholarly dialogue, and to identify promising next steps for research. papers.title: Citation Analysis for “Student Engagement”
papers.authors: David W. Jackson
papers.abstract: For 40 years scholars have published systematic reviews and entire handbooks  on student engagement, though to date there has been no citation analysis of student engagement across all academic disciplines. This configurative synthesis review  separates “non -English language” from “all-language” publications, and it presents finer-grained analyses of four key Categories. Visualizations of citation “bursts” and calculations of “betweenness centrality” confirm some within - and between -Category relationships previously posited, and they also reveal as-yet-undocumented relationships for further exploration.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: For 40 years scholars have published systematic reviews and entire handbooks  on student engagement, though to date there has been no citation analysis of student engagement across all academic disciplines. **Finding**: Visualizations of citation “bursts” and calculations of “betweenness centrality” confirm some within - and between -Category relationships previously posited, and they also reveal as-yet-undocumented relationships for further exploration.

papers.title: Fostering K-12 Students’ Computational Thinking Skills Using Collaborative Technology-rich
papers.authors: Systematic Review, Maryam Babaee, Seyedahmad Rahimi, Salah Esmaeiligoujar
papers.abstract: In today’s technology-driven society, mastering Computational Thinking (CT) skills is crucial for students. To develop these skills, leveraging collaborative technology - rich environments (TREs) can be an effective approach. Examples of those TREs include block-based programming learning environments, immersive digital games, and robotic toolkits. In this systematic review, following PRISMA, we identified 56 studies from the literature. We investigated how collaboration within TREs influences the development of CT skills among K -12 students.  The findings underscore the value of collaborative learning environments within TREs for effectively fostering students’ CT skills, emphasizing the importance of creating impactful learning environments that prioritize collaboration in CT skill development.
papers.summary: **RQ/Objective**: In today’s technology-driven society, mastering Computational Thinking (CT) skills is crucial for students. **Finding**: The findings underscore the value of collaborative learning environments within TREs for effectively fostering students’ CT skills, emphasizing the importance of creating impactful learning environments that prioritize collaboration in CT skill development.

papers.title: ontrolled Trial of Scalable Game Design’s Impact in Elementary Schools
papers.authors: Jou-Yin Chen, Language Center, Mingfong Jan
papers.abstract: The concept of making thinking visible and thinking routines (TRs) have been widely adopted in teaching practice and shown to yield positive learning impact in previous research. However, a gap exists between the high- level theoretical principles and practical application . Thus, our aim is to bridge the gap between theory and practice by developing and testing the thinking routines  instructional design principles of  (TRIDPs) through three design- based research (DBR) iterations in a course on social issues from English movies at a Taiwanese university. We aligned the  3- phase DBR model and conjecture map ping for a systematic evaluation, depicting a detailed design history and trajectory of TRIDPs evolution. Our research has produced six TRIDPs. The iteration process also furthered our understanding of both learning process and outcome in a TRs -embedded classroom.  W e believe our TRIDPs and revised conjecture map offer useful model for those interested in TRs-embedded instruction. Key words: thinking routines, design principles, design-based research, conjecture mapping Is making thinking visible enough? The concept of making thinking visible and thinking routines  (TRs) have been widely adopted in teaching, demonstrating positive learning outcomes in previous research. Project Zero of  Harvard Graduate School of Education has promoted the concept of making thinking visible and proposed many TRs to be used in teaching practice to scaffold students’ thinking and enculturate thinking dispositions in the long run (Ritchhart et al., 2011). TRs, comprising simple questions or prompts, guide students to externalize their thinking, engage in thinking- rich discourse, and make thinking moves such as connecting ideas and considering multiple viewpoints . Our overarching educational goal is to incorporate teaching of thinking into curriculum with adoption of TRs. However, while making thinking visible seems to be an unquestionable guiding principle in teaching practice, its generality may hinder its testability in local contexts (Sandoval, 2004). On the other hand, p revious research on TRs mainly focused on the intervention effects of TRs as learning tasks but provided little insight into furthering the theoretical understanding of the design principles  (DPs) for incorporating TRs at a curricular level. Thus, w e found an urgent need to rethink the TRs  usage by ensuring coherence among curricular components, including course aims, learning tasks, materials, assessment, etc. We aim to propose a TR design framework and design principles to bridge the gap between the high- level theoretical principles and practical application. This study examines the development of thinking routines design principles ( TRIDPs) across three design -based research (DBR) iterations, asking: How may we develop thinking routines design principles? Alignment of DBR and conjecture mapping to capture the evolution of TRIDPs We utilized DBR to iteratively refine instructional and research design and employed conjecture mapping to trace the trajectory of TRIDP evolution. As clarified by Barab and Squire (2004), in DBR, “the design is conceived not just to meet local needs, but to advance a theoretical  agenda, to uncover, explore, and confirm theoretical relationships” (p. 5). The merit of design lies not in theory testing but in refinement or development of theory (Edelson, 2002), and in our case, the establishment and refinement of design principles. However, the refinement of design through multiple iterations may become too messy for a systematic review. Therefore, McKenn ey and Reeves (2012) proposed a 3-phase model of educational design research to visualize the design procedures, which includes three main phases: (1) analysis and exploration, ( 2) design and construction, and (3) evaluation and reflection. Then the final design product is the maturing intervention  and theoretical understanding. Edelson (2002) also suggested considering design procedure, problem analysis, and design solutions in design decision s. McKenney and Reeves’s model , along with Edelson’s view in design decisions , assists us in documenting and evaluating the design procedures. We gather  inspiration from literature review and problem analysis in Phase 1 , depict design solutions including both instructional and research design in Phase 2, and uncover key findings and emergent problems in Phase 3, all of which become sources for adaptation in the next iterative cycle. While the DBR 3-phase model serves a useful guide for iterative cycles, we still need a tool  to evaluate how our TRIDP guides intervention design, so we used conjecture mapping. Conjecture mapping was proposed by Sandoval (2004, 2014) to bridge the gap between the generality of high-level theoretical design principles and the specificity of embodied conjectures  in particular contexts . He explained that “embodied conjecture is a 107 conje cture about how theoretical propositions might be reified within designed environments to support learning” (Sandoval, 2014, p. 215). We adopted conjecture mapping  to specify how the theoretical principle of making thinking visible and the derived TRIDP s are embodied in local instructional design and evaluate whether  the embodiments lead to predicted mediating processes and achieve intended outcome. With our purpose of capturing evolution of TRIDPs in a longer trajectory through multiple iterations, we found a need to align DBR cycles and conjecture mapping. Sandoval (2014) admitted that conjecture mapping itself alone may not be a good representation of movement in a longer trajectory . Therefore, we then referred to Wozniak’s strategy of aligning 3-phase DBR and conjecture mapping (Wozniak, 2015). Wozniak explained that the development of conjecture mapping occurred in Phase 1 and 2 in a DBR cycle, and the evaluation of conjecture mapping is done in Phase 3, which then leads to revision in the next iteration. With this alignment, findings from revision of conjecture mapping and TRIDPs can inform the iterative design of DBR , and vice versa. This way, we can conduct a more systematic review of the refinement of TRIDPs. Research methodology In this section, we will present the research context, the design of conjecture maps, and DBR  iterations. Due to the iterative nature of data collection and analysis, we will discuss data collection and analysis in the findings and discussion sections. Contexts and participants We conducted this research in an English as foreign language  course on social issues from English movies at a Taiwanese university. The study involved three iterative cycles, each conducted within the same course, taught by the same instructor, and spanned over three semesters in three different classes. Iteration 1 included 12 students, Iteration 2 had 20, and Iteration 3 had 24. The course was a 3 -credit semester course, with classes meeting for three hours each week, lasting for 18 weeks. It was delivered in English, and most students were capable of effective self -expression and discussion. We introduced four English movies rich in social issues and guided students in analyzing the plot, characters, and social themes. In Taiwan's educational system, there's an emphasis on teaching thinking in the core curriculum, but integrating it with the curriculum remains a challenge. The transmission model of teaching is still prevalent, and students have limited opportunities to develop their thinking skills. Therefore, our overarching goal is to make thinking visible and create a thoughtful classroom . How TRIDPs guide instructional design and evaluation of conjecture mapping We used conjecture mapping to develop and refine our DPs (Figure 1). We first defined our high-level theoretical principle as: Making thinking visible assists articulation and appropriation of thinking and thus deepens learning. From this, three initial DPs were derived: 1) DP1: Personally relevant or controversial topics of discussion will activate engagement of thinking; 2) DP2: Collaborative work and discourse will provide venue where learners can scaffold and deepen one another’s thinking; 3) DP3: Thinking routines will guide students to externalize their thinking and take thinking moves  (TMs). DP1 highlights the importance of personally connected topics in that they can engage students’ in deeper thinking (Dinsmore & Fryer, 2023). DP2 conforms to sociocultural view  of learning and importance of social community in thinking enculturation (Resnick, 1987). DP3 stems from Project Zero’s application of TRs, which shapes the core of teaching intervention design. We selected four TMs aligning with course nature: building explanations and interpretations, making connections, considering different viewpoints, and reasoning with evidence. Then we followed these DPs to sketch our initial conjecture map. Figure 1 Initial Conjecture Map to Guide TR Instructional Design 108 Thes e DPs guided our design of the embodiments and helped  us predict and evaluate both process and product of design. As shown in Figure 1, The embodiments show  how our initial DPs are translated into instructional design in three aspects: tools and materials, tasks and participant structures, and discursive practice. Take tools and materials for example. F our social issues movies were introduced, and TR guidelines were given to assist students in using TRs. Whiteboards were used to help students externalize and visualize their thinking. DP2 and DP3 played a significant role in shaping task design and discursive practices, promoting both individual and collective thinking following TRs. In the mediating processes, students collaboratively produced movie analyses and engaged in group discussions. To test  our conjectures, we collected evidence to assess (1) design conjectures, determining if they led to student artifact creation and observable interactions, and (2) theoretical conjectures, evaluating whether intended outcomes were achieved. Both expected a nd unexpected findings informed the adaptation or creation of new design conjectures, enhancing our understanding of designed learning, which, in turn, informed revisions to the conjecture map. Data collection and analysis: Systematic review of TRIDPs evolution Alignment of the 3-phase DBR model and conjecture mapping enabled us to have a more systematic review of both design and outcome . Conjecture mapping provides a useful guide to decide what data to collect (Wozniak, 2015). Also, in DBR,  revision of data collection and adaptation of measurements are inevitable for better responsiveness to the changing dynamics of designed learning (Cobb et al., 2003). Therefore, we evaluated and adapted (1) the design conjectures ( the intervention design), (2) the theoretical conjectures (the intervention effects), and (3) data collection and analysis. For example, problems arose in Phase 3 of Iteration 1 led to problem analysis in Phase 1 of Iteration 2, followed by the revised design, including the conjecture map, DPs, task design, and revised data collection . The revised design constructed our implementation in Iteration 2. And the same evaluation process was applied in Iteration 3. Eventually, through iterati ve implementation and evaluation in various contexts, generalization of TRIDPs were produced. Finding and discussion Through our three DBR iterations (Figure 2), seven TRIDPs were produced, comprising three initial DPs derived from theory and three that emerged during iterations. Figure 2 shows the summative product of three iteration cycles and Figure 3 shows the revised conjecture map. Data analysis result of Iteration 1 has been reported in Chen and Jan (2023) and result of Iteration 2 in Chen and Jan (in press). In this paper, we will provide a summary of the previous results and focus on how TRIDPs were tested, refined, and emerged through DBR iteration cycles. Figure 2 Design-based Research Iteration Cycles Evaluation of initial DPs As shown in Figure 2, in Phase 1 and 2 of Iteration 1, we identified initial DPs and sketch a conjecture map. Our initial DPs are: 1) DP1: Personally relevant or controversial topics of discussion will activate engagement of thinking; 2) DP2: Collaborative work and discourse will provide venue where learners can scaffold and deepen one another’s thinking; 3) DP3: Thinking routines will guide students to externalize their thinking and take thinking moves. To test our DPs and conjectures, we collected students’ joint TR products  and observation logs to test the intervention design and collected individual writing to test intervention outcomes. First, we used content analysis to analyze joint TR products to evaluate to what extent students followed TRs to externalize their 109 thinki ng. For example, the TR Circle of Viewpoints was used to guide students to analyze the plot from multiple perspectives and step inside the character. The types of thinking we expected were considering different viewpoints and perspective taking. Thus, we  analyzed students’ joint products by investigating  the number of perspectives students included and how effectively they stepped inside the  perspectives. Second, we maintained a class observation log and field notes to monitor mediating processes and align with our design and initial DPs. Third, we collected students' individual writing in the middle and at the end of the semester and compared their progress in using the expected thinking moves. The analysis results  (reported in Chen & Jan, 2023) showed that the intended outcomes were achieved. Students were able to take expected thinking moves to analyze social issues by following TRs. This indicates our initial DPs led to desired mediating processes and intended outcomes. Problem analysis and revisions of initial DPs and conjecture map in Iteration 2 Achievement of expected outcome came along with unexpected problems, the analysis of which led to development of new DPs and subsequent conjecture mapping. Table 1 is the synthesis of how analysis of identified problems guided development of new DPs. Figure 3 is the revised conjecture map guided by the revised DPs. Table 1 Problem Analysis from Iteration 1 with Subsequent Rrevision and Development of DPs Figure 3 Revised Conjecture Map (Italics used to highlight changes in Iteration 2 and underlines for Iteration 3) First, a s recorded in Phase 3 of Iteration 1 (Figure 2), from our class observation, we found students were unfamiliar with some of TRs we used, which caused  more time and clarification needed and dragged down the effects we expected. We referred to the suggestion of Ritchhart et al. (2006) for repeated use of TRs and considered local students’ lack of previous experience in thinking tasks. Additionally, we needed a  more flexible modification of TRs to be incorporated with a variety of topics for discussion. Thus, we modified TRs and increased the repetition of TRs  and revised DP3 as:  Repeated and adapted use of thinking routines will provide scaffolds and structures to guide students to externalize and take  thinking moves. Second, the TMs we selected were still too generic to serve as course objectives. Conforming to the Sandoval’s suggestions for specificity in embodied conjectures (Sandoval, 2004), we needed a revised set of context-specific course objectives and rubric to communicate thinking objectives with both teachers and students. Then DP4 was developed: Translation of generic thinking moves into context -specific objectives will help communicate thinking and learning objectives Identified problems from Iteration 1 Modified and emergent DPs
